title: The Death of Twitter and the Decline of Public Debate Online
authors: Axel Bruns
venue: M/C Journal
OSINT_Source_Types: Social Media; News Media; Forums & Communities
Tags: Social Media Analysis; Public Discourse; Disinformation; Platform Changes; Freedom of Speech
abstract: Introduction Twitter launched on 21 March 2006 to a largely uncaring public. It remained mostly unknown to all but a self-selecting group of technorati for the following years, until it was plucked from obscurity by the endorsement of U.S. television host Oprah Winfrey. Then at the height of her influence, she famously posted her first, all-caps tweet “HI TWITTERS. THANK YOU FOR A WARM WELCOME. FEELING REALLY 21st CENTURY.” live from her television show on 17 April 2009, with Twitter CEO Ev Williams watching on. The effect was immediate: account sign-ups to the platform spiked, and the Twitter userbase grew rapidly from then on. Although attracting more than 320 million monthly active users during its heyday (Molina), Twitter was never a mass participation platform comparable to Facebook, Weibo, or Instagram. Instead, what distinguished it from its competition was both the particularly influential clientele of local, domestic, and international actors that it was able to attract (e.g. Ausserhofer & Maireder), and the way in which its flat and open platform affordances and network structure at least appeared to (and in some cases genuinely did) enable direct interaction between these elite accounts and the larger mass of ordinary users. While never consciously designed for this purpose (cf. Burgess & Baym), once it was fully established, Twitter provided direct access to the posts of a collection of celebrities, politicians, journalists, business leaders, experts, activists, government and non-government institutions, and corporations that was often nearly complete in many of the regions in which the platform was being used. This also led to it becoming a platform of critical importance for sharing, discussing, and otherwise engaging with news and current events. The substantial changes to Twitter as a company and platform since its takeover by Elon Musk on 27 October 2022 have meant that that platform has died, however. Even the name Twitter itself no longer exists, following its rebrand as ‘X’. This article explores how these changes have affected opportunities for constructive, prosocial online public debate, and examines the extent to which new social platforms are able to fill the space now vacated by Twitter. News, Public Debate, and Prosocial Activism on Twitter The use of Twitter for engagement with news and current events has perhaps been highlighted most prominently in early scholarly analyses of the platform: such work addressed, for example, the role of Twitter in crisis communication during natural disasters and political events (Hughes & Palen), or more generally described the platform as an ‘ambient news’ network (Hermida). Again, the flat and open structure of the platform – where the vast majority of accounts and their posts were publicly accessible by default; and where users could freely follow and tweet at almost any other account, without a need to be accepted as a follower or ‘friend’ (Gruzd et al.) – played a critical role in facilitating such uses, as did the rapidly growing use of hashtags as a user-generated means of coordinating feeds of posts relating to a given topic. Hashtags proved especially critical, indeed, to the bottom-up surfacing of information without the (initial) involvement of major institutional accounts. They enabled key voices to be “crowdsourced to prominence through the pluralizing practices of retweeting, mentioning, and other addressivity markers” by the platform’s ordinary users, as Meraz & Papacharissi have put it (158). In spite of these important uses, Twitter was always more than ‘only’ a news network, however, as Burgess & Baym have documented. Beyond their uses in breaking news (and sometimes overlapping with such uses), for instance, hashtags have always also been crucial to connecting communities – from small and localised interest and identity groups to major, global, prosocial activism like #metoo and #blacklivesmatter (e.g. Jackson & Foucault Welles). In doing so, well beyond their roles in the context of acute events, they also served a purpose in facilitating the longer-term tracking of issues and events. This is demonstrated for example by the six-year campaign in Australia for a Royal Commission of Inquiry into the federal government’s illegal #Robodebt scheme (Dehghan & Bruns). The platform facilitated what Bennett & Segerberg have described as “connective action”, enabling the ad hoc organisation of hashtag followers into crowds with a notable impact on public debate (though not necessarily public policy) related to the issues that such connective action addressed. Through such efforts, as well as more day-to-day thematic attention and networking between accounts focussing on related issues, Twitter also enabled the emergence of a new class of expert voices, community leaders, and issue influencers. This use of social media to build and exert influence was certainly not limited to Twitter alone (Abidin), and of course also produced a substantial amount of ill-informed charlatans opining on topics well outside their area of expertise. But yet again the very public and open nature of communication on Twitter often also served to flush out such misinformation, as genuine experts responded to and debunked misguided views – at least as long as the operators of the Twitter platform also played their part by acting on reports of influence operations and egregious mis- and disinformation sharing. Genuine experts and community leaders found an audience on Twitter, then, especially also because its flat and open structure enabled the rapid horizontal dissemination of their posts not only through hashtagging, but (arguably more importantly) also with the help of retweets (Hemsley). Retweeting distributed other accounts’ tweets to the retweeting user’s network of followers, even if they were not themselves following the retweeted user or any hashtags included in that users’ tweets (cf. Bruns & Moe). This substantially aided the serendipitous discovery of emerging, novel, and unexpected topics and events, and was itself amplified further by the Twitter platform’s identification of current ‘trending topics’, globally or in a user’s geographic region. In a refrain that is recurring throughout Twitter’s history (also cf. Burgess & Baym), Twitter as a platform worked best when its systems responded to the interests and practices of its userbase. Such serendipitous, playful, and social – indeed, joyful – uses of the platform were often overshadowed by the considerable media and scholarly interest in Twitter’s more serious news and business uses. Yet the evidence suggests that social, phatic uses (from simply hanging out online together to mostly good-natured shitposting) accounted for the majority of Twitter activity on any given day (Bruns & Moon). For all the cultural cachet that the hashtag has gained as a media object well beyond Twitter itself, hashtagged tweets were always only a minor subset of all tweets, for instance, and the vast majority of ordinary users did not engage with the platform predominantly for professional purposes. As David Roth put it in one of the many eulogies for the Twitter that was which have been written since the Musk takeover, then, for all the overwrought ways in which Twitter has been described—[Tucker] Carlson called it “the place where our national conversation incubates and develops”…—the comparison that always made the most sense was too small-bore for the big-thinking types. I’ve always thought of Twitter as a house party that I could visit or leave at my leisure. Different things were happening in different rooms, some of them for me and some of them very much not. Over time I learned how to find the scenes and conversations I liked, and came to recognize the people I saw in those rooms as friends. (The owners were of course not around.) This is a fine thing for a website to be, I think. This seems to encapsulate well the general sense of loss that many long-term Twitter users have experienced since the inexorable decline of the platform set in after Elon Musk bought it – yet (like other memories of adolescent house parties) it also creates an image of an antediluvian golden age that likely never existed as such. The Writing on the Wall The sober truth is that Twitter was never well-managed. The owners were indeed never around, or, even if they were, usually failed to show unwanted intruders the door. During its early days, this inattention was perhaps masked by an overall sense of excitement and enthusiasm for this new platform, and by the way management seemed to both take on new ideas (search functions, hashtags, etc.) and open the platform’s technical infrastructure to developers, businesses, and researchers to build third-party tools and extensions and to better understand how people were using the platform (Burgess & Bruns). As Ash notes, even Twitter’s 2013 statement to the US Securities and Exchange Commission in preparation for its public listing on the stock exchange still makes the commitment that the mission we serve as Twitter, Inc. is to give everyone the power to create and share ideas and information instantly without barriers. Our business and revenue will always follow that mission in ways to improve – and not detract from – a free and global conversation. (Twitter, Inc.) This commitment waned considerably as Twitter’s management, in search of a longer-term business plan, began to crack down on third-party uses of its data, and sought to monetise such data for themselves – not least also in response to shareholder pressure to perform financially. By 2015, “no longer is Twitter speaking to barriers of freedom, but rather, they focus on generating revenue. A marked shift in rhetoric is now made visible” in its quarterly earnings reports (Ash), especially as Twitter’s development slowed while the company invested in ill-fated ventures like video platforms Vine and Periscope that sought to expand to new userbases rather than serve existing users (cf. Scolari). Poorly thought-through and widely opposed decisions such as the redesign of the ‘star’ button (as a form of bookmarking tweets) to a ‘heart’, implying emotional attachment (Bucher & Helmond), and stubborn inaction in the face of user demand – exemplified most obviously by the company’s notorious refusal to introduce any, even limited, functionality to edit tweets after posting (Martineau) – were signs of further trouble to come. Some such trouble also originated externally, not least in the growth in coordinated influence operations designed to affect public opinion for instance in the 2016 Brexit referendum and U.S. presidential election (Bastos; Golovchenko et al.), and the rapid rise in abuse and hate speech especially in the wake of Donald Trump’s election. Not only did Twitter management appear to do too little, too late: some of its inaction seemed to stem from a misguided, pseudo-libertarian valuation of unconstrained ‘free speech’ above all else, and/or a concern for the business and political implications of acting more forcefully against mis- and disinformation, abuse, hate speech, and other obvious ills. Twitter’s status as Trump’s favourite platform was good for business and brand recognition in the short term, in other words, no matter the long-term damage that platforming Trump and other high-volume sources of blatant disinformation and hate speech might also cause for both company and community. It is notable in this context that, but for a handful of high-profile and at times poorly handled collaborations (cf. Liao), Twitter largely also failed to engage with the substantial volume of leading scholarship on prosocial as well as problematic user practices that its earlier, more permissive collaboration settings had encouraged. Especially after 2016, substantial computational social science scholarship addressed the challenges of identifying and combatting mis- and disinformation operations (e.g. Kim et al.; Starbird et al.) and other forms of what Facebook came to call ‘coordinated inauthentic behaviour’ (Gleicher), while other researchers dissected the company’s use of appeals to ‘free speech’ as a justification for its continued platforming of outright fascists (Konikoff), yet Twitter’s leadership largely ignored any of this work. It also actively frustrated its user community’s attempts to rekindle the DIY spirit of the platform’s early days and develop communal approaches to combatting problematic actors, for instance by creating collaborative blocklists (Geiger). It was only towards the end of this late period in Twitter’s pre-Musk trajectory that the company appeared to rethink its relationship especially with researchers (and it is possible that this volte face was prompted to some extent by the coming Digital Services Act in the European Union, with its requirements for Very Large Online Platforms to provide better data access to researchers). In 2021, Twitter introduced a powerful new Application Programming Interface specifically dedicated to research purposes (Perez, “Twitter”), as well as a no-code Tweet Downloader functionality that would provide datasets directly in human-readable file formats without the need for any programming. These genuinely useful facilities would soon be dismantled again, however, as Twitter’s fortunes changed irrevocably following its acquisition by Elon Musk in 2022 (Stokel-Walker). Their brief flourishing serves as a reminder of a better path not taken. The Decline of Online Public Debate Open, prosocial, constructive public debate flourished briefly in online spaces such as Twitter during the first half of the 2010s. This substantially aided phenomena such as the Arab Spring, Me Too, and Black Lives Matter, as well as countless smaller and more localised societal movements. Those last two examples also point to the fact that these developments were never truly global, however: they occurred predominantly in the democratic countries of the Global North, while similar developments elsewhere were often snuffed out by more repressive regimes, at times even with the help of Twitter and other platforms that acquiesced all too easily to the take-down demands made by such governments. Available space in this article does not permit a full discussion of Twitter’s use across the diverse political contexts of the Majority World. Twitter was used to pursue social change, protest government oppression, and organise resistance against authoritarian regimes in a broad range of contexts: for instance, activism in Indonesia towards the criminalisation of sexual violence (Azmi); resistance against government repression of public debate in Saudi Arabia (Uniacke); diasporic opposition against autocratic leaders in Russia and Iran (Dehghan and Glazunova). The temporary success of protest campaigns and movements, from the Arab Spring onwards, in attracting a global audience to their cause was aided not least by the deployment of singular hashtags to bundle and amplify critical information and calls to action – but it increasingly also produced a two-fold backlash from contrarian actors. On the one hand, it indicated a pressing need to develop effective countermeasures against the influence of such campaigns, while on the other, it pointed to the potential of instrumentalising these same processes in support of far more reactionary and disruptive purposes. While earlier examples can readily be identified, too, the second half of the 2010s is widely seen as the period during which these efforts produced their first major harvest. Much as earlier prosocial campaigns had attracted and enrolled a public yearning for change, now domestic influence campaigns in the United States, the United Kingdom, and elsewhere – potentially assisted by the Russian ‘Internet Research Agency’ troll farm (Bail et al.) and other foreign actors – engaged the partisan supporters of reactionary and populist causes in what Starbird et al. came to call “participatory disinformation”. Through a mixture of genuine influencers, inauthentic accounts, and bots, they gave ordinary partisans licence to push false narratives that supported their own side and distracted or denigrated their opponents. If nothing else, the sheer volume of content produced by such efforts – whether by the Russian ‘Internet Research Agency’, the Saudi regime’s ‘troll army’ (Benner et al.), or Indonesian political parties’ extensive cohorts of ‘buzzers’ (Burgess & Souisa) – was often already sufficient to overwhelm any meaningful discussion that might otherwise have occurred in the communicative spaces Twitter provided. Public debate ahead of the Brexit referendum and the first election of Donald Trump to the U.S. presidency in 2016 was undermined in this way, and similar patterns of disinformation, division, and decoherence are observable for most major public debates – in the Global North and the Majority World – since then, especially perhaps for debates about climate action and responses to the COVID-19 pandemic (Graham & FitzGerald, “Exploring”). This backlash against the potential prosocial uses of Twitter and other social media platforms for genuine public debate amongst a set of actors well beyond the elite that populate the “virtual stage of mediated communication” provided by the classic Habermasian public sphere (Habermas) was entirely foreseeable, perhaps. It represents only the latest, social media-enhanced iteration of the “fear, uncertainty, and doubt” playbook supposedly first used by IBM to denigrate its competitors in the 1970s – an approach which by now is so well established it has even earnt a standing acronym in marketing research: FUD (Pfaffenberger). Its major innovation is simply to capitalise on the very affordances of social media platforms such as Twitter to institute a participatory FUD campaign, where the polarising and divisive messages produced by authentic and inauthentic influencers are now willingly spread online by partisans themselves. Indeed, in doing so, it revives the classic Soviet communication strategy of agit-prop – agitation and propagation – for a new communicative environment (Svegaard). Yet foreseeable or not, this instrumentalisation of platform affordances against societal cohesion turned out to be difficult to defend against – especially also because the extreme ‘free speech’ positions embraced by Twitter and other platform operators. Their resistance against well-intentioned regulatory interventions by democratic government authorities, their belligerence towards independent, critical, public-interest research, and their dismissal of their own user communities’ requests for more proactive interventions against disruptive and inauthentic accounts shut off many of the possible avenues that could have been taken in the fight against those reactionary groups which sought to undermine meaningful online public debate. Notoriously, for instance, Twitter CEO Jack Dorsey reluctantly sanctioned the take-down of Donald Trump’s account only after the latter had encouraged the violent insurrection against the legitimate U.S. election certification process on 6 January 2021 (Paul, “Twitter”). Viewed with the benefit of hindsight, it is clear that such naïve inaction materially aided these disruptive actors’ efforts to undermine online public debate and further damage societal cohesion. Platforms and platform regulators failed, and still fail, to adequately protect the public from those who seek to disinform and divide for base political reasons. It is bitterly ironic in this context both that Twitter’s failure to act against those who sought to undermine it – and here, especially against inauthentic bot accounts – in turn also became a key issue in Elon Musk’s efforts to acquire the platform (Milmo), and that Musk’s own dismantling of any even rudimentary defences against coordinated inauthentic intrusions has subsequently led to the rebranded X becoming overwhelmed with newly created bot accounts (Graham & FitzGerald, Bots). Online Public Debate beyond Twitter Such growing dysfunction in online public debate is not, and never was, limited to Twitter alone, of course. Meta and Alphabet (as owners of platforms such as Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp, and YouTube) have been similarly culpable for their negligence in protecting their users from abuse and disinformation, and for their opposition to legitimate democratic governments’ regulatory initiatives requiring them to do so. However, Twitter’s unique – flat and open – structure of public communication has meant that it came to occupy a special place in the social media ecology, even in spite of its considerably smaller userbase. When news broke of natural disasters, political scandals, violent conflicts, scientific breakthroughs, celebrity deaths, or other major developments, people flocked to Twitter and not those other platforms. When campaigns sought public visibility, community involvement, and crowdsourced amplification, they did so on Twitter. When citizens tried to get journalists to pay attention to emerging issues, convince corporations to improve their practices, or encourage politicians to change their views, they addressed them on Twitter. This positioning is still well removed from Twitter’s occasional self-aggrandisement as “the digital town square” (Burgess), but it does mark Twitter as a distinct place where public debate was likely to take place in a way that it could not on platforms like Facebook, Instagram, and WhatsApp (because debate there is not predominantly public), nor on YouTube or TikTok (because their affordances privilege the posting of public content rather than extensive and ongoing debate). Town square or not, Twitter’s pre-Musk management allowed this public space to atrophy through its pursuit of profit over community, and its inattention to the growing encroachment of disruptive and divisive forces. Its various platform interventions, often strongly opposed by the user community, represent what Cory Doctorow has described as the “enshittification” of a platform for commercial gain. For instance, Twitter’s 2016 transition from a simply chronological to an algorithmically curated default activity feed – which was subsequently found to privilege right-wing politics (Huszár et al.) – maximised content visibility for major accounts over ambient awareness of updates from those accounts users had chosen to follow and interact with. This constitutes a clear turn away from the mission “to give everyone the power to create and share ideas and information instantly without barriers” (Twitter, Inc.). Under Elon Musk, as enshittification turned into enxittification and X transformed altogether into a fascist hangout, the speed of decline increased substantially. The algorithm was tweaked further, not least to promote Musk’s own tweets regardless of whether users were following him or not (Paul, “Elon Musk”). Status as a major, verified account with Twitter’s previously prestigious ‘blue tick’ was now for sale for as low as US$8 (Mogyoros). And far-right accounts exploiting these new realities to push disinformation and abusive content were even rewarded with a share of X’s (dwindling) advertising revenue (Lorenz). In response, a growing number of alternative platform options have sought to position themselves as more or less seamless replacements. These include Mastodon, with its decentralised and federated network of bespoke instances that are each able to set their own community standards and rules; Threads, adopting Mastodon technology for a Twitter-style platform under the auspices of Meta (and with the corporate baggage that this entails); and Bluesky, another federatable but to date more centralised platform whose corporate structure is intended to prevent a Musk-style take-over by hostile and autocratic techbros. This effort to replace Twitter with something else that looks and feels almost exactly like Twitter, just without the stench of Musk, both demonstrates the extent to which ‘old’ Twitter in its style, functionality, and affordances for public debate had captured the attention of social media users, and betrays a lack of imagination about what better alternatives could look like. As Christianna Silva wrote in a perceptive Mashable article, “the same type of guy keeps making the same social media platforms and I am tired” (Silva) – a sentiment that, given Twitter founder Jack Dorsey’s early involvement in Bluesky, could even be shortened to ‘the same guy keeps making the same platform’. If, as she suggests, “the solution to Twitter's downfall isn’t five Twitter clones”, but something new that genuinely improves on the user experience of Twitter and comparable platforms, what might this entail? This question assumes, first, that in spite of the move towards richer and more immersive multimedia formats (with platforms like Instagram and TikTok) there remains a demand and purpose for text-centric social media platforms like Twitter. In addition, other distinct aspects of Twitter – such as the flat, open, and not necessarily reciprocal nature of its network, which enables a considerably greater presence of weak-tie connections – also contribute to its unique user experience, and encourage the platform’s use for predominantly public connection and discussion, including but not limited to journalistic purposes. These should also be retained. Indeed, it is notable that these features are amongst those most faithfully replicated by Mastodon, Threads, or Bluesky; the emergence of third-party tools to transfer users’ established Twitter networks of followers and followees to these new spaces clearly also speaks to a continuing user interest in such aspects. A text-centric, weak-tie, predominantly public platform still fills a unique niche in the social media ecosystem that has been vacated with the death of Twitter, then. Any new platforms seeking to replace Twitter will be subject to the same attempts to disrupt and suppress genuine public debate that old Twitter was, however; they must be better prepared for this. This is unlikely for Threads, which is compromised by parent company Meta’s inconstant and politically expedient commitment to protecting users from abuse and disinformation. It is complicated for Mastodon, where such efforts are at the discretion of each instance operator, most of whom are amateur enthusiasts with strictly limited resources. And it is already proving controversial for Bluesky, whose approach to platform moderation is as yet not fully formed (Perez, “Bluesky”). These new platforms’ inability to address questions of community standards and moderation as an integral part of the platform design is perhaps unsurprising given the long history of insufficient content moderation policies on mainstream social media platforms. But it also constitutes a significant missed opportunity. Any platform that commits to effective and consistent moderation and embeds this deeply into its operations may well find this to be a significant selling point for prospective new users seeking to escape the meltdown of meaningful public debate on Twitter and elsewhere. Indeed, what the early years of Twitter showed most clearly is that the platform was most successful when it worked closely with its users, when it listened to their needs and wishes, when it incorporated user innovations like retweets, hashtags, and search functions into the platform infrastructure proper, and when it enabled third-party developers to build powerful new functionality around that infrastructure by providing a well-documented Application Programming Interface (API). Emerging platforms show at least some signs that they have learnt from this. So far, Bluesky’s own API is powerful and wide open to potential users. Mastodon’s federated structure might be understood as a distributed experiment to explore a variety of approaches to working with users, some of which will succeed while others will fail. Both operate on shared and extensible protocol frameworks for building social media platforms that encourage third-party experimentation. Any such openness may also be targeted by reactionary groups seeking to undermine the potential prosocial uses of these platforms, however, and the central challenge to the platform operators will be how to prepare for and respond to such attempts when (not if) they are made. Will they naïvely take the same laissez-faire, ‘free speech absolutist’ approach as their predecessors, even as large parts of the user community itself encourage them to crack down on abuse? Will they continue to platform disinformation, abuse, and hate because real action against prominent problematic accounts might result in political or commercial consequences? Alternatively, can they develop policies that balance free speech and freedom from harmful speech, and implement them fairly and consistently? Can they find ways to genuinely engage and consult their communities in decisions that affect the running of the platform? A Difficult Path Ahead The historical trajectory of Twitter over these past twenty years, and of social media and their predecessor channels over an even longer period, has made it abundantly clear that any prosocial public debate that is genuinely open to more than the entrenched elites of the Habermasian public sphere will be targeted by those who seek to defend their own public influence and agenda-setting power from being scrutinised and diluted, and instrumentalised by those who see an opportunity to misdirect and derail public discourse for their own benefit. For now, this has severely curtailed the genuine potential that spaces for online public debate like Twitter once showed (even in spite of their now obvious flaws). This decline has occurred at a time when traditional arenas for public debate – such as commercial and public-service mainstream media channels – are themselves severely threatened by failing business models, corporate hollowing-out, journalistic self-censorship, and political obstruction. In combination, the struggles of both social and mainstream media have aided the current global democratic backsliding towards autocracy. And yet, all hope is not lost. From Belarus to Brazil, from the United States to Hungary, clearly communities and societies around the world continue to resist the autocratic transformation of once democratic systems, and in doing so also continue to experiment with new forms and platforms for public communication and debate. As Twitter, now X, fades into irrelevance as a far-right fringe platform overrun by AI slop and performative Musk worship, the social media landscape is more diverse and fragmented than it has been for many years. That fragmentation also presents a considerable opportunity to explore and test platform models and configurations that constitute a genuine departure and avoid the mere replacement of Twitter with yet another Twitter clone. Those new entrants into the social media space that proactively address these challenges in the most innovative way are likely to be those that will win out in the end. title: “Trying to go at full speed with the handbrake on”: Living with persistent symptoms after COVID-19, a qualitative interview study
authors: Dilara Gülmez; Emelie Sarenmalm; Elena Nowacki; Emmanuel Dudoignon; Morgane Michel; Björn Peters; Lenka Vanek; Janosch Niknam-Saeidi; Amelie Kurnikowski; Justyna Siwy; Astrid Erber; Mariann Gyöngyösi; Ulrich Kropiunigg; Manfred Hecking
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: COVID-19; Health; Qualitative research; Caregiving; Gender issues
abstract: Abstract Background: Despite individuals experiencing a gradual reduction in persistent symptoms following SARS-CoV-2 infection, a subset remains at increased risk of death and health loss up to three years post-infection. Given prior evidence of gender-related disparities in acute COVID-19 outcomes and informed by survivorship concept, we examined psychosocial aspects of Long COVID by considering gender-related differences in participants’ narratives. Methods: In this multi-center qualitative study, 27 patients with persistent symptoms following acute COVID-19 and three primary caregivers were interviewed using a semi-structured interview guide across centers in Austria, France and Sweden. Qualitative analysis was informed by Charmaz’s constructivist grounded theory and stratified by self-reported gender. Results: The study cohort consisted predominantly of individuals previously hospitalized for acute COVID-19 assessed at a mean follow-up of 3.4 ± 0.6 years post-infection. Functional constraints coincided with shifts in self-concept prompting retrospective reflection and a search for reassurance predominantly among women; altered roles and responsibilities increased caregiver strain and heightened structural vulnerability in the context of prolonged recovery. Perceived neglect in healthcare prompted both women and men to engage in self-advocacy in aid- and health-management. Survival-oriented positive future outlooks and resilience following near-death-experiences were salient among men. Neglect of health needs was associated with a premature pressure to perform due to caregiving demands among women, and with prioritization of the breadwinner role and masculinity-linked stoic ideals of invulnerability among men. Conclusion: Both patient and caregiver narratives revealed intersecting challenges warranting holistic, coordinated care attentive to systemic barriers, social relations, and gender-related patterns.
Keywords: Long COVID; Qualitative study; Gender disparities; Patient narratives; Healthcare system

title: Secure Robotics: Navigating Challenges at the Nexus of Safety, Trust, and Cybersecurity in Cyber-Physical Systems
authors: Adam Haskard; Damith Herath
venue: ACM Computing Surveys
Tags: cybersecurity; safety; automation; robotics; trust
abstract: The growing pervasiveness of robotic and embodied artificial intelligence systems in daily life and within cyber-physical environments highlights a complex web of challenges at the intersection of robotic safety, human-to-robot trust, and cybersecurity. This article explores these challenges by emphasising the crucial role of security in establishing and maintaining trust between humans and robots, which is integral to successfully adopting and operating these systems in human environments. Safety considerations include mitigating the risks of physical harm and environmental damage due to robotic malfunctions or cyberattacks, particularly in autonomous robots requiring high built-in safety measures. From a cybersecurity perspective, these systems face unique challenges due to their complex, interconnected software and hardware components that necessitate robust protection against data breaches to ensure secure data communication. Additionally, the dynamic interaction of these systems with the physical environment adds a layer of complexity, which makes the safety, security, and reliability of these interactions a vital component of the overall security strategy. This article reviews these areas within the cyber-physical systems paradigm by focusing on engineering fail-safe mechanisms, the importance of trust and ethical responsibility in human-robot interactions, and the need for resilient cybersecurity measures. At this nexus, a table of crossover challenges illustrates the intricacy of integrating safety, trust, and security in robotic systems. This article introduces “secure robotics” as a new paradigm to address these collective challenges with a novel model to provide a structured methodology for evaluating and enhancing robotic system performance that symbolises the convergence of theoretical constructs with empirical analysis. By defining secure robotics, this article establishes a framework for advancing robotics in the cyber-physical era in alignment with current technological trends while anticipating future developments. This framework positions secure robotics as a key contributor to the evolution of cyber-physical systems.
Keywords: secure robotics; cyber-physical systems; human-robot trust; cybersecurity; safety considerations

title: Cyber Security and the Internet of Things: Vulnerabilities, Threats, Intruders and Attacks
authors: Mohamed Abomhara; Geir M. Køien

abstract: Internet of Things (IoT) devices are rapidly becoming ubiquitous while IoT services are becoming pervasive. Their success has not gone unnoticed and the number of threats and attacks against IoT devices and services are on the increase as well. Cyber-attacks are not new to IoT, but as IoT will be deeply interwoven in our lives and societies, it is becoming necessary to step up and take cyber defense seriously. Hence, there is a real need to secure IoT, which has consequently resulted in a need to comprehensively understand the threats and attacks on IoT infrastructure. This paper is an attempt to classify threat types, besides analyze and characterize intruders and attacks facing IoT devices and services.

title: A Comprehensive Review of Cyber Security Vulnerabilities, Threats, Attacks, and Solutions
authors: Ömer Aslan; Semih Serkant Aktuğ; Merve Ozkan-Okay; Abdullah Asim Yilmaz; Erdal Akin
venue: Electronics
Tags: cybersecurity; vulnerability assessment; threat detection; emerging technologies
abstract: Internet usage has grown exponentially, with individuals and companies performing multiple daily transactions in cyberspace rather than in the real world. The coronavirus (COVID-19) pandemic has accelerated this process. As a result of the widespread usage of the digital environment, traditional crimes have also shifted to the digital space. Emerging technologies such as cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), social media, wireless communication, and cryptocurrencies are raising security concerns in cyberspace. Recently, cyber criminals have started to use cyber attacks as a service to automate attacks and leverage their impact. Attackers exploit vulnerabilities that exist in hardware, software, and communication layers. Various types of cyber attacks include distributed denial of service (DDoS), phishing, man-in-the-middle, password, remote, privilege escalation, and malware. Due to new-generation attacks and evasion techniques, traditional protection systems such as firewalls, intrusion detection systems, antivirus software, access control lists, etc., are no longer effective in detecting these sophisticated attacks. Therefore, there is an urgent need to find innovative and more feasible solutions to prevent cyber attacks. The paper first extensively explains the main reasons for cyber attacks. Then, it reviews the most recent attacks, attack patterns, and detection techniques. Thirdly, the article discusses contemporary technical and nontechnical solutions for recognizing attacks in advance. Using trending technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, cloud platforms, big data, and blockchain can be a promising solution for current and future cyber attacks. These technological solutions may assist in detecting malware, intrusion detection, spam identification, DNS attack classification, fraud detection, recognizing hidden channels, and distinguishing advanced persistent threats. However, some promising solutions, especially machine learning and deep learning, are not resistant to evasion techniques, which must be considered when proposing solutions against intelligent cyber attacks.
Keywords: cybersecurity; vulnerabilities; cyber attacks; machine learning; deep learning; solutions

title: Cybersecurity of Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems: A Review
authors: Hakan Kayan; Matthew Nunes; Omer Rana; Pete Burnap; Charith Perera
venue: ACM Computing Surveys
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Government Data; Academic Literature
Tags: Cybersecurity; Industrial Systems; Vulnerabilities; Research Directions
abstract: Industrial cyber-physical systems ( ICPSs ) manage critical infrastructures by controlling the processes based on the “physics” data gathered by edge sensor networks. Recent innovations in ubiquitous computing and communication technologies have prompted the rapid integration of highly interconnected systems to ICPSs. Hence, the “security by obscurity” principle provided by air-gapping is no longer followed. As the interconnectivity in ICPSs increases, so does the attack surface. Industrial vulnerability assessment reports have shown that a variety of new vulnerabilities have occurred due to this transition. Although there are existing surveys in this context, very little is mentioned regarding the outputs of these reports. While these reports show that the most exploited vulnerabilities occur due to weak boundary protection, these vulnerabilities also occur due to limited or ill-defined security policies. However, current literature focuses on intrusion detection systems ( IDSs ), network traffic analysis ( NTA ) methods, or anomaly detection techniques. Hence, finding a solution for the problems mentioned in these reports is relatively hard. We bridge this gap by defining and reviewing ICPSs from a cybersecurity perspective. In particular, multi-dimensional adaptive attack taxonomy is presented and utilized for evaluating real-life ICPS cyber incidents. Finally, we identify the general shortcomings and highlight the points that cause a gap in existing literature while defining future research directions.
Keywords: Industrial Cyber-Physical Systems; Cybersecurity; Vulnerability Assessment; Attack Taxonomy; Security Policies

title: A systematic literature review on advanced persistent threat behaviors and its detection strategy
authors: Nur Ilzam Che Mat; Norziana Jamil; Yunus Yusoff; Miss Laiha Mat Kiah
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity
Tags: Cybersecurity; Threat Detection; Literature Review
abstract: Abstract Advanced persistent threats (APTs) pose significant security-related challenges to organizations owing to their sophisticated and persistent nature, and are inimical to the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of organizational information and services. This study systematically reviews the literature on methods of detecting APTs by comprehensively surveying research in the area, identifying gaps in the relevant studies, and proposing directions for future work. The authors provide a detailed analysis of current methods of APT detection that are based on multi-stage attack-related behaviors. We adhered to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines and conducted an extensive search of a variety of databases. A total of 45 studies, encompassing sources from both academia and the industry, were considered in the final analysis. The findings reveal that APTs have the capability to laterally propagate and achieve their objectives by identifying and exploiting existing systemic vulnerabilities. By identifying shortcomings in prevalent methods of APT detection, we propose integrating the multi-stage attack-related behaviors of APTs with the assessment of the presence of vulnerabilities in the network and their susceptibility to being exploited in order to improve the accuracy of their identification. Such an improved approach uses vulnerability scores and probability metrics to determine the probable sequence of targeted nodes, and visualizes the path of APT attacks. This technique of advanced detection enables the early identification of the most likely targets, which, in turn, allows for the implementation of proactive measures to prevent the network from being further compromised. The research here contributes to the literature by highlighting the importance of integrating multi-stage attack-related behaviors, vulnerability assessment, and techniques of visualization for APT detection to enhance the overall security of organizations.
Keywords: Advanced Persistent Threats; APTs; Detection Strategies; Vulnerability Assessment; Multi-stage Attacks

title: Role of Artificial Intelligence in the Internet of Things (IoT) cybersecurity
authors: Murat Kuzlu; Corinne Fair; Ozgur Guler

abstract: Abstract In recent years, the use of the Internet of Things (IoT) has increased exponentially, and cybersecurity concerns have increased along with it. On the cutting edge of cybersecurity is Artificial Intelligence (AI), which is used for the development of complex algorithms to protect networks and systems, including IoT systems. However, cyber-attackers have figured out how to exploit AI and have even begun to use adversarial AI in order to carry out cybersecurity attacks. This review paper compiles information from several other surveys and research papers regarding IoT, AI, and attacks with and against AI and explores the relationship between these three topics with the purpose of comprehensively presenting and summarizing relevant literature in these fields.

title: Evaluating and Securing Power Systems against Vulnerabilities Introduced by Large Language Models
authors: Manpo Li; Xuerui Yang; Xiaochen Yang; Shugui Zhang
venue: Informatica
Tags: LLMs; Security Risks; Power Monitoring; Machine Learning; Cyber Attacks
abstract: An exciting new direction for improving operational efficiency and decision-making is the use of Large Language Modeling (LLMs) to contemporary power systems. Nevertheless, there may be unanticipated security risks associated with this move. Using LLMs to power networks may pose certain risks, which this paper examines. It stresses the need of doing research and developing remedies immediately. It is a challenging but vital job to secure large language models in a power monitoring context. Through the implementation of thorough security measures, the promotion of a security-conscious culture, and the continuous monitoring of new threats while technologies, we may maximize the benefits of LLMs while minimizing their hazards. It is our duty as information security experts to pioneer this new field and make sure that our security protocols adapt to the increasing sophistication of our AI systems. Security flaws in LLM that allow rapid injection attacks are among the most critical ones. These types of attacks take advantage of LLMs' fundamental features by deliberately feeding them data that will cause them to operate in an unexpected way or leak private information. Many LLMs have seen extensive usage with the introduction of commercially accessible systems like ChatGPT. One crucial area of cybersecurity that is seeing a rise in the use of LLMs is power monitoring systems. It is critical to safeguard these systems against cyber-attacks since they are essential for the stability of society and the nation's energy supply. In order to keep these systems resilient and reliable, it is essential to detect unexpected vulnerabilities, especially zero-day attacks. One potential way to improve these detection capabilities is via LLMs. It integrates power-system standards and threat intelligence with traditional anomaly detection, LLM-assisted reasoning over code/configs/logs, and protocol-aware telemetry. In order to uncover undisclosed power monitoring system weaknesses, we used models with LSTM with GRU. Since these models are masters of sequential data analysis, they are ideal for this job. Sequential data includes things like sensor readings, system logs, and network traffic. By identifying unusual activity that differs from typical system operation, LSTMs and GRUs are able to discover new, "zero-day" vulnerabilities, in contrast to conventional security technologies that depend on predetermined attack signatures. Here, we built an LLM model using TinyLlama Chat 1.1. The LLM takes the processed packet data and the extracted context as input and outputs a user-friendly summary of the packet file. Through the use of machine learning models, the program provides a concise, well-organized, and straightforward overview of the network's operations.
Keywords: Large Language Models; Power Systems; Cybersecurity; Anomaly Detection; Zero-Day Vulnerabilities

title: Cyber Threat Intelligence Using AI
authors: V. Rakesh Reddy; Charitha Sai; Purandeshwar Reddy; Gorapati Revanth; G.Revanth -
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research

abstract: The rapid growth of the internet and IoT devices has increased connectivity but also raised the number of cyber threats. Traditional security systems often detect attacks only after they occur, making early detection difficult. This project proposes an AI-based Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) system to identify potential cyber attacks at an early stage. The system collects data from multiple sources such as network logs, malware databases, and open-source intelligence. Using deep learning techniques like Recurrent Neural Networks (RNNs), it learns attack patterns and predicts possible threats in advance. This proactive approach helps security teams respond faster, reduces false alarms, and improves the overall efficiency of cyber threat detection.

title: From Anomaly to Attack Path: LLM-Based Network Traffic Investigation for APT Detection
authors: Benedikt Pletzer; Jürgen Mottok
venue: Proceedings of the 19th European Workshop on Systems Security
Tags: APT Detection; Security; Network Security; Machine Learning
abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) pose a growing challenge to critical infrastructure security. Their extended timescales, stealth, and multi-stage tactics limit the effectiveness of traditional Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDS), as signature-based methods miss novel techniques and anomaly detection alone produce a flood of low-confidence, low-specificity events. We propose a system that combines unsupervised anomaly detection with automated, large language model (LLM)-driven investigation to analyze suspicious network flows and reconstruct attack paths from network-level observations. Flagged flows are examined at both the feature and payload level using a locally hosted language model. Investigation results are aggregated in a graph database to reconstruct the attack progression through the network. Evaluation on the CICAPT-IIoT dataset shows that the system identifies all labeled malicious flows while uncovering mislabeled traffic containing clear indicators of compromise, suggesting detection capability without prior attack knowledge. We further discuss risks introduced by deploying language models in security-critical applications, including prompt injection via malicious payloads and data poisoning attacks.
Keywords: Advanced Persistent Threats; network traffic; anomaly detection; large language model; attack path reconstruction

title: Geoclimatic and Cognitive Shifts: An Analysis of Their Interrelationship in the Era of Global Crisis
authors: D. D. Stepanyuk; P. S. Seleznev
venue: Humanities and Social Sciences. Bulletin of the Financial University
Tags: global crisis; human behavior; sustainability; environmental psychology; cognitive sociology
abstract: This article examines and analyzes the typology of global geoclimatic shifts, classifying the types of environmental and climatic changes that change the face of the planet. The authors identified 4 types of geoclimatic shifts, such as gradual climatic trends, extreme changes in weather conditions, turning points in the Earth’s system, and changes in biosphere and ecosystem regimes. The authors also consider global cognitive shifts that classify changes in human behavior, values, and collective psychology in response to the global crisis. The types identified by the authors are as follows: climate anxiety, environmental grief and the psychology of crisis, digital transformation and cognitive overload, changes in values, worldview, and moral principles. For each category in the article, the authors identified the key driving factors, their characteristics and the observed consequences for environmental stability, human health, food and water security, as well as the sustainability of infrastructure. The authors draw on modern scientific literature in the fields of the environment, behavioral sciences, cognitive sociology, and moral psychology. A key analytical contribution is the study of the effects of the interaction between geoclimatic and cognitive shifts. In the article, the authors analyzed how climatic stress factors — extreme heat, lack of resources, population displacement, and exposure to natural disasters — can increase psychological stress, change moral priorities, and transform institutional trust, while cognitive models such as increased risk, cascades of misinformation, and failures of collective action, in turn, can influence the results of mitigation and adaptation. In conclusion, the authors consider how these shifts interact with each other (for example, how climatic stressors cause psychological reactions or social changes), and also consider how such a typology can help in research, policy development, and political sustainability planning.
Keywords: geoclimatic shifts; cognitive shifts; environmental changes; climate anxiety; psychology of crisis

title: Hardware techniques to mitigate cyber and data thefts to enable digital technology adoption
authors: Jaya Chakraborty
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
Tags: cybersecurity; technological framework; data governance; metaverse security; vulnerability mitigation
abstract: This paper examines the threat vectors specific to devices in metaverse ecosystem, that include factors such as identity theft, compromised biometric credentials, smart device vulnerabilities and finally the biggest challenge posed by AI impersonation. Furthermore, in the context of persistent consumer geotags or sensor-based data collection; it analyses the regulatory gaps inherent in General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR) frameworks. This paper proposes onion-layered strategies to identify isolate-test-mitigate threats - with inner layer metaverse devices being in close proximity to humans and outer layer devices that surround us in the external environment. It highlights gaps in techno-commercial, infrastructural, organizational, and governance-level to recommend risk averse solutions. The outcome is an 8-step framework mapped to Vulnerability- Uncertainty- Complexity- Authenticity (VUCA) based on the device threat impact score. This framework can be referenced by businesses to prepare a future-looking roadmap that will enable a stable, reliable and secure metaverse adoption.
Keywords: cyber theft; data protection; metaverse; identity theft; biometric security; AI impersonation; GDPR; risk mitigation

title: Enhancing network security based on anomaly detection using deep learning for intelligent IDS/IPS systems
authors: Trong Thang Ha
venue: Tạp chí Khoa học và Công nghệ Trường Đại học Công nghệ Đông Á
Tags: Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Network Security Solutions
abstract: Intrusion Detection Systems (IDS) and Intrusion Prevention Systems (IPS) are critical security solutions designed to monitor and manage network activities in order to detect and respond to attacks or abnormal behaviors. An IDS primarily monitors network traffic and generates alerts upon detecting suspicious activities, whereas an IPS can proactively respond to threats by automatically blocking packets, terminating connections, disabling accounts, or isolating devices from the network. However, traditional IDS/IPS systems are limited in their ability to detect complex anomalous patterns in network traffic and often respond ineffectively in dynamic and heterogeneous network environments. This research proposes an intelligent IDS/IPS framework for LAN environments, integrating a Deep Learning‑based Autoencoder to perform anomaly detection on network traffic features. As an unsupervised learning approach, it enables the identification of anomalies without requiring pre‑labeled attack data, while an automated alert mechanism and real‑time response capability enhance the effectiveness of threat detection, monitoring, and prevention in a more proactive and efficient manner.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection Systems; Anomaly Detection; Deep Learning; Network Security; IDS/IPS; Autoencoder

title: CyberForce: Intelligent Malware Detection Using Federated Reinforcement Learning
authors: Dr. Bushra Tahseen; Chakali. Hemavathi
venue: Research Digest on Engineering Management and Social Innovations
Tags: Intelligent Systems; Distributed Learning; Cyber Threats; Adaptive Strategies
abstract: The rapid evolution of malware and cyber threats has made traditional centralized detection systems less effective due to privacy concerns, data silos, and limited adaptability. To address these challenges, this study proposes Cyber Force, a federated reinforcement learning-based framework for intelligent malware detection. The system leverages federated learning to enable multiple distributed devices or organizations to collaboratively train models without sharing sensitive data, thereby preserving privacy while improving detection performance. Reinforcement learning is integrated to dynamically adapt detection strategies based on environmental feedback, allowing the system to continuously improve its decision-making capabilities. The proposed framework combines decentralized data training with adaptive learning mechanisms to detect both known and unknown malware variants effectively. By utilizing local training on edge devices and aggregating model updates through a central server, the system ensures scalability and robustness. Experimental analysis demonstrates that the Cyber Force framework achieves higher detection accuracy, reduced communication overhead, and enhanced privacy compared to traditional centralized approaches. This research contributes to the development of next-generation cybersecurity systems capable of handling evolving malware threats in distributed environments.
Keywords: Malware Detection; Federated Learning; Reinforcement Learning; Cybersecurity; Privacy Preservation

title: SmartCPS-ADAPT: An Intrusion Detection System for Cyber-Physical Systems
authors: Upasana Mahajan; J. Somasekar; Vikram Neerugatti
venue: Journal of Artificial Intelligence and Technology
Tags: Security; AI; Edge Computing; Network Resilience
abstract: The rapid growth of cyber-physical systems (CPS) and internet of things Edge-Cloud environments has amplified concerns regarding cyber threats, making intrusion detection systems (IDS) a vital component of network resilience. However, recent studies reveal a research gap in existing IDS frameworks: many fail to adapt to evolving attacks, exhibit imbalanced detection performance, or incur high computational costs. To address this challenge, this work aims to develop a robust deep learning-based classification model that accurately detects cyberattacks in CPS. Hence, this work proposed SmartCPS-ADAPT, which leverages Convolutional Neural Network-Bi-Directional Long Short-Term Memory (CNN–BiLSTM) for spatial-temporal feature extraction, an adaptive extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) classifier for handling evolving data distributions, and a drift detection mechanism for continuous learning. Experimental evaluation on the CICIoT2023 dataset demonstrates superior performance, achieving 100% accuracy in binary classification and 99.85% accuracy in multi-class classification. The findings confirm that SmartCPS-ADAPT significantly outperforms existing approaches, ensuring reliable detection of diverse cyber attacks. In conclusion, the SmartCPS-ADAPT establishes a highly effective IDS model that addresses adaptability, robustness, and accuracy in CPS security.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection System; Cyber-Physical Systems; Deep Learning; CNN-BiLSTM; Adaptive Classifier; Cybersecurity

title: AI-Based Operating System: Architecture, Intelligence Integration, Challenges, and Future Perspectives
authors: Arahan Babbar
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
Tags: AI; Operating Systems; Security; Autonomous Intelligence; Performance Optimization
abstract: The accelerated development of computing workloads that includes highly concurrent tasks, diverse hardware architectures, data flow in real time, and intelligent applications has highlighted the inefficiencies of the conventional operating system (OS) model. Designed on the foundations of rules-driven heuristics that were developed in the heydays of the batch processing mainframe computers, current OSs like Linux and Windows NT fail to maximize their capabilities and provide adaptive and proactive security management and user experience in today’s world. This paper explores, designs, and analyses a fully-fledged architecture for an AI-Operating System or AI-OS – a novel generation of OS in which artificial intelligence algorithms including machine learning, deep reinforcement learning, large language models, and probabilistic inference engines form part of the kernel and services around it. Unlike ad hoc integrations of individual ML components into existing OS subsystems, AI-OS represents a holistic redesign guided by a set of unifying principles: safety-bounded intelligence, unified telemetry, online adaptive learning, graceful degradation, and transparent explainability. We present a five-layer hierarchical architecture spanning hardware abstraction to natural language user interaction, and elaborate the design of six AI-infused core subsystems: (1) reinforcement learning-driven process scheduling, (2) predictive memory management, (3) intelligent file and storage management, (4) AI-enforced security and anomaly detection, (5) a natural language system interface powered by a locally deployed LLM, and (6) autonomous fault detection and selfhealing. We further address the substantial engineering challenges that arise when deploying ML models in a kernel context — including real-time inference constraints, formal safety verification, privacy-preserving online learning, and hardware heterogeneity — and propose concrete mitigation strategies for each. Experimental evaluation on a 16-node cluster running a modified Linux 6.6 kernel with AI-OS extensions demonstrates: a 14.7% improvement in aggregate CPU throughput, a 19.3% reduction in 99th-percentile scheduling latency, a 37.7% decrease in memory page fault rates, a 96.4% zero-day threat detection rate with only 0.08% false positives, an 87% rate of automated fault resolution, and a 9.8% reduction in overall energy consumption — all with a scheduling overhead increase of merely 0.3 percentage points. The findings provide empirical evidence to support the research hypothesis of the significant system-level performance gains possible via AI-OS technology while ensuring the safety and correctness requirements necessary for operational systems. In addition to its technical contribution, this paper also addresses the ethical, social, and governance issues related to the application of autonomous intelligence in the context of an operating system. Finally, it lays out a path forward for future research in this area
Keywords: AI-Operating System; machine learning; deep reinforcement learning; security management; kernel architecture

title: Lightweight Multi-Channel BiLSTM-Attention with Coordinated Defense for Intrusion Detection in Distributed Photovoltaic Communication Networks
authors: Danni Liu; Shengda Wang; Chunhui Shi; Jia Li; Xiuhong Jiang
venue: Informatica
Tags: Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Edge Computing; Data Security; Network Defense
abstract: To address intrusion and data tampering threats in distributed photovoltaic (PV) communication networks, this paper proposes a lightweight multi-channel BiLSTM-Attention–based intrusion detection and coordinated defense framework. An attack-oriented, risk-aware feature modeling method constructs multi-dimensional temporal inputs by combining protocol semantics, operational interaction behaviors, and deviation-based risk indicators, which are processed by a BiLSTM backbone with time-step attention and channel-level attention fusion. Model pruning and attention sparsification are adopted to obtain a compact architecture suitable for edge deployment, while a dual-threshold, detection-driven defense coordination mechanism links anomaly scores to graded response policies and closed-loop control. Experiments on a hybrid dataset composed of real PV communication logs and PV-adapted UNSW-NB15 and CIC-IDS2018 traffic show that the proposed model achieves 94.8% accuracy, 94.2% recall, and a 95.6% F1-score with an average inference time of 16.2 ms and a false positive rate below 3.6%. Compared with a vanilla BiLSTM-Attention baseline, the proposed framework improves F1-score by 3.2 percentage points and reduces inference latency by about 11%, while maintaining higher robustness under noisy and imbalanced conditions. These results indicate that the framework can provide accurate, real-time intrusion detection and coordinated security defense for distributed photovoltaic communication networks in resource-constrained deployment scenarios.Povzetek:An improved lightweight multi-channel BiLSTM-Attention framework enhances intrusion detection and coordinated security defense in distributed photovoltaic communication networks through risk-aware temporal modeling, multi-channel attention fusion, and model pruning for edge deployment.
Keywords: BiLSTM; Intrusion Detection; Photovoltaic Networks; Attention Mechanism; Coordinated Defense

title: R-Snort: A Performance-Optimized Multi-Agent NIDS Architecture for SOHO and Edge-of-Things Networks Using Snort 3 on Raspberry Pi 5
authors: Julio Gómez López; Deian Orlando Petrovics Tabacu; Nicolás Padilla Soriano; Alfredo Alcayde García
venue: Computers
Tags: Intrusion Detection; Cybersecurity; Open Source; Performance Optimization; Distributed Systems
abstract: Network Intrusion Detection Systems (NIDSs) are critical to ensuring the resilience of modern digital infrastructures. Although traditionally deployed in large-scale corporate environments, the expanding threat landscape requires the integration of robust security measures into Small Office/Home Office (SOHO) and Edge-of-Things (EoT) networks. However, these environments often face significant constraints in terms of specialized hardware and technical expertise. This article presents R-Snort, an open-source NIDS based on Snort 3, optimized for low-cost Raspberry Pi 5 hardware. Its multi-agent architecture enables distributed deployment with centralized traffic analysis and cross-agent attack correlation, while an intuitive web interface simplifies alert visualization and system management for non-expert administrators. Its main contributions are: (1) a performance-optimized NIDS agent achieving 1 Gbps throughput; (2) a distributed multi-agent architecture enabling centralized event correlation and detection of multi-vector attacks; and (3) an IaC-based automated deployment framework with an intuitive web interface, democratizing professional-grade security for SOHO and EoT environments.
Keywords: NIDS; SOHO; Edge-of-Things; Raspberry Pi; Snort 3

title: Hybrid optimization-based quantum-driven multi-relational graph attention networks for enhanced cyber attack detection in medical IoT networks
authors: R. Krishna Kumari; C. R. Komala; E. Afreen Banu; M. Sivaramkrishnan; M. Siva Ramkumar; K. Sekar; Khursheed Muzammil; Saiful Islam; Amanuel Zewdie
venue: Scientific Reports
Tags: medical IoT; cybersecurity; machine learning; quantum computing; feature selection
abstract: The swift implementation of Internet of Medical Things (IoMT) devices has reshaped the way healthcare is provided. Along with the benefits, the use of IoMT devices has introduced new risks stemming from advanced cyberattacks. The conventional intrusion detection systems (IDSs) have numerous issues, including scalability problems, features that are irrelevant and redundant, and a poor response to evolving attack patterns. All these issues contribute to poor real-time detection performance. To deal with these issues, this paper presents a Hybrid Optimization–Based Quantum–Driven Multi–Relational Graph Attention Network for IoMT Security (MREQGAN-DSA) for IoMT environments. This model addresses the problems arising in IoMT environments for IoMT security and integrates the following three novel techniques: Cat Hunting Optimization with Prism Refraction Search (CHO–PRS) for the refined feature selection, Multi-Relational Equivariant Quantum Graph Attention Network (MREQGAN) for attack classification aware of symmetries, and Duck Swarm Algorithm (DSA) for the adaptive dynamic optimization of hyperparameters. The model is evaluated on NSL-KDD and WUSTL-EHMS-2020 benchmark datasets and obtains an average accuracy of 99.81% on the NSL-KDD dataset and 99.77% on the WUSTL-EHMS-2020 dataset, thereby greatly enhancing the detection metrics of well-known precision, F1-score, and recall, along with the existing literature of IoMT intrusion detection techniques. This study discusses the implementation of advanced quantum-inspired learning and bio-inspired optimization in the MREQGAN-DSA framework to address the IoMT security problem. Thus, the framework is presented as a foundation for smart healthcare systems that are both secure and efficient.
Keywords: IoMT; cyber attack detection; quantum-driven; graph attention networks; intrusion detection; optimization algorithms

abstract: Abstract: The quick expansion of information technology and internet usage in the digital age has greatly increased susceptibility to cyber threats. The study, "A Study on Cyber Threat Trend Analysis Using Historical Data in Defend Shield Cyber Security," looks at the progression of cyber threats over a five-year period, from 2021 to 2025, using historical data. Using quantitative techniques to examine patterns and correlations between major variables like the kind of cyber threat, the frequency of attacks, the response time, and the severity levels, the study takes a descriptive and analytical approach. Sectors like information technology, banking, and e-commerce have been severely affected by these dangers. Additionally, the results highlight the crucial role of timely response in minimizing potential damage by showing a strong link between effective threat detection systems and successful prevention methods.
