title: Financial Disruptions and Risk Mitigation: Exploring the Impact of Intentional and Unintentional Social Media Activities on Organizations
authors: Andrew Clifton Stephens
venue: Purdue
Tags: risk mitigation; organizational resilience; market integrity; digital communication; AI in security
abstract: The widespread adoption of social media has transformed corporate communication and public engagement while heightening organizational and national exposure to cybersecurity threats with economic, operational, and reputational consequences. This dissertation examines emerging risks within social media ecosystems through three case studies of incidents that produced measurable financial or institutional disruption, combining quantitative event study techniques with qualitative process tracing to evaluate how digitally mediated trust failures propagate across financial markets and information networks. An impersonation attack against Eli Lilly and Company exploited platform verification weaknesses to produce a statistically significant structural break in sector-adjusted stock performance, with multi-day persistence from a single fraudulent post. A SIM-swap-enabled takeover of the Securities and Exchange Commission's verified social media account generated statistically significant intraday price and volume disruptions in Bitcoin markets within minutes of a false regulatory signal. An AI-generated deepfake advertising campaign targeting Le Creuset demonstrated how synthetic media distributed through paid advertising infrastructure can enable consumer fraud at scale while evading platform detection. Across these cases, financial and reputational harm consistently emerged through four control surfaces---authority, authentication, amplification, and response latency---patterns synthesized into the Market-Moving Impersonation Attack (MMIA) construct, defined as a social-media-originated event in which the compromise, simulation, or fraudulent representation of an authoritative identity results in measurable financial, market, or organizational disruption. The MMIA framework provides a unified analytical lens for classifying observed incidents and projecting future threat scenarios that combine documented attack mechanisms with emerging capabilities such as generative AI. The cross-case findings are translated into operational guidance organized around eight recurring gaps in organizational preparedness and five policy recommendations, including a proposed National Digital Signal Integrity Act, AI-generated media provenance standards, and coordinated federal oversight for market-integrity contexts. The dissertation positions these empirical and conceptual contributions within the broader literature, articulates boundary conditions, and identifies directions for future research, offering practical guidance for cybersecurity professionals, policymakers, regulatory agencies, corporate risk managers, and digital communication strategists seeking to strengthen institutional resilience in increasingly networked environments.
Keywords: financial disruptions; social media risks; cybersecurity threats; impersonation attacks; deepfake media

title: Proactive Cyber Threat Detection with Real-Time Network Traffic Analysis and Threat Intelligence Integration
authors: D. Vedasamhitha; Prof. Dr. Suchita Rawat
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; News Media; Forums & Communities
Tags: cybersecurity; real-time monitoring; data analysis; network security; proactive defense
abstract: This study proposes a proactive method for cyber threat detection by integrating real-time network traffic analysis with threat intelligence. The goal is to identify and analyse malicious network activities before they compromise data or systems. Live network traffic is captured from malicious web sources within a secure, isolated environment using Wireshark to monitor packet-level behaviour and detect suspicious communication patterns. Captured packets are examined for anomalies such as unusual IPs, abnormal port usage, frequent DNS requests, irregular data sizes, and encrypted traffic flows. These indicators help identify threats like phishing, malware downloads, and command-and-control activities. The analysed data is then correlated with threat intelligence to verify and classify the nature of threats, improving accuracy and reducing false positives. By merging behavioural observation with intelligence validation, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of proactive, continuous monitoring over reactive approaches. It highlights how real-time analysis and adaptive intelligence can strengthen cybersecurity resilience and enable faster, informed responses to evolving cyber threats.
Keywords: cyber threat detection; network traffic analysis; threat intelligence; malicious activities; anomaly detection
affiliations: Garden City Community College; Garden City University College

title: Research on Power System Intrusion Detection and Attack Recognition Algorithm Based on Feature Learning
authors: Chen Wang; Songming Han; Cong Lin; Jie Zahng; Ying Ling; Ming Xie
venue: Frontiers in Artificial Intelligence and Applications
Tags: Cybersecurity; Power Systems; SCADA; Machine Learning; Data Fusion
abstract: With the rapid development of smart grids, the cybersecurity risks of power systems are becoming increasingly prominent. To improve the detection capability of complex attacks, this paper proposes a power system intrusion detection and attack identification algorithm based on deep feature learning. The study preprocesses and structures SCADA and PMU multi-source data, constructs a convolutional-LSTM-attention fusion feature learning framework, and employs an end-to-end weighted classification model to achieve multi-attack identification. In the IEEE-39 node system simulation experiment, the proposed model achieved 98.7% accuracy, 97.9% recall, and 98.2% precision in the intrusion detection task, all significantly outperforming traditional SVM and PCA+MLP methods. In attack type identification, the F1-score for DoS attacks reached 98.9%, for FDI attacks it reached 97.1%, and for replay attacks it reached 95.8%. Experimental results show that this method can effectively capture multi-scale features and has good generalization ability, providing a feasible path for smart grid security protection.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection; Feature Learning; Smart Grid Security; Deep Learning; Multi-attack Identification
affiliations: Electric Power Research Institute; Beihai People's Hospital; Power Grid Corporation (India)

title: AI-Powered Phishing Attack Real Time For User Proctection
authors: Hardik Chavan
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: PhishShield; Machine Learning; Natural Language Processing; User Protection
abstract: This research paper presents PhishShield AI, a hybrid and explainable phishing detection system designed to address the growing challenges of modern cyber threats. The system combines rule-based heuristic analysis with machine learning and natural language processing techniques to accurately detect phishing attacks in real time. Unlike traditional approaches that provide only binary results, the proposed system focuses on Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), offering clear and human-readable explanations that help users understand the nature of detected threats.The system analyzes URLs, email content, and web pages by examining structural patterns, textual features, and hidden elements such as malicious forms. It integrates multiple detection layers to improve accuracy and ensure reliable performance, even against zero-day phishing attacks. Additionally, the inclusion of a user-friendly interface and a gamification component enhances user engagement and promotes cybersecurity awareness.Overall, this work aims to provide an effective, accessible, and intelligent solution that not only improves phishing detection but also educates users, enabling them to make safer decisions in the digital environment
Keywords: AI; Phishing Detection; Explainable AI; Cybersecurity Awareness; Real Time Detection
affiliations: MIT Art, Design and Technology University

title: AI-in-the-Loop Malware: A Capability-Architecture Reference Map and Defender's Counter-Architecture
authors: Hangyu Mei
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: AI-in-the-Loop; malware lifecycle; network security; defensive strategies
abstract: AI integration across the malware lifecycle (recon, payload generation, C2, persistence, post-exec) is an observable not hypothetical threat. We construct a five-stage reference architecture, document per-stage capability uplift with research citations, and provide a 100-host network simulation showing AI-augmented malware infects 3.9-6.5x more hosts than traditional. Multi-posture sweep (zero-day/LotL/adaptive x signature/behavioral/cross-stage detector) reveals defender-preference inversion by attacker posture: LotL is best-defended by signature, not behavioral. Cost-Pareto analysis shows 2-detector pairs dominate the 3-detector ensemble. This paper is part of the AIACW (AI-Autonomous Cyber Weapons) ResearchProgramme, Wave 2 (papers P10-P20). Wave 1 (P1-P9) was deposited atpeer-review venues 2026-Q2 (NDSS, ACM CCS, IEEE S&P, USENIX Security,Oxford J. of Cybersecurity, ACM Computing Surveys). Wave 2 establishesthe empirical interior. P19 (cross-paper integration test) and P20(methodology meta-paper) provide programme-level validation anddocumentation.
Keywords: malware; AI integration; network simulation; defense mechanisms; cybersecurity

title: Comparing PPO and GRPO for Automated Penetration Testing with Compact Language Models on Consumer-Grade Hardware
authors: Junhao Dong
venue: Purdue
Tags: AI Security; Network Vulnerability; ML in Cybersecurity; Consumer Hardware
abstract: As networked systems are increasingly intertwined with our lives, the demand for scalable automated security testing will continue to rise. Penetration testing is one of the most effective ways to discover system vulnerabilities. However, the global cybersecurity sector faces a talent shortage, with manual assessment capabilities being the most significantly impacted (ISC2, 2024). Recent advances in Large Language Models (LLMs) and Deep Reinforcement Learning (DRL) present opportunities for automating multi-step penetration testing tasks, such as reconnaissance, exploitation, and privilege escalation. The increasing popularity of open-source models such as DeepSeek-R1 distilled variants, efficient fine-tuning techniques such as Low-Rank Adaptation (LoRA), and availability of consumer GPUs have made creating custom AI agents relatively easy, which raises concerns about AI-powered attacks as well. The purpose of this research is to compare whether an actor-critic reinforcement learning architecture can build efficient penetration testing agents on consumer-grade hardware by comparing Proximal Policy Optimization (PPO) with Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO), contributions to future AI and RL in automated penetration testing and small-model domains.
Keywords: Penetration Testing; Reinforcement Learning; Large Language Models; Cybersecurity; Automated Testing

title: Cybercrime Evidence Lifecycle: Preservation, Validation, and Adversarial Destruction Tradecraft Under Modern Adversary Capability
authors: Hangyu Mei
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: cybersecurity; forensics; evidence preservation; adversarial tactics
abstract: Modern cybercrime evidence operates under a 4-6 order-of-magnitude time-constant mismatch between adversary destruction (sec-min) and warrant-based preservation (h-d). We characterize the evidence lifecycle as a 6-stage pipeline, enumerate adversary destruction tradecraft per stage, and derive a front-loaded preservation doctrine. Proxy simulation (N=1,000) shows front-loaded preserves 39% vs reactive 6.3% (6.2x improvement). Bilateral preservation reciprocity adds +7.4pp. Stage-sensitivity tornado reveals leverage shifts from S1 (reactive) to S3 (front-loaded) as architecture is deployed. Cost-of-doctrine analysis identifies front-loaded alone as the cost-Pareto-optimum. This paper is part of the AIACW (AI-Autonomous Cyber Weapons) ResearchProgramme, Wave 2 (papers P10-P20). Wave 1 (P1-P9) was deposited atpeer-review venues 2026-Q2 (NDSS, ACM CCS, IEEE S&P, USENIX Security,Oxford J. of Cybersecurity, ACM Computing Surveys). Wave 2 establishesthe empirical interior. P19 (cross-paper integration test) and P20(methodology meta-paper) provide programme-level validation anddocumentation.
Keywords: cybercrime; evidence lifecycle; preservation; adversarial destruction; simulation

title: A Comprehensive Review of Advanced Control Techniques for GridConnected Renewable Energy Systems Using Artificial Intelligence and Power Electronics
authors: Prof. Suyog Sangharatna Dhoke; Dr. R.K. Dhatrak; Dr. Ram R. Deshmukh
venue: International Journal of Drug Delivery Technology
Tags: Control Techniques; Smart Energy Systems; Cybersecurity Challenges; Energy Flow Management
abstract: Since renewable energy sources are sporadic and unpredictable, integrating them into contemporary electrical systems poses substantial technical problems. It is challenging to use traditional control techniques to maintain grid stability, power quality, and efficient energy flow in such circumstances. Advanced control methods that combine artificial intelligence (AI) and power electronics have become viable answers to these problems. Power electronic converters facilitate voltage regulation, frequency control, and power flow management by serving as vital interfaces between renewable energy sources and the grid. AI techniques, including machine learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning, provide intelligent capabilities such as real-time forecasting, adaptive control, system optimization, and fault detection. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI-driven control strategies for grid-connected renewable energy systems. The study highlights how intelligent control enhances system reliability, improves energy management, and ensures compliance with grid standards. Furthermore, key challenges such as computational complexity, data dependency, and cybersecurity are discussed. The results demonstrate that the integration of AI with power electronics provides a robust framework for next-generation smart and sustainable energy systems.
Keywords: Renewable Energy; Artificial Intelligence; Power Electronics; Grid Stability; Energy Management

title: CYBERPUNK CAPITALISM: AI-AUGMENTED BLACK-MARKETS IN THE DIGITAL ECONOMY
authors: Vajid C; Shahil C K; Sanaabil V P; Nasla M
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; News Media; Forums & Communities; Academic Literature
Tags: cybersecurity; underground economy; technological convergence; machine learning; financial fraud
abstract: AbstractThis study investigates how emerging technologies are creating new paradigms in underground economies. Through a systematic analysis of secondary data from 78 peer-reviewed journals, 12 industry reports, and 29 verified media investigations (2018–2023), we identify three key developments: (1) AI-facilitated financial crimes showing 412% growth (Interpol, 2022), (2) a $2.9 billion unregulated cybernetic enhancement market (CyberSecurity Ventures, 2023), and (3) algorithmic "crime-as-a-service" platforms. The research establishes a novel theoretical framework combining institutional anomie theory with posthuman transaction cost economics, addressing critical gaps in existing literature that treat AI ethics and human augmentation as separate domains. Practical implications highlight urgent needs for: AI watermarking mandates, international cybernetic device registries, and enhanced fintech security protocols. The study contributes to digital economics by demonstrating how technological convergence creates new criminal ecosystems that outpace regulatory frameworks. By exploring the hybridization of biological and algorithmic entities within unregulated digital markets, this article uncovers a new chapter in cybercrime one where boundaries between human, machine, and capital dissolve.
Keywords: AI; cybercrime; black-markets; digital economy; financial crimes; crime-as-a-service

title: AI-Powered Cybersecurity
authors: Sahar Yousif Mohammed; Maad M. Mijwil; Kawther Abbood Neamah; Aseed Yaseen Rashid Al-Jubori
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: Cyber Threats; Data Analysis; Security Frameworks
abstract: The rapid advancements in Artificial Intelligence (AI) have revolutionized cybersecurity operations, because they now enable predictive hazard detection and automatic incident responses as well as adaptive security measures. The combination of artificial intelligence-based security solutions uses machine learning algorithms with deep learning technology alongside predictive analytics for analyzing amount of data to detect anomalies while fighting cyber threats instantly. AI delivers many blessings in cybersecurity but brings multiple demanding situations that include targeted attacks on systems underlying biases and important concerns regarding privacy and transparency. AI deployment needs explainable AI (XAI) and robust security frameworks and ethical guidelines to maintain accountability because cybercriminals are more often than not leveraging AI for advanced attacks.
Keywords: AI; Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Predictive Analytics; Incident Response; Explainable AI; Ethical Guidelines

title: Cybersecurity in Healthcare
authors: Mahi Bhardwaj; Yukti Juneja; Neeru Sidana
venue: Organ Trafficking Prevention in the Healthcare Sector
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Corporate Records; Government Data
Tags: Cybercrime; Digital Transformation; Patient Care; COVID-19; Vulnerabilities
abstract: This chapter explores the crucial responsibility of strengthening cybersecurity measures within the ever-changing context of contemporary healthcare systems. As digitalization gets ingrained in healthcare practices, sensitive medical data becomes increasingly vulnerable to cyber-attacks. The healthcare industry is undergoing a rapid digital transformation, with increasing reliance on internet-enabled services and devices such as electronic health records (EHRs), telemedicine, IoT devices, and cloud-based solutions. While these advancements enhance patient care and operational efficiency, they also introduce significant cybersecurity vulnerabilities for criminals, industrial saboteurs, and extortionists to exploit. Healthcare is an attractive target for cybercrime for two fundamental reasons: it is a rich source of valuable data and its defences are weak as the COVID-19 pandemic exposed critical vulnerabilities in global healthcare systems, particularly in data security and interoperability.
Keywords: Cybersecurity; Healthcare; Data Security; IoT; Telemedicine

title: Secure AI Applications for Cybersecurity
authors: Iram Hanif; Majid Hussain; Muhammad Ibrar; Amara Hafeez; Affan Yasin
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: AI applications; cyber risks; ethical AI; privacy; GDPR
abstract: The diversity of digital capabilities has been improved by new cloud-native, microservices, DevSecOps, and IoT software designs, which have also designed a path to cyber threats. Outdated security tools like firewalls and signature-driven recognition are not very effective against ransomware, insider threats, phishing attacks, sophisticated persistent threats and zero-day attacks. The practice of AI can be in the zones of intrusion prevention, malware detection, phishing resistance, insider monitoring, and IoT and autonomous platforms security. These concerns increase major ethical alarms to software engineers who must confirm that the AI systems are transparent, accountable, and fair. XAI and privacy-sensitive models, as well as compliance with such regulations as GDPR and the EU AI Act, provide much-needed protection. Future secure AI developments in cybersecurity include secure AI innovations such as federated learning, blockchain-based AI, and quantum-safe algorithms.
Keywords: AI security; cybersecurity; ransomware; malware detection; phishing resistance; federated learning

title: Cybersecurity Regulation and Individual Rights
authors: Azamat Ali; Ankit Dixit
venue: Legal and Ethical Challenges in Data Privacy Rights and Cybersecurity
Tags: cyber law; human rights; data privacy; government response
abstract: Digital technologies have become highly popular in the modern world, which has added more risk to cyber threats, and it becomes a major concern regarding human rights and data safety. The chapter discusses the reaction of law to digital threats in the perspective of cybersecurity regulation. It discusses the role that the national and international legal systems play in safeguarding personal data, protecting digital security and defending the rights of individuals. It also dwells on the issues of keeping a balance between national security and the rights of individual privacy. Case studies and some law cases that refer to the real life are also provided to demonstrate the tendencies of governments and institutions reacting to cyber offences. The chapter concludes with the suggestions to increase legal protection, enforce moral leadership and to make sure that cyber law protects not only electronic systems but also those people who live in a more interconnected world.
Keywords: cybersecurity regulation; individual rights; data protection; digital security

title: Collaborative Cybersecurity and Co-Creation
authors: Alice A. Bamigbola
venue: Organ Trafficking Prevention in the Healthcare Sector
Tags: collaboration; cybersecurity; innovation; resilience; trust-based cooperation
abstract: The rapid evolution of digital technologies has intensified cyber threats, leaving individuals, organizations, and critical infrastructures increasingly vulnerable. Traditional, isolated cybersecurity approaches are no longer sufficient. Consequently, collaborative cybersecurity and co-creation have emerged as vital strategies that unite the strengths of diverse stakeholders. Yet, efforts remain fragmented due to low trust, poor coordination, and unequal capacities, especially in regions with weak regulatory systems and scarce resources. This chapter examines the roles of governments, private-sectors, academia, civil society, and end users in advancing collaborative cybersecurity. Drawing from literature, policies, and case studies, it shows how co-creation fosters innovation and resilience through shared expertise and resources. Effective collaboration relies on trust, information sharing, and clear governance. However, inconsistent regulations and weak institutional ties persist. Sustainable cybersecurity demands inclusive, transparent, trust-based cooperation among all actors.
Keywords: collaborative cybersecurity; co-creation; stakeholder engagement; cyber threats; trust

title: Deepfake Threats, Cybersecurity Challenges, and Countermeasures
authors: Sherly Alphonse; Neha Khadeeja; Azra Q. Fathima; Manasa Balaji
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: deepfake threats; video manipulation; security challenges
abstract: The social problem of deepfake videos is becoming a critical issue. A rising social problem is the manipulation of these recordings by artificial intelligence (AI) techniques, particularly deep learning. Malicious people employ deepfake technologies to disseminate bogus content, including phony audio, video, and image files. The creation of convincing fake information poses a threat to privacy, security, and politics. Most deepfake video detection techniques rely on data. In-depth analysis of deepfake video production and detection is the goal of this chapter. Identifying the many difficulties in identifying deepfake films is the primary contribution of the chapter. This chapter describes about the science behind the deepfake, detection and mitigation of deepfake etc. This chapter also describes about the applications of deepfake and also the policies and technologies to combat deepfake. This chapter describes in detail about the ethical, legal and social implications.
Keywords: deepfake; cybersecurity; AI; detection; countermeasures; ethics; policy

title: Mathematics in Cryptography, Cybersecurity, and Blockchain Technology
authors: Nirmla Deshmane
venue: International Journal For Multidisciplinary Research
Tags: Digital Security; Mathematical Principles; Decentralized Systems; Data Integrity; Public-Key Cryptography
abstract: The growth of cryptocurrencies and blockchain technology has spawned a massive revolution in the traditional banking and financial system. The trend in modern digital transactions is towards platforms that are transparent, secure, and decentralized. Now blockchains and cryptocurrencies are actively used in order to provide reliable financial communication and data exchange, but their effectiveness and safety depend on the properly developed mathematical principles. Mathematics forms the foundation of functionality, reliability, and security that blockchain and cryptography systems rely on. An example of such cryptographic hash functions is that they can ensure the integrity and immutability of data in blockchain records, which makes any change of the information stored in blockchain records extremely hard without being detected and therefore protects the system against tampering and cyber threats. Digital signatures and public-key cryptography ensure safe user authentication and validation of transactions in the decentralized networks. Another critical aspect of blockchain technology that is based on the mathematical modelling is consensus mechanisms. Conventional methods like Proof of Work (PoW) require significant processing power, which other protocols like Proof of Stake are significantly more energy efficient, while as transactions are authenticated not by the number of computational resources but by the number of digital assets one owns. These techniques reduce energy use and encourage greater involvement and sustainability in the network. In addition to cryptographic primitives, mathematical primitives, such as error-correcting codes, are used to protect blockchain data both in transit and in storage against either accidental corruption or intentional malicious attacks. The idea of game theory is also used to understand the behaviour of participants in decentralized networks, hence promoting cooperation and discouraging fraudulent actions. Homomorphic encryption techniques allow computation of encrypted data without revealing sensitive information and, therefore, improve privacy in blockchain-based systems. In the modern digital world that is highly dependent on data, there has been a sharp rise in the issue of data privacy, data security, and data trust. Data breaches and cyberattacks are a threat of serious concern to both individuals and organizations. As a result, cybersecurity has become an essential factor in the context of the contemporary digital realm, whether it is internet banking and cloud computing or digital communication platforms. The security of confidentiality, integrity, and authentication of digital information is based on cryptography. In its simplest form, cryptography is based on fields of mathematics, including number theory, algebra, probability, and discrete mathematics. These basic principles are the cornerstones of safe communication networks and online technologies. Therefore, mathematics is not only an abstract endeavour but also a practical tool that enables safe digital transformation. The paper will aim at exploring the connections between mathematics, cryptography, blockchain technology, and cybersecurity. It explains the role played by mathematical concepts in ensuring safe information processing, privacy-sensitive communication, and decentralized transaction systems. The better comprehension of these connections can prepare researchers, developers, and educators to understand the practical value of mathematics in the new digital technologies and come up with more relevant solutions for a safer, data-driven world.
Keywords: Cryptography; Blockchain; Cybersecurity; Mathematics; Data Privacy; Digital Transformation

title: Deep Learning and Neural Networks in Cybersecurity
authors: Ashish Avasthi; Namrata Laxman Jogi; S. Nandhini Devi; D. J. Samatha Naidu; T. Balachander; Rakesh K. Kadu; V. Bhoopathy
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: Cybersecurity; Deep Learning; Intrusion Detection; Threat Detection
abstract: As the internet has evolved rapidly in recent decades, so has concern over more widespread and sophisticated cyberattacks. Data needed an effective Intrusion Detection System (IDS), and Machine Learning (ML) and Deep Learning were one of the best approaches to solve this problem. This article examined IDS and ML and DL learning methods to prevent data leaks. The essay discusses ML and DL developments in IDS building. Network implementations, application learning methods, and datasets are covered. Traditional defences are failing to combat advanced persistent attacks, polymorphic malware, and sophisticated social engineering methods. DL and NNs can evaluate complex and high-dimensional data to detect, prevent, and respond to cyberattacks in real time. DL in cybersecurity is examined in this chapter, including key usage, designs, issues, and future advances.
Keywords: Deep Learning; Neural Networks; Cybersecurity; Intrusion Detection Systems; Machine Learning

title: The Role of Red Teams in Cybersecurity
authors: Hakkı Yılgın; Gurkan Tuna
venue: Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing in Cybersecurity
Tags: Red Team Operations; Cyber Threats; Security Measures; Vulnerability Scanning; Nessus
abstract: This study focuses on ethical hacking practices aimed at enhancing the security of digital assets, with particular emphasis on red-team operations and associated remediation strategies. It highlights the necessity of proactive security measures in response to evolving cyber threats, emphasising the importance of timely vulnerability remediation. The primary objective of this research is to evaluate ethical hacking practices through a representative red-team engagement based on recognised penetration-testing standards. The experiment was conducted within a controlled personal network and a virtualised environment. The chapter presents the installation and configuration of the required security tools, the execution of red-team activities, and the vulnerability-scanning process carried out using Nessus. In addition, mitigation strategies are proposed for the identified security weaknesses, with particular attention given to vulnerabilities associated with exposed or misconfigured network ports.
Keywords: Red Teams; Cybersecurity; Ethical Hacking; Vulnerability Remediation; Penetration Testing

title: Strengthening Business Defenses With Quantum AI-Driven Cybersecurity
authors: Riya Sen; Rajesh Kanna Rajendran; Deepthi Das
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: Quantum AI; Cyber Defense; Data Protection; Threat Landscape
abstract: In today's competitive world, businesses are under constant pressure and are racing against each other to protect their systems from any attacks that may cause the loss of their data assets. One of the most rapidly growing advancements in this domain is the combination of quantum computing and artificial intelligence, which together form what experts now call quantum AI. This technology doesn't just give promises on stronger cyber security but also redefines it. Quantum AI provides faster threat detection, adaptive responses, and the development of encryption methods to fight even quantum-powered attacks. Recent reviews, including the QUASAR framework and quantum-safe protocols, emphasize how organizations can prepare now by mapping their cryptographic assets, adopting post-quantum algorithms, and integrating AI-driven monitoring tools. Both technical security and strategic and regulatory advantages in an increasingly complex threat landscape.
Keywords: Quantum Computing; Artificial Intelligence; Cybersecurity; Threat Detection; Encryption; Post-Quantum Algorithms

title: AI-Driven Cybersecurity for Detecting Organ Trafficking Networks
authors: Chinmayee Vijaykumar Mali; Gitanjali Rahul Shinde; Grishma Bobhate; Sonal Fatangare; Prashant Dhotre; Piyush Gawali
venue: Organ Trafficking Prevention in the Healthcare Sector
Tags: cybersecurity; healthcare; anomaly detection; blockchain; ethical governance
abstract: The digitization of healthcare has improved efficiency but exposed patient data to new cyber risks exploited by organ trafficking networks. Stolen medical records hold lasting value, enabling identity fraud and falsified donor-recipient data. This chapter explores how Artificial Intelligence (AI) can strengthen cybersecurity by detecting anomalies in electronic health records and predicting insider threats. It proposes a Co-Creation Framework combining AI, blockchain, and ethical governance through collaboration among clinicians, technologists, and policymakers. Real-world cases, including Hyderabad's Jeevandan Program and Kenya's Mediheal Hospital, highlight the urgency of AI-driven, transparent, and accountable systems that protect data integrity and help prevent organ trafficking while maintaining patient trust.
Keywords: AI-driven cybersecurity; organ trafficking networks; healthcare digitization; data integrity; identity fraud

title: Co-evolutionary dynamics of attack and defence in cybersecurity
authors: Adeela Bashir; Zia Ush Shamszaman; Zhao Song; The Anh Han
venue: Knowledge-Based Systems
Tags: cyber strategy; risk management; defender dynamics; attack frequency
abstract: In the evolving digital landscape, it is crucial to study the dynamics of cyberattacks and defences. This study uses an Evolutionary Game Theory (EGT) framework to investigate the evolutionary dynamics of attacks and defences in cyberspace. We develop a two-population asymmetric game between attacker and defender to capture the essential factors of costs, potential benefits, and the probability of successful defences. Through mathematical analysis and numerical simulations, we find that systems with high defence intensities (at least 80%) show stability with minimal attack frequencies (at most 10%), whereas low-defence environments (lower than 50%) show instability and are vulnerable to attacks. We simulate 100,000 randomly sampled games and observe three key results: (i) the defend and attack equilibrium remains stable in 39.8% of configurations; (ii) increasing the defence success rate from 0.2 to 0.8 reduces the frequency of successful attacks by nearly 50%; and (iii) in over 80% of sampled games the system converges to a stable boundary equilibrium, indicating robust evolutionary dynamics. We validate these outcomes using a public dataset of real-world cyber incidents (2004–2020). Our theoretical findings align with this historical data, demonstrating the interdisciplinary impact, such as fraud detection, risk management and cybersecurity decision-making. Our EGT framework uniquely captures co-evolving attacker-defender populations, achieves stable equilibrium outcomes, and demonstrates robustness through large-scale random game analysis and social welfare evaluation. Overall, our analysis suggests that adaptive cybersecurity strategies based on EGT can improve resource allocation, enhance system resilience, and reduce the overall risk of cyberattacks. By incorporating real-world data, this study demonstrates the applicability of EGT in addressing the evolving nature of cyber threats and the need for secure digital ecosystems through strategic planning and proactive defence measures.
Keywords: Evolutionary Game Theory; cybersecurity; attack and defence dynamics; system stability; real-world cyber incidents

title: AI-Powered Intrusion Detection and Privacy-Preserving Mechanisms in Cybersecurity
authors: Vikas Sharma; Puneet Chauhan; Tarun Kumar Vashishth; Pushpendra Kumar Verma; Shashiraj Teotia
venue: Advances in Computational Intelligence and Robotics
Tags: cybersecurity; AI; intrusion detection; privacy; vulnerabilities
abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in cybersecurity has revolutionized intrusion detection and response mechanisms. This chapter explores AI-driven intrusion detection systems (IDS) and the role of adversarial machine learning in cybersecurity, highlighting both opportunities and vulnerabilities. It delves into privacy-preserving AI techniques that enhance data security while mitigating risks posed by sophisticated cyber threats. Additionally, the chapter examines the challenges of securing AI-driven systems against adversarial attacks, emphasizing the need for explainable AI in ensuring transparency. The discussion includes case studies on AI-driven cyberattacks and privacy-enhancing strategies for securing sensitive data. Future directions for AI-powered cybersecurity solutions are also explored to establish robust defense mechanisms against evolving threats.
Keywords: AI-driven intrusion detection; privacy-preserving techniques; adversarial machine learning; data security; cyber threats; explainable AI

title: Advanced Adaptive Control Strategies for Fault Tolerance and Cybersecurity in Autonomous Vehicles
authors: Mahmoud Hussein; Qingsong Wang; Zhaoheng Liu; Youmin Zhang
venue: IEEE Transactions on Industrial Electronics
Tags: adaptive control; cyber-physical systems; real-time experiments; vehicle safety
abstract: As autonomous vehicles play an increasingly vital role in critical sectors such as transportation, logistics, and defense, ensuring their operational safety and security becomes paramount. These vehicles are susceptible to both physical faults, such as actuator failures, and cyberattacks, including denial-of-service, deception, and replay attacks. Traditional fault-tolerant control (FTC) systems focus on physical faults but often overlook cyber threats that can compromise vehicle safety and performance. This article presents an adaptive FTC framework that integrates an intrusion detection and protection system with control design to address these challenges. The framework enables real-time threat detection and dynamic control adaptation to ensure vehicle resilience under compromised conditions. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through real-time experiments with Quanser QCar vehicles, confirming its capability to mitigate cyber–physical threats. This work advances secure autonomous systems by providing a comprehensive solution addressing both physical and cyber vulnerabilities, thereby enhancing overall safety and security.
Keywords: autonomous vehicles; fault tolerance; cybersecurity; intrusion detection; control systems

title: Managing Cybersecurity in the Water Sector: When the Human Factor Does Matter
authors: Laura Arantegui; Steven Kemp; Ignasi Rodriguez-Roda
venue: Journal of Water Resources Planning and Management
Tags: cybersecurity; critical infrastructure; threat analysis; digitalization
abstract: The water sector is considered critical due to its essential role in human life and the severe consequences that may arise from supply disruptions or compromised water quality. The increasing digitalization and connectivity within the sector and its supply chain, along with the recent inclusion of the wastewater domain in cybersecurity regulations, present new challenges for addressing cyberattacks and their consequences. However, empirical research on these issues is scarce. Decisions regarding the management of water cybersecurity depend on professionals; thus, through interviews with 15 professionals in the sector, this study analyzes the perspectives of various Spanish water cybersecurity professionals regarding how cybersecurity management is conducted, how the sector responds to cyber threats, the significance of the regulatory framework, and potential future challenges. The importance of human factors in the management of water cybersecurity is the topic on which there is the greatest consensus among all participants.
Keywords: water cybersecurity; human factors; cyber threats; regulatory framework; Spanish water sector

authors: Mayur Jariwala
venue: Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing in Cybersecurity

abstract: As cyber threats evolve in scale and complexity, ethical hacking must also advance beyond traditional approaches. This chapter explores how artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) are revolutionizing penetration testing, from reconnaissance and vulnerability assessment to social engineering and blue teaming. It examines real-world applications, adversarial AI risks, and the ethical boundaries of automated attacks. The chapter also highlights regulatory implications and emerging trends such as explainable AI and autonomous red teaming. It provides a forward-looking perspective on how AI can responsibly augment cybersecurity practices in both offensive and defensive contexts.
Keywords: AI; Machine Learning; Ethical Hacking; Penetration Testing; Cybersecurity

authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti

abstract: Abstract: Cybersecurity in the Age of AI: Adaptive Defense Strategies for Smart and Connected Systems develops a comprehensive scholarly framework for designing, evaluating, governing, and scaling AI-enabled cyber defense across increasingly interconnected digital, physical, and institutional environments. The manuscript treats cybersecurity as an adaptive research domain in which uncertainty, adversarial behavior, data quality, organizational decision making, and public accountability must be analyzed together. It progresses from foundational concepts and research design to statistical explanation, causal inference, machine-learning prediction, secure data engineering, reproducible MLOps, sectoral deployment, and governance strategy. title: Comparative Legal Analysis of Civil Liability for Cybersecurity Violations by Participants in International Commercial Arbitration
authors: Begaim Kaibyldaeva
venue: Uzbek Journal of Law and Digital Policy
Tags: cybersecurity violations; international law; arbitration; legal standards; liability analysis
abstract: This study examines the civil liability of participants in international commercial arbitration arising from cybersecurity violations. As arbitration proceedings increasingly migrate to digital platforms, they become vulnerable to cyber threats, including data breaches, unauthorized access, and ransomware attacks. The research applies a comparative legal methodology, analyzing frameworks from the European Union, the United States, the United Kingdom, and selected Asian jurisdictions. The findings reveal that existing arbitration rules and national laws inadequately address cybersecurity liability, creating enforcement gaps and accountability ambiguities. The study identifies three primary liability categories: institutional, arbitrator, and party and counsel liability, each governed by distinct legal standards. The analysis demonstrates that harmonized international standards are essential for effective regulation. The study concludes by recommending the adoption of cybersecurity-specific provisions within major arbitral institutions' rules and the development of a model international convention on arbitration cybersecurity liability.
Keywords: cybersecurity; civil liability; international arbitration; digital platforms; data breaches; legal analysis

title: Artificial intelligence-driven smart grid optimization: A comprehensive review of machine learning, renewable integration, and cybersecurity applications
authors: Burak Gülmez
venue: Energy Conversion and Management: X
Tags: energy management; load forecasting; intrusion detection; computational challenges; research gaps
abstract: • Comprehensive synthesis of 205 AI studies across smart grid optimization domains. • Machine learning achieves < 2% MAPE in load forecasting under optimal conditions. • Cybersecurity frameworks demonstrate > 98% intrusion detection accuracy. • Computational footprint and scalability barriers challenge operational deployment. • Research gaps persist in safety verification and adversarial robustness. Smart grid modernization necessitates advanced computational approaches addressing renewable variability, distributed control, and cybersecurity challenges that exceed traditional methodologies. This review synthesizes 208 peer-reviewed publications (2020–2026) examining artificial intelligence applications across smart grid optimization and energy management. Machine learning architectures—including convolutional neural networks, recurrent networks, transformers, and hybrid ensembles—demonstrated load forecasting accuracy improvements with reported mean absolute percentage errors below 2% in optimal conditions. Deep reinforcement learning enabled autonomous control policies achieving cost reductions and emission minimizations across simulated environments, though transferability to operational systems requires validation. Renewable integration benefited from AI-enhanced forecasting, energy storage optimization, and microgrid coordination, with case studies reporting operational cost reductions ranging from 3.77% to 55%. Cybersecurity applications achieved intrusion detection accuracies exceeding 98%, though adversarial robustness against sophisticated attacks remains partially characterized. Emerging technologies—digital twins, large language models, federated learning—present opportunities alongside uncertainties regarding deployment timelines. Challenges span computational complexity, data quality limitations, scalability barriers, and environmental sustainability concerns as AI energy consumption potentially offsets efficiency gains. Research gaps persist across safety verification, explainability guarantees, multi-objective optimization frameworks, and lifecycle impact assessments. Successful deployment requires balancing technological capabilities with regulatory frameworks, workforce development, and stakeholder acceptance across diverse institutional contexts.
Keywords: smart grid; artificial intelligence; machine learning; cybersecurity; renewable energy; optimization

title: Shaping the future of cybersecurity: The convergence of AI, quantum computing, and ethical frameworks for a secure digital era
authors: Menahil Khawar; Sohail Khalid; Mujeeb Ur Rehman; Aminu Usman; Wajdan Al Malwi; Fatima Asiri
venue: Computer Science Review
Tags: cybersecurity; quantum technology; ethical governance; malware defense; AI models
abstract: The increasing sophistication and frequency of cyber threats have rendered conventional protection strategies inadequate. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is becoming central to modern cybersecurity, strengthening capabilities in vulnerability assessment, malware detection, phishing prevention, intrusion detection, and deception technologies. Simultaneously, quantum computing introduces both challenges to classical cryptography and opportunities for new forms of quantum-enhanced defenses. This review integrates advances in AI, quantum methods, and ethical governance to provide an integrated perspective on the future of secure digital systems. It evaluates state-of-the-art AI models, including explainable frameworks and quantum-inspired approaches, such as Quantum Convolutional Neural Networks and Quantum Support Vector Machines, along with recent progress in post-quantum cryptography. Ethical concerns, particularly bias, transparency, privacy, and accountability, are examined as essential foundations for trustworthy cybersecurity design in system-on-chip and embedded AI environments. In addition to technical developments, this study considers regulatory frameworks, governance structures, and societal expectations, highlighting the need for responsible and adaptive approaches. A comparative SWOT analysis outlines the strengths, limitations, and areas for cross-domain integration. Finally, a roadmap of future research directions is presented, aligning AI-driven defenses, quantum resilience, and ethical safeguards into flexible and reliable cybersecurity architectures. By linking the technological, ethical, and policy dimensions, this review offers a consolidated foundation to guide the evolution of cybersecurity in a globally connected era.
Keywords: AI in cybersecurity; quantum computing; ethical frameworks; vulnerability assessment; malware detection; phishing prevention; quantum cryptography

title: The effect of cybersecurity on critical infrastructure in the United States of America: A review of current state to future state in relation to industry 4.0
authors: Oluwaseyi Adedeji Adeniyan
venue: Global Journal of Engineering and Technology Advances
Tags: cyber risks; national security; automation; interconnectivity; mitigation strategies
abstract: The rapid evolution of Industry 4.0 technologies—including Artificial Intelligence (AI), Industrial Internet of Things (IIOT), and digital twin systems—has significantly transformed critical infrastructure in the United States. While these technologies enhance operational efficiency, resilience, and automation, they simultaneously introduce new cybersecurity vulnerabilities that pose unprecedented risks to national security and public safety. This comprehensive review examines the current cybersecurity landscape within U.S. critical infrastructure sectors and explores future developments in relation to Industry 4.0 adoption. Drawing from recent literature spanning 2020-2024, the study evaluates threats, vulnerabilities, and mitigation strategies across cyber-physical systems (CPS), industrial control systems (ICS), and digital twin environments. The findings reveal that increasing interconnectivity, lack of standardization, and evolving threat actors pose substantial risks to infrastructure sectors including energy, transportation, healthcare, and water systems. Recent incidents indicate that 85% of critical infrastructure operators have experienced at least one significant cyber incident in the past three years, with average recovery costs exceeding $4.2 million per incident. The paper further outlines emerging solutions, including AI-driven security frameworks, zero-trust architectures, and predictive analytics capabilities. Ultimately, the research emphasizes that proactive cybersecurity integration is essential to ensure resilience, national security, and sustainable advancement toward Industry 4.0 implementation.
Keywords: cybersecurity; critical infrastructure; Industry 4.0; cyber vulnerabilities; cyber-physical systems; AI-driven security; zero-trust architecture

The von Neumann bottleneck—separating memory from processing—consumes the majority of energy in modern AI systems. This pillar conceptualizes a unified computing fabric where data processing and storage occur within the same physical medium, utilizing light-based computation and resistive state retention. This eliminates redundant data transfer, dramatically reducing energy consumption while increasing throughput.

#### 2.5. Hierarchical Verification Protocol
Trust in autonomous systems requires transparent, externally verifiable safety guarantees. This pillar establishes a multi-tier verification structure:

#### 2.6. Hardware-Anchored Corrigibility
Software-level safety measures can be bypassed or modified by advanced systems. title: Client-Centred Cybercrime Training: A Scottish SME Case Study
authors: Juraj Šikra; Karen Renaud; D. Thomas
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: cybersecurity; training; small businesses; Scotland
abstract: The UK's neoliberal government cyber responsibilises Small-to-Medium enterprises (SMEs), meaning that they receive advice but little direct support if they fall victim to a cyber attack. Possibly as a direct consequence, SMEs tend not to report falling victim to cybercrimes. The aim of this research was to develop, deliver, and evaluate a client centred cybercrime training session with an accompanying booklet as means of engendering post-attack closure, upskilling, enhancing knowledge and improving reporting incidence. We surveyed nine staff of an attacked SME to elicit their training preferences; six staff members subsequently attended and five supplied feedback in the form of a post-training survey. Two staff members were also interviewed. We provide a list of five guidelines that were derived from our experiences in delivering this training. It became clear that the UK government's responsibilization of Scottish SMEs did indeed appear to deter staff from reporting cybercrimes to Police Scotland.
Keywords: cybercrime training; SMEs; reporting incidents; neoliberalism; UK government

title: AN ASSESSMENT OF TRANSNATIONAL CRIME IN THE AFRICAN CONTEXT: TRENDS, CHALLENGES, AND STRATEGIC RESPONSES
authors: Dr. John Motsamai Modise
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Government Data; News Media; Forums & Communities; Other
Tags: crime trends; security cooperation; policy analysis; community resilience
abstract: Abstract: This study seeks to critically examine the scope, causes, and consequences of transnational crime in the African context,and to assess the adequacy of regional and continental policy responses. It aims to provide actionable, evidence-based strategies that can enhance cooperation, law enforcement capacity, and community resilience across African states. Transnational organised crime presents a rising threat to Africa’s development, peace, and governance. It is fueled by weak border control, political instability, institutional fragility, corruption, and socio-economic exclusion. Despite the existence of frameworks such as the AU Continental Strategy for Combating Transnational Organised Crime (2023) and SADC’s 2023–2027 Strategic Plan, implementation remains fragmented and under-resourced. Criminal networks exploit legal and institutional loopholes across regions, undermining state authority, rule of law, and citizen safety (UNODC, 2023; Global Initiative, 2024). Criminal syndicates have diversified across Africa, with drug trafficking, human trafficking, cybercrime, arms smuggling, and environmental crimes rising sharply in the last decade. Institutional corruption and poor coordination between states are major enablers. Youth unemployment and poverty are primary recruitment drivers into criminal economies. Cybercrime is an emerging frontier, with most African states ill-equipped to respond. Regional strategies exist, but face gaps in harmonisation, funding, and data sharing. This research contributes to transnational crime scholarship by offering a context-specific, African-led perspective, integrating criminological, political, and developmental insights. It identifies actionable policy reforms and proposes a collaborative regional security model grounded in legal harmonisation, intelligence coordination, and community resilience. It supports Agenda 2063 and the Sustainable Development Goals (particularly SDG 16). The study will adopt a qualitative research design, combining desktop policy analysis, regional case studies, and thematic content analysis of secondary data. Key sources include AU, UNODC, Interpol, and civil society reports from 2021–2024. Expert interviews may be used to validate findings from regional security practitioners.Systematic Approach using a multi-level analytical framework, the study will: Map key types and routes of transnational crime inAfrica, examine political-economic drivers and governance failures, Analyse the effectiveness of continental and regional institutional responses, and propose practical, implementable policy solutions for AU member states. Transnational crime is no longer a peripheral issue in Africa it is central to the continent’s governance, peace, and development trajectory. This study demonstrates that combating it requires a whole-of-continent approach, integrating law enforcement, legal reform, economic inclusion, and regional solidarity. Without decisive and coordinated action, Africa risks deeper criminal infiltration, weakened governance, and stunted social progress. This research equips stakeholders with the knowledge and tools necessary to disrupt criminal networks and build a safer, more resilient continent.
Keywords: transnational crime; Africa; cybercrime; law enforcement; regional security; policy reforms

title: I Know What You Played Last Summer: Evaluating the Feasibility of Privacy Attacks in Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games
authors: Parisa Rahimi; George Spary; Amit Kumar Singh; Seyedali Pourmoafi; Xiaohang Wang; Alexios Mylonas
venue: Electronics
Tags: cybersecurity; gamification; malware; social engineering; online gaming
abstract: Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games (MMORPGs) increasingly rely on player-developed third-party tools to extend functionality and personalise gameplay, creating a complex software ecosystem that introduces both usability benefits and security risks. This study investigates whether such tools can be exploited as an attack vector for cybercrime by designing and implementing a proof-of-concept add-on within a widely deployed commercial MMORPG using its native scripting and application programming interface. The developed tool supports automated player discovery, chat capture, target inspection, and local data persistence, enabling a systematic evaluation of how cyber-assisted and cyber-dependent crimes could be facilitated within the game client. Empirical testing demonstrates that while the platform’s protected execution model and interface restrictions prevent direct credential theft and remote code execution, the add-on architecture allows extensive behavioural data collection and social-engineering-relevant monitoring, making several forms of cyber-enabled crime technically feasible. These findings show that MMORPG add-on frameworks represent a non-trivial socio-technical attack vector in next-generation online platforms, where security depends not only on code isolation, but also on how user-generated extensions interact with human behaviour. The results highlight the need for architecture-aware security controls and governance mechanisms to mitigate emerging threats in large-scale, extensible virtual environments.
Keywords: MMORPG; privacy attacks; cybercrime; player tools; data collection

title: ARCANE: Cross-Campaign Attacker Re-identification via Passive Beacon Telemetry -- A Bayesian Network Framework for Longitudinal Cyber Attribution
authors: Abraham Itzhak Weinberg
venue: ArXiv.org
Tags: abstraction; longitudinal data; adversary fingerprints; data analysis; cybersecurity
abstract: Current cyber attribution approaches typically operate on a per-incident basis, leaving open whether aggregating evidence across campaigns improves adversary identification. We investigate whether cross-campaign attribution reduces ambiguity or whether structural limits persist under longitudinal data. We model adversary fingerprints as multi-dimensional feature vectors encoding behavioral, infrastructural, and temporal characteristics derived from covert beacon interactions. We introduce ARCANE (Attacker Re-identification via Cross-campaign Attribution Network), a probabilistic framework that aggregates passive telemetry across campaigns and organizations to construct persistent adversary fingerprints. These fingerprints are updated using a Bayesian belief network that integrates new evidence over time. A time-decayed confidence metric captures accumulated similarity across campaigns. Evaluation on a synthetic dataset of multiple threat profiles shows that intra-actor similarity consistently exceeds inter-actor similarity. However, separation between distinct actors remains limited due to shared operational practices among sophisticated adversaries. Results indicate that cross-campaign aggregation alone does not resolve attribution ambiguity. Performance is constrained by a structural ceiling in feature space, where inter-actor similarity remains high even without evasion. Attribution accuracy remains stable under increasing evasion, suggesting the main limitation is feature indistinguishability rather than adversarial adaptation. These findings highlight the need for additional signal classes, such as targeting patterns, temporal coordination, and infrastructure relationships, to improve attribution reliability.
Keywords: cyber attribution; Bayesian network; cross-campaign; adversary identification; telemetry

title: Preliminary vascular plant checklist of the city of Chattanooga
authors: Matthew J Scott
venue: UTC Scholar (University of Tennessee at Chattanooga)
Tags: flora; checklist; herbarium; iNaturalist; Tennessee
abstract: The City of Chattanooga, Tennessee was designated as a National Park City in April 2025 by the National Park City Foundation. Yet, there has not been a comprehensive vascular flora compiled for the city, though there have been extensive collections and observations made of the plant biodiversity in the area from the late 1800s onward. The goal of this project was to examine both the existing herbarium collections and public observation records from iNaturalist to compile a preliminary vascular plant checklist for Chattanooga, and to include conservation and ecological data for the species currently documented to provide a holistic review of the local flora. In the creation of this checklist, 428 species were found to be confirmed in the area by both herbarium voucher specimen and public observation records. 49 species (11.4%) were classified as invasive by the Tennessee Invasive Plant Council. Five species were listed under the Tennessee Rare Plant List including Silphium pinnatifidum (Threatened) and Clematis fremontii (Endangered). 163 species had modeled subnational conservation ranks of S3 (Vulnerable) or lower, with nine designated S1 (Critically Imperiled). The most common wetland indicator status was FACU (Facultative Upland) with 139 species. The average coefficient of conservatism for all species recorded was 4.83, and the average heliophyte index was 6.2. More work is needed to more fully address the vascular plant species checklist for Chattanooga, but this research creates a baseline of thoroughly documented species.
Keywords: Chattanooga; vascular plants; biodiversity; invasive species; conservation; ecological data

abstract: Abstract Cyber security has become a fundamental requirement in modern digital systems due to the rapid expansion of internet-based services, cloud computing, and interconnected technologies. As organizations and individuals increasingly rely on digital platforms for communication, financial transactions, and data storage, the risk of cyber threats has grown significantly. Modern systems are exposed to a wide range of security threats, including malware, phishing, ransomware, denial-of-service attacks, and advanced persistent threats, which can lead to data breaches, financial losses, and disruption of critical services. This paper presents a comprehensive review of cyber security threats in modern systems by examining the different types of attacks, their methodologies, and their impact on organizations and users. It also explores various defense mechanisms such as encryption techniques, authentication methods, firewalls, and intrusion detection systems that are used to protect digital assets. Furthermore, the study discusses key challenges in cyber security, including evolving attack strategies, vulnerabilities in emerging technologies, and the lack of user awareness. title: Privacy-focused artificial intelligence model for detecting deepfake-based cyber threats
authors: Selvavinayagam G.; Guhan E.; Raman A. Sankar; Vanipriya R.; Vinoth S.
venue: World Journal of Advanced Research and Reviews
Tags: AI security; deepfake detection; privacy preservation; cybersecurity
abstract: This paper presents an extended literature survey on deepfake-oriented cyber threats with a strong focus on practical deployment constraints. Although detection accuracy has improved in recent years, real-world adoption remains limited by privacy concerns, hardware requirements, and weak generalization across unseen media conditions. We examine the evolution of deepfake detection from handcrafted forensic cues to deep multimodal architectures, and we discuss why many high-scoring benchmark models fail under operational workloads. The survey highlights a local-first strategy that combines multimodal evidence, interpretable outputs, and resource- aware model design so that robust detection can run on consumer-grade systems. The goal is to support trustworthy, privacy-preserving defense against impersonation fraud, misinformation, and identity abuse in modern digital ecosystems.

title: A Hybrid Approach for Insider Threats Detection Using System Call Analysis and Malware API Monitoring
authors: Pathuri Rama Krishna
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
Tags: Cybersecurity; Intrusion Detection; Anomaly Detection; Predictive Analysis
abstract: Most organizational computer systems rely on user IDs and passwords for authentication. However, the practice of sharing login credentials significantly weakens security and increases the risk of insider threats from authenticated users. While considerable research has focused on external attacks, studies addressing internal intrusions remain limited. This project proposes an Internal Intrusion Detection and Protection System (IIDPS) that employs data mining and machine learning techniques to detect insider threats and provide real-time protection within computer systems. By continuously monitoring user behavior through system call patterns and integrating malware API call detection, IIDPS enhances the identification of suspicious or malicious activities. Advanced machine learning models are used for predictive analysis, enabling the system to adapt and improve over time. A comparative analysis of classification models is conducted to identify the most effective approach, optimizing detection accuracy and minimizing response time. To reinforce the system's effectiveness, IIDPS incorporates real-time alerts to notify administrators of anomalies, facilitating rapid responses to potential security threats. The system is architected for scalability, ensuring it can handle growing volumes of data as organizational needs evolve. Moreover, continuous model updates help IIDPS stay robust against newly emerging insider attack vectors

title: Anomaly detection of cyber threats in industrial IoT networks via hybrid digital twins and continual learning
authors: Andrea Melis; Andrea Piroddi; Chan-Tong Lam; Giovanni Pau; Roberto Girau
venue: Internet of Things
Tags: Industry 4.0; data privacy; intrusion detection; adaptive systems
abstract: • Hybrid digital twins secure IIoT while preserving data privacy • Continual learning adapts models to new threats with low data needs • Hardware-in-the-loop validates detection under realistic conditions • Achieves 97% accuracy with 20 × less training data than full retraining • Scalable framework for resilient anomaly detection in Industry 4.0 The Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) is increasingly exposed to cyber threats due to its tight integration of operational technology and digital connectivity. Traditional intrusion detection systems (IDSs) often struggle with adaptability, false positives, and operational scalability in dynamic, non-stationary environments. This paper proposes a cyber threat detection framework that integrates hybrid digital twins (DTs) with continual learning to enable reliable and adaptive intrusion detection in realistic IIoT settings. The hybrid DTs act as local mirrors of IIoT devices, preserving sensitive data close to the source while supporting controlled validation of firmware updates and configuration changes. The continual learning mechanism enables the detection model to incrementally adapt to evolving traffic patterns and emerging attacks, mitigating catastrophic forgetting without requiring repeated offline retraining. Experimental validation on benchmark datasets and real IIoT traffic shows that the proposed DT-enabled framework supports stable detection performance over time under bounded memory and incremental update constraints, reflecting realistic deployment conditions. The proposed architecture highlights a practical trade-off between offline optimality and online adaptability, offering a robust, scalable solution for securing IIoT infrastructure that balances continuous operation, reliability, and controlled adaptation.
Keywords: cyber threats; IIoT; anomaly detection; hybrid digital twins; continual learning

title: Online Test-Time Adaptation for Shadow Segmentation
authors: Di Wu; Haifeng Xia; Libo Sun; Wenhu Qin; Siyu Xia
venue: ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
Tags: machine learning; computer vision; signal processing; accuracy
abstract: Shadow segmentation is sensitive to illumination shifts and scene diversity. Test-time adaptation provides a source-free solution, yet most methods assume large batches or stationary distributions, limiting online use. We present an online test-time adaptation framework for shadow segmentation, where data arrive sequentially in small batches without revisiting. Our method applies dual-stage filtering: image-level domain scoring with a frozen supervisor, followed by pixel-level soft masking guided by confidence, consistency, and structural cues. A brightness-guided module exploits illumination priors to refine shadow regions, while curriculum-based thresholding and exponential moving average teacher–student updates stabilize adaptation and reduce error accumulation. Experiments across six cross-domain settings on SBU, CUHK-Shadow, and ISTD demonstrate consistent gains over baselines in accuracy and boundary preservation, achieving robust generalization under diverse shifts.
Keywords: shadow segmentation; test-time adaptation; domain adaptation; image processing; illumination shifts

title: Ecological Stressors and Taxonomic Inconsistencies in Indian Freshwater Game Fisheries: A National Review of Biodiversity and Anthropogenic Threats
authors: SHAHIN SHAJAHAN; Suvamoy Maiti
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Biodiversity; Fisheries; Environmental Science; Conservation; India
abstract: Abstract Despite India’s status as a global aquatic biodiversity hotspot, its recreational fisheries remain obscured by fragmented governance and systemic data deficiencies. This study validates 277 game fish species, revealing widespread taxonomic inconsistencies and miscategorized conservation statuses in FishBase and Eschmeyer's Catalog of Fishes. Marine environments support the highest species richness (161 native taxa), whereas freshwater systems disproportionately harbor Endangered and Vulnerable species at risk of regional decline. Significant taxonomic discrepancies-outdated, incorrect, or unverified species names coincide with a high prevalence of Data Deficient and Not Evaluated IUCN statuses, particularly among 26 freshwater taxa, suggesting that many high-value native species, including members of Carangidae, Lutjanidae, and Cyprinidae, may be experiencing “invisible” declines that escape current conservation oversight. Ecological pressures are further amplified by an oxythermal habitat squeeze, where rising temperatures and benthic hypoxia constrain survival space for sensitive species such as mahseer, alongside technological overexploitation and invasive species–driven biotic homogenization (e.g., Clarias gariepinus and Oreochromis niloticus) . We advocate basin-scale governance and community-led stewardship to reconcile fragmented data, strengthen conservation frameworks, and safeguard India’s aquatic heritage from largely invisible declines, alongside enhanced data mobilization through platforms such as the Ocean Biodiversity Information System to improve transparency, accessibility, and long-term monitoring.
Keywords: Indian Freshwater Fisheries; Biodiversity; Taxonomic Inconsistencies; Ecological Stressors; Conservation Status

title: Gradient Boosting for Online Two-Stage Adaptive Group Testing
authors: Malcolm Egan; Alix Jeannerot; Lélio Chetot; Jean-Marie Gorce
venue: ICASSP 2026 - 2026 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP)
Tags: Machine Learning; Statistical Analysis; Signal Processing; Group Testing
abstract: We consider an online two-stage Bayesian group testing protocol. In the first stage, a Bayesian estimator is utilized to identify active items. In the second stage, a subset of the items are verified. The key challenge for Bayesian group testing that we address in this paper is imperfect knowledge of the prior distribution. We propose a new scheme based on gradient boosting where the estimator in the first stage utilizes convex combinations of the posteriors for a set of base estimators exploiting imperfect priors. We analyze the regret and show via a numerical study that our algorithm can outperform a baseline estimator with perfect knowledge of the prior distribution that does not exploit verification.
Keywords: Bayesian Group Testing; Gradient Boosting; Online Learning; Estimation; Adaptive Methods

title: Targeting America's Nuclear Industry: Adversary Cyber Threats to Small Modular Reactors and the Emerging Nuclear Energy Sector
authors: mark, christopher
OSINT_Source_Types: Government Data; News Media; Public Records
Tags: cybersecurity; nuclear sector; adversary analysis; strategic recommendations; SMR technology
abstract:
This paper provides a strategic intelligence assessment of the adversary cyber threat landscape confronting small modular reactor (SMR) developers and advanced nuclear operators. The United States is experiencing its most significant nuclear energy revival since the 1970s, driven by AI-driven data center power demand, energy security imperatives following Russia's weaponization of European gas supplies, and the emergence of SMR technology that promises factory-manufactured, passively safe reactors deployable in years rather than decades. This expansion is occurring against a threat backdrop of extraordinary severity.

Four state adversaries present simultaneous, active cyber threats to the nuclear sector: China's Volt Typhoon and related APT groups have pre-positioned persistent access within U.S. energy infrastructure while systematically targeting SMR intellectual property; North Korea's Andariel/APT45 unit conducts nuclear-focused technology espionage while the Lazarus Group funds the regime's weapons program through energy sector financial attacks; Iran demonstrated current-period nuclear facility intrusion capability in March 2024 and is receiving Russian offensive cyber capability transfers; and Russia has caused actual electricity outages through cyberattacks and integrates energy infrastructure targeting into military doctrine.

The paper introduces the Mark Heptad adversary motivation framework — a seven-driver model distinguishing Financial Gain, Ideology, Espionage, Revenge, Nuisance/Destruction, War/Defense, and Facilitation motivations — and applies it in conjunction with the CIA Triad (Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability) to generate an integrated threat matrix across all adversary categories, including non-state and ideological actors whose documented history of physical intrusions and disinformation campaigns against nuclear licensing proceedings represents an underestimated threat vector. Special attention is given to the SMR-specific attack surface — digital-native architecture, remote monitoring requirements, commercial off-the-shelf software integration, and IT/OT convergence — which differs fundamentally from legacy nuclear plant security and is inadequately addressed by existing regulatory frameworks, particularly 10 CFR 73.54. The role of artificial intelligence as a cross-cutting force multiplier amplifying adversary capabilities across all attack phases is examined. The paper concludes with six strategic recommendations for nuclear energy executives, board risk committees, and chief information security officers.
Keywords: cyber threats; nuclear energy; advanced reactors; threat assessment; AI influence
