title: Strengthening the Transportation Cybersecurity Workforce: A Mixed-Methods Analysis of Workforce Development, Organizational Preparedness and Cross-Sector Collaboration
authors: Amjad Ali; Larry Liu; Blessing Ojeme; Chidozie Anadozie; Fremah Agyemang; Satish Ukkusuri; Eunhan Ka; Shagun Mittal
venue: Future Transportation
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Government Data; News Media
Tags: Cybersecurity; Critical Infrastructure; Operational Technology; Workforce Capacity
abstract: The rapid digitalization of transportation systems has expanded the cyberattack surface of critical infrastructure while exposing significant shortages in transportation-specific cybersecurity workforce capacity. Existing workforce studies rarely integrate transportation-sector workforce development, organizational preparedness, operational technology (OT) challenges, and interdisciplinary collaboration within a unified analytical framework. In response to this gap, this study employs a mixed-methods approach that integrates Term Frequency–Inverse Document Frequency (TF-IDF) text analysis of publicly available workforce development documents, qualitative interviews with academics, policymakers, and transportation cybersecurity professionals, and organizational survey analysis to examine workforce development challenges across transportation subsectors. The findings reveal persistent information technology (IT) and operational technology (OT) competency gaps, curriculum–industry misalignment, organizational staffing shortages, disparities in cybersecurity preparedness, and the critical importance of experiential learning and dedicated cybersecurity staffing. The study further emphasizes the need for interdisciplinary education, organizational capacity building, and sustained collaboration among academia, government, and industry to strengthen the transportation cybersecurity workforce’s readiness and resilience. Collectively, the findings position transportation cybersecurity workforce development as a systems-coordination challenge that requires long-term strategic investment, cross-sector collaboration, and workforce innovation to enhance the security, resilience, and operational continuity of transportation systems.

title: Securing Ethiopia's Digital Government EcosystemthroughaContext-Aware Cybersecurity Framework for the MesobEcosystemunder the Digital Ethiopia 2030 Strategy
authors: Tilahun Ejigu Belay; Shalu Gupta

abstract: Ethiopia is making rapid strides towards digital transformation under the Digital Ethiopia 2030 (DE2030) Strategybyexpanding digital government services, interoperable platforms and applications, and cloud computing, digital identitysystems, and integrated public service infrastructures. The Mesob Digital Collaboration Ecosystemhas becomeastrategic platform that allows for the secure collaboration, sharing of information and coordinated provisioningof services between government institutions and stakeholders. At the same time as growing connectivity among digital systems has opened doors for new opportunities, it has also opened the door for cyber threats like data breaches, ransomware attacks, unauthorized access, API vulnerabilities and attacks against critical national infrastructure. This paper proposes a Context-Aware Cybersecurity Framework that would enhance the security, resiliencyandinteroperability of Ethiopia's digital government ecosystem. The framework encompasses adaptive security featuressuch as Zero Trust Architecture, Identity and Access Management (IAM), secure interoperability security, continuousmonitoring, threat intelligence, and risk-based access control, all designed to tackle the evolving nature of cybersecurity in today's interconnected digital landscape. The framework proposed has the potential to contribute to a secure and stable digital governance, the protectionof critical digital infrastructures, and the sustainable digital transformation process, as outlined in the DE2030 strategy. It also offers a localized cybersecurity model which is aligned to Ethiopia's technological, institutional and digital governance context to increase cyber resilience and build trust in digital public services

title: Balancing cybersecurity, wireless charging, and safety: Digital twin-driven techno-economic analysis of electric vehicles
authors: Shameem Hasan; Abu M. Fuad; B.M. Khalid Hasan Drobo; Md. Reshad Al Muttaki; Sadia Afrin; Alvi Ibn Amzad Anil; Omar Farrok
venue: Energy Conversion and Management: X
Tags: cybersecurity risks; AI intrusion detection; environmental sustainability; multi-layer defense
abstract: Widespread decarbonization of global transportation necessitates electric vehicles; nevertheless, greater connectivity renders them vulnerable to cybersecurity risks. This study presents the first integrated framework simultaneously addressing cybersecurity, wireless charging safety, techno-economic performance, and environmental sustainability. The critical findings from this study are identified as follows: levelized energy costs are found to range from USD 0.004 to USD 0.237/kWh; a 99.4 % accuracy is achieved by AI-powered intrusion detection; annual CO 2 reductions reaching 435,884 kg in optimal configurations are observed; and novel threats, including oscillatory load attacks and harmonic injection, are shown to be introduced by wireless charging. Digital twin analysis reveals that optimal cybersecurity investment occurs at a 0.10 security level, yielding 652.9 % return on investment. Multi-layer defense architecture proves essential, with battery management systems requiring a minimum of three-layer protection, achieving 68.7 % effectiveness. The study demonstrates that cybersecurity, wireless charging safety, economic feasibility, and environmental performance cannot be optimized independently. Integrated security-by-design approaches with regulatory baseline standards and regional cost adjustments enable sustainable EV commercialization while maintaining grid stability and consumer trust.
Keywords: cybersecurity; electric vehicles; digital twin; techno-economic analysis; wireless charging

title: Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing Handbook: A Practical Guide to Cybersecurity Assessment, Vulnerability Analysis, and Ethical Hacking Methodologies

abstract: Ethical Hacking and Penetration Testing Handbook is a comprehensive and practical guide designed for students, educators, researchers, IT professionals, and cybersecurity enthusiasts who want to develop a strong foundation in ethical hacking, penetration testing, and cybersecurity assessment. This book provides a systematic understanding of modern cybersecurity concepts, from the fundamentals of ethical hacking to vulnerability assessment, penetration testing methodologies, security reporting, legal considerations, and emerging technologies. Each chapter is written in a clear and structured manner, supported by real-world examples, illustrations, tables, and review questions to enhance learning. Whether you are preparing for a cybersecurity career, pursuing academic studies, or seeking to strengthen your organization's security posture, this handbook offers valuable insights into professional security assessment practices and responsible cybersecurity techniques. What You Will Learn • Fundamentals of cybersecurity and ethical hacking principles • Cyber threats, attack methodologies, and hacker classifications • Reconnaissance, footprinting, information gathering, and scanning techniques • Vulnerability assessment and penetration testing methodologies • Authentication security, wireless security, and web application security • Common web vulnerabilities, including SQL Injection, Cross-Site Scripting (XSS), and Cross-Site Request Forgery (CSRF) • Security assessment tools, post-exploitation concepts, and professional reporting • Legal responsibilities, ethical considerations, and cybersecurity compliance frameworks • Emerging technologies such as Artificial Intelligence, Zero Trust Architecture, Cloud Security, and Internet of Things (IoT) Security • Career opportunities and professional development in ethical hacking and cybersecurity Key Features Comprehensive coverage of ethical hacking and penetration testing concepts Easy-to-understand explanations supported by professional figures and tables Real-world case studies and practical examples Review questions and practical exercises for self-assessment Suitable for undergraduate and postgraduate students, faculty members, researchers, and cybersecurity professionals Written with an emphasis on ethical practices, responsible disclosure, and professional cybersecurity standards, this handbook serves as a valuable resource for learning, teaching, research, and career development in the rapidly evolving field of information security.

title: The public health psychological challenges of protecting wastewater treatment plants from cybersecurity criminal risks
authors: Darrell Norman Burrell; Sharon Burton; Calvin Nobles; Allison J. Huff; Won Song; Kylei Conti
venue: Brazilian Journal of Business
Tags: cyber risks; environmental safety; system fragility; information technology; operational technology
abstract: Local wastewater treatment plants have become increasingly vulnerable to cyber intrusions due to rapid digitization, insufficient segmentation, and persistent reliance on legacy industrial control systems. Recent incidents in Florida, Pennsylvania, and Texas demonstrate that malicious actors can remotely manipulate chemical dosing, disable alarms, and disrupt critical operations, creating direct pathways to environmental contamination and acute public health harm. Smaller municipalities, lacking dedicated cybersecurity resources, face disproportionate risk as adversaries increasingly exploit default credentials, vendor access pathways, and converged information technology–operational technology environments. This commentary synthesizes emerging threat trends, highlights the systemic fragility created by inadequate governance and supply-chain oversight, and evaluates the cascading consequences of disruption, including regulatory noncompliance and erosion of public trust. Findings underscore the need for layered controls, cyber-informed engineering practices, and rehearsed incident response to mitigate escalating risks. Securing Supervisory Control and Data Acquisition–enabled wastewater systems is therefore a critical public health and safety imperative.
Keywords: cybersecurity; wastewater treatment; public health; incident response; industrial control systems; cyber intrusions

title: Quantum Cryptography, Quantum Communications and Nano-Enabled Cybersecurity: Global Frameworks for DefenceTech, FinTech and SpaceTech
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti
venue: International Journal of Academic and Industrial Research Innovations(IJAIRI)
Tags: quantum security; cryptography; cybersecurity frameworks; threat modeling; nano-technology
abstract: Abstract: This study develops a scope of analytical framework for integrating quantum cryptography, quantum communications, post-quantum cryptography and nano-enabled hardware security into global cybersecurity architectures for DefenceTech, FinTech and SpaceTech. The research problem is framed by the convergence of three pressures: the long-lived confidentiality exposure created by harvest-now-decrypt-later attacks, the rapid standardization of post-quantum algorithms, and the need for hardware-rooted trust in physically exposed devices, satellites, edge nodes and payment infrastructures. The paper synthesizes quantum key distribution, quantum-network standardization, crypto-agile migration, physical unclonable functions and sectoral governance into a single evaluation model. It uses a public-source calibrated realistic dataset of 18 high-value scenarios across defence, finance and space systems. The dataset is not represented as confidential operational telemetry; rather, it is explicitly constructed from publicly available threat, standards and engineering indicators to support transparent modelling. The methodology combines literature review, structured scenario analysis, weighted risk scoring, residual-risk modelling, expected annual loss estimation and feasibility-sensitive control selection. Mathematical equations are used to express QKD channel attenuation, secret-key-rate intuition, cryptographic migration risk, expected loss and multi-criteria optimization. Results indicate that hybrid PQC adoption produces the broadest near-term risk reduction, QKD offers the strongest value where long-lived secrets and controlled optical paths exist, and nano-enabled roots of trust are especially relevant to contested devices and supply chains. The study proposes a staged global framework in which crypto-agility, hybrid PQC, QKD network governance and nano-PUF attestation are treated as complementary layers rather than competing security paradigms. The conclusion identifies future work in real operational benchmarking, satellite-QKD testbeds, standards-aligned implementation assurance and machine-verifiable security reasoning. title: The Influence of Top Management Support, System Usability, and Cybersecurity Readiness on the Digital HRM Effectiveness of Banking Sector Employees
authors: Kushariyadi Kushariyadi; Iwan Henri Kusnadi; Enny Diah Astuti; Agus Setiono; Ayu Ratna Wulandari; Ahmad Nur Budi Utama
venue: Journal of Information System, Technology and Engineering
Tags: Human Resource Management; Digital Transformation; Cybersecurity
abstract: This study really wants to find out, in a kind of overarching way, how Top Management Support, System Usability, and Cybersecurity Readiness influence the Digital HRM Effectiveness for people working in the banking sector, yes, more or less. The research was conducted in a quantitative manner, through a survey approach aimed at banking workers. Purposive sampling was also used, but somehow it feels like it’s leaning a bit too much on one segment, like it’s overly directed toward that specific group. The data were gathered via an online survey, then processed using multiple linear regression. Before any hypothesis testing could even begin, validity and reliability checks were done, and of course the usual assumption scans were included, like normality, heteroscedasticity, and multicollinearity. So overall, it seems the dataset is a solid match. The findings indicate that Top Management Support, System Usability, and Cybersecurity Readiness all have a positive, and fairly strong impact on Digital HRM Effectiveness. That influence shows up in both partial effects and also, at the same time, through the combined model. Put more plainly, the results suggest that digital HRM in banking tends to be powered by manager backing, system clarity, and cybersecurity preparedness. In the end, this study contributes to the theoretical conversation on digital human resource management and also on how organizations undergo digital transition. It additionally provides hands-on direction for the banking industry, particularly for strengthening the real-world effectiveness of digital-based HRM.

title: Pre-service Teachers’ Digital Leadership Perceptions and Cybersecurity Responsibility: Evaluating A Curriculum Intervention in Resource-Constrained Contexts
authors: Joyce Robertson Kanyerere; Nyarai Tunjera; Agnes Chigona
venue: International Journal of Current Educational Studies
Tags: Education; Cyber Awareness; Digital Citizenship; South Africa; Mixed Methods
abstract: Recent global digital transformations in education have rapidly shifted the focus toward pre-service teachers' roles as digital citizens. Within resource-constrained South African institutions, digital risks are intensified by insecure personal devices. The purpose of this study was to design, implement, and evaluate a focused curriculum intervention to strengthen cybersecurity awareness and perceptions of digital leadership among pre-service teachers through a structured 12-hour, four-module curriculum. This mixed-methods study employed a pre-test/post-test design with 470 pre-service teachers from two South African universities, using a sequential data-collection procedure integrated into the analytical phase. Quantitative data were gathered using the Cybersecurity Awareness Knowledge Test and the Teacher Digital Leadership Perception Scale. Qualitative data from 30 semi-structured interviews were analyzed using thematic analysis. Significant, large-magnitude improvements were observed for cybersecurity knowledge (pre: M=11.47, post: M=19.63, t(469)=34.00, p<0.001, d=2.34) and digital leadership perceptions (pre: M=52.31, post: M=71.28, t(469)=27.90, p<0.001, d=1.86). Qualitative themes highlighted increased risk recognition, enhanced professional self-efficacy, and a strong sense of community responsibility. However, structural constraints moderate the prospective translation of these perceptions into classroom practice. The study concludes that while the intervention significantly enhances baseline knowledge and responsibility dispositions, systemic resource deficits must be addressed to support long-term implementation.
Keywords: Cybersecurity; Digital Leadership; Pre-service Teachers; Curriculum Intervention; Resource-Constrained Contexts

title: Cybersecurity Knowledge Deficits, Information Management Failures, and Organizational Moderators Among Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises in Lagos, Nigeria
authors: Chinonso Njoku Jude; Onyedikachukwu Chukwueke Ugonna
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: SMEs; Cybersecurity; Lagos; Information Management
abstract: Abstract This study evaluated the effect of cybersecurity awareness on the information management practices of small and medium sized enterprises (SMEs) in Lagos, Nigeria. A quantitative descriptive survey design was adopted, with data collected from 331 valid respondents drawn from SMEs across three major Lagos business districts using a multistage stratified sampling technique. The adapted Human Aspects of Information Security Questionnaire (HAIS-Q) served as the primary data collection instrument. Findings revealed a moderate overall cybersecurity awareness level (M = 3.03) among SME employees, with incident reporting constituting the most acutely deficient focus area. Information management practices were found to be broadly inadequate (M = 2.41), with incident response, backup and recovery recording the most severe deficits. A statistically significant, moderately strong positive relationship was established between cybersecurity awareness and information management practices (r = 0.618, p < .001), with awareness accounting for approximately 38% of the variance in practice scores. Hierarchical moderated regression analysis revealed that training availability, leadership support, and formal cybersecurity policy significantly amplify the behavioral dividend of higher awareness levels, while resource constraints attenuate it. The study concluded that awareness is a pivotal but institutionally conditioned determinant of information management quality in Lagos SMEs. Keywords: Cybersecurity awareness, information management practices, Protection Motivation Theory, HAIS-Q

title: Modeling artificial intelligence enabled cybersecurity behavior in the information society using PLS-SEM and artificial neural network approach
authors: Mahfujur Rahman Faraji; Koushik Bandapadya; Md. Mahfuzur Rahman; Sharjil Bin Yousuf; Mohammad Sohel; Md Zainal Abedin; Mohammad Rakibul Islam Bhuiyan
venue: Discover Sustainability
Tags: AI; cybersecurity; behavioral intention; sustainable development
abstract: This study examines how perceived ease of use (PEU), performance expectancy (PE), artificial intelligence (AI) perceptions, perceived vulnerability (PV), and awareness of cybersecurity (ACS) shape behavioral intention and secure information society behavior (ISB) in a developing-economy context. By integrating the three models such as technology acceptance model (TAM), protection motivation theory (PMT), and the unified theory of acceptance and use of technology (UTAUT), the research aligns individual adoption dynamics with SDGs 8, 9, 16, and 17. Adopting a quantitative non-probability convenience-purposive sampling, the research surveys 368 Bangladeshi digital users via an online questionnaires and analyzes the data through a hybrid PLS-SEM and Python-based ANN framework to cover both linear and non-linear effects within an integrated three models. This study provides the first TAM–PMT–UTAUT integration for AI-cybersecurity adoption in Bangladesh (n = 368), revealing performance expectancy (PE) as the dominant awareness of cybersecurity (ACS) predictor, followed by PEU and AI perception. Awareness of cybersecurity (ACS) drives Information Society Behavior (ISB), but perceived vulnerability (PV) unexpectedly weakens this path via threat overload—contrasting high-resource findings—while awareness of cybersecurity proves insignificant. Python-based artificial neural network (ANN) visualizations uncover non-linear patterns, outperforming in predictive validity. These findings offer critical implications for policymakers and developers designing user-centric, AI-enabled security solutions. Ultimately, this research highlights how targeted behavioral interventions and competence-focused training can safeguard critical infrastructure, thereby advancing sustainable development objectives in emerging information societies.
Keywords: artificial intelligence; cybersecurity behavior; technology acceptance model; protection motivation theory; Bangladesh

title: Leadership Activities Aimed at Ensuring Cybersecurity in a General Education School / Vadovų veikla užtikrinant kibernetinį saugumą bendrojo ugdymo mokykoje
authors: Rasa Skališienė; Šarūnė Kazlauskė; Ilona Klanienė; Kęstutis Mockus
venue: Regional Formation and Development Studies
Tags: education; cyber safety; intervention strategies; principal roles
abstract: The article analyses the importance of cybersecurity in schools and the role of the school principal in ensuring a safe digital environment. The study was conducted using semi-structured interviews with principals of general education schools. The research results revealed that educational institutions are increasingly facing cyberthreats, such as phishing emails, malicious links, or misleading messages about alleged dangers. These threats can disrupt the educational process, pose risks to data security, and damage the institution’s reputation. The findings show that school leaders’ activities in ensuring cybersecurity focus on organising preventative and interventional measures, mobilising the community, developing internal procedures and response algorithms, and cooperating with institutions. It was observed that principals often lack experience and feel psychological stress and legal responsibility for potential consequences. Different perspectives on the principal’s role emerged, from that of a key leader to one in which there is a shared community responsibility model. However, there is agreement that effective cybersecurity assurance is based on the principal acting as an educator, threat manager, prevention organiser and community mobiliser, actively involving the entire school community in building a culture of security.

title: Proof-of-Exploit: Cryptographically Verified LLM Cybersecurity Evaluation via Tiered Risk Metrics in the Operational-Risk Framework
authors: Joshua White; Kara Zaffarano; John Stacy; Xiaomin Bian
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy
Tags: Crypto Security; Risk Metrics; Exploit Validation; AI in Cybersecurity; NIST AI RMF
abstract: Existing Large Language Model cybersecurity evaluations rely on text-based plausibility scoring systems that fail to validate operational exploit viability. In this paper, we present the Operational Risk Framework (ORF), advancing beyond our prior MalcodeEval work through three (3) innovations: (1) ECDSA-P384 cryptographic execution validation providing non-repudiable proof-of-exploit, (2) MITRE ATT&CK-aligned tiered scoring with CVSS v4.0-derived severity weights, (3) and six-phase progressive validation tracking 217 Indicators of Compromise within isolated VM environments. The utility of this framework is demonstrated through detailed case studies that have revealed granular disparities in capabilities and multi-stage attack progression, often obscured by standard pass/fail binary metrics. This work contributes systematic LLM-to-CVSS mapping and open cryptographic protocols toward NIST AI RMF 2.0 development.

title: Artificial Neural Network-Based Intelligent Framework for Multiclass Network Intrusion Detection in Modern Cybersecurity Systems
authors: Ankit Kumar Singh; Aastha Singh; Avanish Kant Agnihotri; Amit Trivedi; Mohd Nadeem
venue: Recent Progress in Science and Engineering
Tags: Intrusion Detection; Neural Networks; Cyber Threats; Cloud Computing; IoT
abstract: The advent of cloud computing, the Internet of Things (IoT), and digital services has led to an increase in the number and complexity of cyberattacks. The intrusion detection methods currently used, based on machine learning and artificial intelligence, include SVM, random forest, deep learning, convolutional neural networks, and LSTM. These methods are more advanced than the signature method since they are more efficient. However, despite these advancements, several issues with intrusion detection systems remain. They include high false-positive rates, computational complexity, limited scalability, inability to detect zero-day attacks, and poor real-time performance. To overcome such challenges, this paper suggests the development of an intelligent system for network intrusion detection using artificial neural networks (ANNs). This method is intended to increase the accuracy of cyber threat detection and minimize the number of false positives through adaptive and nonlinear learning. Data preprocessing, data encoding, feature normalization, feature selection, and feedforward neural networks are some of the methods employed in the classification of data traffic into malicious and normal traffic. The types of intrusions considered in this study include DoS, Probe, R2L, and U2R attacks. According to experiments performed using intrusion detection benchmark data, the proposed ANN algorithm delivers accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score values of 97.6%, 96.8%, 97.2%, and 97.0%, respectively, while maintaining a low false-positive ratio of only 2.1%. The comparative analysis further demonstrates that the ANN classifier outperforms other classification techniques, such as random forests, decision trees, and support vector machines. The findings thus demonstrate that the ANN can be successfully used for detecting attacks and improving the security of networks, cloud computing, and the IoT.
Keywords: Network Intrusion Detection; Artificial Neural Networks; Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; False Positives

title: Digitalized Quality Management for Cybersecurity Conformity Assessment: ISO/IEC 17025-Based Automated Workflows, Evidence Analytics, and EN 18031 Readiness for the Radio Equipment Directive
authors: Aymen Gatri; David Lübeck; Mukayil Kilic
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity and Privacy
Tags: ISO standards; cybersecurity; conformity assessment; automation
abstract: Cybersecurity conformity assessment is increasingly shaped by the Radio Equipment Directive (RED) delegated act, the EN 18031 harmonized standards, the Cyber Resilience Act, and industrial standards such as International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) 62443. ISO/IEC 17025:2017 provides a general laboratory competence framework, but its application to qualitative cybersecurity testing, rapidly changing toolchains, and automation-assisted evidence workflows remains under-specified. This paper proposes a digitalized quality-management framework that translates ISO/IEC 17025 clauses into cybersecurity-native controls for scope definition, method governance, toolchain control, evidence traceability, decision rules, technical review, and corrective-action feedback. An accreditation-style single-laboratory case study integrates a European Telecommunications Standards Institute (ETSI) TS 103 701 assessment workbook, an IEC 62443 corrective-action dataset, ISO/IEC 17025 internal audit findings, and laboratory governance records. In the ETSI workbook, the Conformity Statement Ambiguity Index (CSAI) decreases from 0.976 in the draft state to 0.050 after review, with 37 previously inconclusive provisions moving to PASS. This result is interpreted as improved determinability within the assessed workflow, not as cross-laboratory validation. The study contributes a clause-to-workflow operationalization of ISO/IEC 17025, an analytic design for heterogeneous assurance artefacts, and an EN 18031 evidence-mapping approach for Radio Equipment Directive readiness.
Keywords: cybersecurity conformity assessment; ISO/IEC 17025; quality management; evidence analytics; Radio Equipment Directive

title: <b>Navigating the Cybersecurity Landscape in Africa's Digital Renaissance: Challenges, Strategies, and Future Prospects</b><b></b>
authors: Faty Top; Balikis Alarape; Sahar Bukhari; Aruna M Jarju
venue: Journal of Climate Innovation and Technology
OSINT_Source_Types: Government Data; News Media; Public Records
Tags: Cybersecurity Challenges; Digital Renaissance; Economic Impact; Legislative Gaps
abstract: The African continent is undergoing a significant digital transformation, fueled by the rapid adoption of digital technologies across various sectors such as finance, education, and government (Africa Digital Transformation Strategy, 2023). This transformation, accelerated by the COVID-19 pandemic, has led to increased Internet penetration and a surge in mobile subscribers (GSMA, 2021). In 2021, Africa had 612 million people with Internet access, representing 43% of the population. However, alongside these advancements come substantial cybersecurity challenges. Despite the potential of digital technologies to drive economic growth and innovation, Africa faces critical issues related to cybersecurity infrastructure, legislative gaps, and a lack of public awareness about information security (ECA, 2022). The prevalence of cybercrime is on the rise, with cyberattacks in Africa more than doubling over the past five years (Africa Cybersecurity Report, 2023). Africa experienced a 23% increase in the average number of cyberattacks per week per organization in the second quarter of 2023 compared to the same period in 2022. Challenges such as inadequate cybersecurity protocols, limited legislative coverage, and a shortage of cybersecurity professionals pose significant threats to businesses and governments (KPMG, 2020). Approximately 90% of African businesses operate without cybersecurity protocols, leaving them vulnerable to cyberthreats (Africa Cybersecurity Report, 2023). The consequences of cyberattacks range from disruptions in business operations to substantial financial losses, with cyberattacks costing African countries an average of 10% of their GDP in 2022 (ECA, 2022). This article explores the digital transformation landscape in Africa, the vulnerabilities it introduces, and the imperative for proactive cybersecurity measures to mitigate cyber risks and safeguard digital assets.
Keywords: Cybersecurity; Africa; Digital Transformation; Cybercrime; Threats

title: Controles avanzados de ciberseguridad en SoftwareONE Ecuador: fortalecimiento de la protección corporativa.
authors: Henry Nelson Revelo-Quiñónez
venue: Portal de la Ciencia
Tags: cyber threats; advanced controls; security gaps; digital transformation; data protection
abstract: The accelerated digital transformation process has exponentially increased organizations' exposure to highly sophisticated cyber threats. This article analyzes the current state of corporate cybersecurity at SoftwareONE Ecuador and identifies the main security gaps in the technology services sector in the country, where the average cybersecurity maturity of companies falls below 60%. Using a descriptive-analytical approach and specialized secondary sources, it proposes the implementation of advanced cybersecurity controls aligned with ISO/IEC 27001:2022 and NIST Cybersecurity Framework 2.0 standards, with emphasis on reducing vulnerabilities associated with phishing, ransomware and unauthorized credential access. Expected results include a significant reduction in vulnerabilities in the local technological infrastructure, strengthening of confidentiality, integrity and availability principles, and proactive compliance with Ecuador's Personal Data Protection Law. This work constitutes a methodological contribution applicable to subsidiaries of multinational companies with emerging operations in Ecuador

Intelligent transport, autonomous vehi- cles, sustainable mobility, and transport optimization are examined. title: Cybercrime in the Banking Sector: A Systematic Review and Future Research Directions
authors: Mazurina Mohd Ali; Noor Hasniza Haron; Susi Handayani
venue: GATR Accounting and Finance Review
Tags: cybersecurity; banking; literature review; research gaps
abstract: Objective - The purpose of this study is to examine cybercrimes in the banking sector. The focus is on conducting a systematic review, synthesizing knowledge on the impacts of cybercrime, and identifying research gaps. Methodology/Technique - Specifically, this study applied a PRISMA-guided systematic literature review (SLR) to identify relevant studies, which included inclusion and exclusion criteria and defined data sources. This study found two main clusters of literature. First are cybersecurity risk, technology, and management in banking. This cluster can be divided into four themes: (i) cyber risk assessment and management, (ii) cybersecurity technologies and defense mechanisms, (iii) digital transformation and its impact on cybersecurity, and (iv) innovation and strategic management in cybersecurity. Findings - The second cluster is human, regulatory, and economic dimensions of cybercrime in banking. This cluster can also be divided into four themes: (i) cybercrime types, threats, and fraud prevention, (ii) regulation, compliance, and audit, (iii) human factors and cybersecurity awareness, and (iv) economic and insurance aspects of cybersecurity. Furthermore, regulatory compliance remains a challenge, necessitating robust cybersecurity measures and collaboration between stakeholders. Novelty - The findings of this study may contribute to the banking sector, businesses, government agencies, and the public by enhancing awareness and cooperation, both of which are vital in combating cybercrime and safeguarding banks. The study also proposes a robust research agenda for the future. title: CYBER SECURITY DISCLOSURE: THE ROLE OF STAKEHOLDER PRESSURE AND GOVERNANCE QUALITY
authors: Muhammad Fadhly Rizky Octavio; Noorfaiz Athallah Koeswandana
venue: Akurasi : Jurnal Studi Akuntansi dan Keuangan
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; News Media; Corporate Records
Tags: cybersecurity; governance; banking; data analysis; stakeholder influence
abstract: This study explores how customer pressure, public digital pressure, and the quality of corporate governance influence cybersecurity disclosure in Indonesia’s banking sector. Using a quantitative panel data design, this study analyzed 115 observations by banks listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange over 2020–2024. Cybersecurity disclosure was measured using word frequency analysis by Voyant Tools, while customer pressure was proxied by total customer deposits, public digital pressure by Google Trends scores, and corporate governance quality by the LSEG Management Score. Panel data regression by robustness checks through lagged regression and Propensity Score Matching were employed. Outcomes confirm that CP, PDP, and CGS each positively and significantly influence CSD. Differences in disclosure among state-owned and non-state-owned banks were also identified. Overall, the outcomes extend legitimacy theory to cybersecurity disclosure in emerging-market banking and support the use of Google Trends as a practical proxy for public digital pressure.
Keywords: cybersecurity disclosure; stakeholder pressure; corporate governance; Indonesia banking sector; quantitative analysis

title: Fundamentals of Machine Learning and Data Analytics for Security
authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana
venue: Cybersecurity 5.0
Tags: Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Data Analysis; Threat Detection
abstract: The fast development of digital technologies has radically changed the situation in cybersecurity by introducing a new phase of the cybersecurity system when the role of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) becomes a key player in the protection against threats proactively. This chapter addresses the fundamentals of machine learning and data analytics in the context of cybersecurity and how these technologies have allowed systems to respond, predict, and detect attacks faster and more precisely than ever before. It provides the background of the algorithms: supervised, unsupervised, and reinforcement learning, and their application in the fields of anomaly detection, malware identification, and intrusion prevention. Another important observation in the chapter is the incorporation of data analytics models, including feature engineering, dimensionality reduction, and predictive modeling, which increase the interpretability and performance of the ML-based defense processes. Moreover, it addresses the issues of data quality, adversarial attacks, and model transparency and provides some insights into the creation of resilient and explainable AI security models. Communicating the theoretical support of ML to the real-life use of cybersecurity, this chapter offers a complete conceptual base in the way intelligent data-driven systems are defining the future of Cybersecurity 5.0.
Keywords: Machine Learning; Data Analytics; Cybersecurity; AI; Anomaly Detection; Malware Identification; Intrusion Prevention

title: Understanding cyber security in the modern digital era
authors: Dr. Archana Bendale; G B Kale; Supriya Somanath Aringale
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: Cybersecurity Awareness; IoT Security; Data Breaches
abstract: Abstract: The rapid growth of the Internet and digital technologies has made data sharing easier but has also increased cybersecurity risks. This study examines the importance of cybersecurity in protecting digital systems, data, and users from evolving cyberthreats. It highlights the rise in cybercrime, including issues such as data breaches, online harassment, and crimes targeting vulnerable groups, especially women and children. The paper discusses key cybersecurity techniques such as password protection, antivirus software, firewalls, and malware detection tools. It also explores major challenges such as advanced persistent threats, zero-day attacks, and security risks associated with IoT devices. Additionally, the role of social media in increasing cyber vulnerabilities was analyzed. The study concludes that, along with technical solutions, strong legal frameworks, user awareness, and proactive measures are essential to ensure a safe and secure digital environment. title: Mitigating vanishing similarity in quantum kernels for DDoS attack detection
authors: Arturo Rodríguez-Almazán; Guillermo Rivas; Pablo Plaza; Angélica González-Arrieta; Ricardo S. Alonso
venue: Quantum Machine Intelligence
Tags: cybersecurity; quantum computing; DDoS detection; data-driven
abstract: Abstract Distributed Denial-of-Service (DDoS) attacks remain one of the most critical threats to modern cybersecurity. While machine learning techniques have proven effective for detection, classical approaches struggle with the growing complexity and scale of these attacks. Quantum computing, particularly quantum kernel methods, offers a promising alternative; however, the current state of the art faces a major challenge: vanishing similarity, which severely limits model expressiveness in high-dimensional spaces. This work introduces a novel quantum kernel inspired by multiple kernel learning, designed to mitigate vanishing similarity by constructing kernels in reduced-dimensional subspaces and combining them through averaging. The methodology is validated on the Canadian Institute for Cybersecurity dataset (NTP-based DDoS attacks). The proposed kernel effectively preserves classification capability in high-dimensional feature spaces, paving the way for practical applications of quantum kernels.
Keywords: DDoS attacks; quantum computing; machine learning; quantum kernel methods; vanishing similarity

title: Cyber Diplomacy and National Sovereignty in AUKUS Alliance: Balancing Regional Strategic Interests with Collective Cyber Security Goals
authors: DR.KEZZOUTE MHAMMED
venue: Journal of Cybersecurity, Digital Forensics and Jurisprudence
Tags: AUKUS Alliance; Collective Security; Cyber Defense; National Interests; Geostrategy
abstract: We must closely study the balance of interests within the AUKUS alliance, and the role of cyber diplomacy in this game of interests and power. Knowing that the alliance is constrained to address the challenges and issues of global instability, it primarily aims to strengthen the members' capabilities in cybersecurity and cyber defense. At this point, the desired balance among the members raises several questions and concerns. Regulatory frameworks, national interests, geopolitical and strategic issues, hegemony, and U.S. dominance all seem to be obstacles to the harmony and coherence of the alliance in achieving its objectives. In our study, we examine how the members manage these difficulties to eliminate obstacles to decision-making and deep cooperation. We also hope to understand how these states manage to maintain their sovereignties while contributing coherently and effectively to the alliance's collective cybersecurity strategy. Respect for national interests and the avoidance of establishing a hegemonic paradigm, etc., will be the main questions to examine in this work with a view to serving as a model for strengthening global cybersecurity and cyber governance.

title: Deep Learning for Malware and Ransomware Defense
authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana
venue: Cybersecurity 5.0
Tags: Deep Learning; Cyber Threats; Artificial Intelligence; Security Systems
abstract: The high rate of cyber threat development, especially malware and ransomware, has surpassed traditional defense and detection systems. Deep learning (DL) has become a revolutionary technology in cybersecurity, and it provides intelligent, adaptive, and automatic threat detection. In the present chapter, the author examines the application of DL to improve the protection against malware and ransomware, including convolutional neural networks (CNNs), recurrent neural networks (RNNs), generative adversarial networks (GANs), and Transformer-based models. It talks about how these models can process large and complicated data sets—such as code patterns, behavioral logs, and network traffic—to determine some hidden signs of bad behavior. Moreover, the chapter also discusses such issues as adversarial attacks, data imbalance, and explainability, as well as new trends (federated learning, multimodal analysis, and hybrid defense systems). Combining DL with cybersecurity models will enable organizations to create proactive, resilient, and scalable security against constantly evolving cyber threats and move toward the future of Cybersecurity 5.0, a future where intelligence-driven and autonomous security systems exist.
Keywords: Deep Learning; Malware Defense; Ransomware; Cybersecurity; Neural Networks

title: Insider Threat Detection Based on Behaviour Analytics Using Machine Learning
authors: Arsalan Siddiquee; Deepjyoti Choudhury
venue: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
Tags: Cybersecurity; Artificial Intelligence; Threat Detection; Behavioural Biometrics; Ethical AI
abstract: Cybersecurity has traditionally focused on defending organizations from threats that originate outside the network perimeter. Firewalls, intrusion detection systems, antivirus software, and access controls have evolved rapidly to counter increasingly sophisticated external attacks. Yet, some of the most damaging security incidents continue to arise from within organizations—through trusted users, compromised accounts, or malicious insiders who already possess legitimate access. These insider threats remain among the most difficult challenges in modern cybersecurity because they often evade conventional security mechanisms. This book grew out of our research into behavioural analytics as a means of addressing this challenge. Rather than asking whether a user possesses valid credentials, the central question explored here is whether the user's behaviour matches the identity they claim to be. Writing style, particularly in organizational email communication, offers a rich behavioural signature that can reveal subtle inconsistencies when an account is used by someone other than its legitimate owner. The work presented in this book builds upon extensive experimentation using the Enron Email Corpus, one of the most widely studied datasets in cybersecurity research. During the course of this research, an important methodological issue became apparent: many previous studies unknowingly benefited from author-identifying information embedded within email headers, resulting in inflated classification performance. Removing this hidden source of information fundamentally changed both the experimental design and the interpretation of results. This discovery reinforced an essential principle of scientific research—that reliable conclusions depend as much on careful data preparation as on sophisticated machine learning models. Throughout these chapters, readers will find not only the implementation of multiple machine learning techniques—including classical statistical models, ensemble learning methods, and gradient boosting algorithms—but also the practical engineering considerations required to transform research into deployable security solutions. Equal emphasis is placed on reproducibility, computational efficiency, privacy preservation, ethical deployment, and regulatory compliance, because effective cybersecurity extends beyond predictive accuracy alone. This book is intended for postgraduate students, cybersecurity practitioners, machine learning researchers, and professionals interested in behavioural biometrics, insider threat detection, and applied artificial intelligence. While the discussion includes technical details, every effort has been made to explain the underlying concepts before introducing algorithms and implementation choices, making the material accessible to readers with a general background in computer science and cybersecurity. The field of behavioural security is evolving rapidly. Artificial intelligence now enables systems to recognise patterns that would be impossible for human analysts to detect manually, yet these capabilities also introduce important ethical responsibilities. Behavioural monitoring must always be balanced with privacy, transparency, fairness, and accountability. For this reason, the final chapters discuss not only how such systems can be built, but also how they should be governed in real-world environments. No research is ever truly complete. Every answer uncovers new questions, and every improvement reveals new challenges. It is my hope that this book serves both as a practical guide for those developing behavioural security systems and as a foundation for future research into explainable, privacy-preserving, and trustworthy machine learning for cybersecurity. If these pages encourage readers to question assumptions, build more reliable systems, and pursue responsible innovation, then they will have fulfilled their purpose.
Keywords: Insider Threats; Behavioural Analytics; Machine Learning; Cybersecurity; Email Communication; Data Preparation

title: <b>Risk Assessment and Mitigation in Smart Manufacturing Systems Using a Qualitative Risk Matrix Approach</b><b></b>
authors: Sharvani Jagtap; Aarya Chavan
venue: International Research Journal of Innovation in Science and Technology
Tags: Manufacturing Security; Risk Management; Operational Safety; Industry 4.0
abstract: Industry 4.0 technologies, including the Internet of Things (IoT), cyber-physical systems (CPS), artificial intelligence (AI), and automation, have significantly transformed modern manufacturing by improving productivity, flexibility, and operational efficiency. However, the increasing connectivity and complexity of smart manufacturing systems have also introduced new technical, operational, cybersecurity, and safety-related risks that require systematic assessment and management. This paper presents a structured framework for risk identification, assessment, and mitigation using a qualitative risk matrix approach. The proposed methodology classifies manufacturing risks into major categories and evaluates them based on their probability of occurrence and potential impact to support effective risk prioritization. Appropriate mitigation strategies, including predictive maintenance, enhanced cybersecurity measures, system redundancy, real-time monitoring, and workforce training, are discussed to improve system reliability and operational safety. The study highlights that systematic risk assessment enables early identification of critical vulnerabilities, supports informed engineering decision-making, and contributes to more resilient, reliable, and sustainable smart manufacturing systems. The proposed framework provides a practical reference for manufacturing engineers and industrial practitioners implementing risk management within Industry 4.0 environments.
Keywords: Risk Assessment; Smart Manufacturing; Qualitative Risk Matrix; Cybersecurity; IoT; CPS; Industry 4.0; Mitigation Strategies

abstract: Cyber threats are evolving rapidly, making traditional perimeter-based security models inadequate for protecting modern enterprise environments. Zero Trust Security Architecture: Principles, Technologies, and Enterprise Implementation provides a comprehensive guide to designing, implementing, and managing Zero Trust security in cloud, hybrid, and on-premises infrastructures. Written by experienced academicians and researchers, this book combines theoretical foundations with practical implementation strategies, making it an ideal resource for students, researchers, cybersecurity professionals, and IT practitioners. This book covers: • Fundamentals of Zero Trust Security and cybersecurity principles• Evolution from traditional security to Zero Trust Architecture• Identity and Access Management (IAM), MFA, SSO, RBAC, ABAC, and PAM• Zero Trust network design, micro-segmentation, and Software Defined Perimeter (SDP)• Endpoint, device, and application security• Cloud security and Zero Trust for hybrid and multi-cloud environments• Continuous monitoring, SIEM, SOAR, and threat intelligence• AI and Machine Learning applications in Zero Trust Security• Zero Trust maturity models and enterprise implementation frameworks• NIST SP 800-207, Google BeyondCorp, Microsoft Zero Trust, and CSA frameworks• Case studies, best practices, implementation challenges, and future trends Who should read this book? • Undergraduate and postgraduate students in Computer Science, Information Technology, Cybersecurity, and Artificial Intelligence• Faculty members and academic researchers• Security architects, network administrators, and IT professionals• Cloud engineers and DevSecOps practitioners• Professionals preparing for cybersecurity certifications and enterprise security roles With clear explanations, real-world examples, diagrams, and implementation guidance, this book equips readers with the knowledge and skills required to design secure, resilient, and scalable Zero Trust environments for modern digital enterprises. Build a security strategy based on one simple principle: Never Trust, Always Verify

authors: Achraf akkaoui; Yassine Zahidi; Mohamed El Moufid; Wafaa Dachry; Hassan Gziri; Hicham Medromi
venue: F1000 Research Ltd
Tags: healthcare; technology trends; future directions; medical technology
abstract: This paper examines the rapid advancements and integration of emerging technologies in the medical field, particularly focusing on Artificial Intelligence (AI), the Internet of Medical Things (IoMT), Augmented Reality (AR), and cybersecurity. The study leverages data from Scopus and Web of Science databases to highlight the trends, challenges, and future directions in the development of medical devices. Significant progress has been made in enhancing patient care through the integration of AI and IoMT, which facilitate predictive analytics, personalized treatment plans, and real-time data monitoring. AR is transforming medical training and surgical precision, while cybersecurity measures are becoming increasingly vital to protect sensitive health data. Despite these advancements, the field faces challenges such as data privacy concerns, infrastructure limitations, and interoperability issues. The study also explores Africa’s contributions, with a particular emphasis on Morocco’s emerging role in this technological landscape. Three major research clusters identified include AI and AR, IoT and cybersecurity, and embedded systems, each playing an important role in the evolution of medical technologies. By analyzing publications from 2010 to 2024, the paper provides insights into the current state and future potential of advanced medical technologies, aiming to offer a foundation for further research and innovation in this rapidly evolving field.
Keywords: emerging technologies; medical devices; cybersecurity; AI; IoMT; AR; data privacy; infrastructure

title: Mathematical Tools for Cyber security in Engineering Systems: A Review of Recent Trends and Applications
authors: Anushka A. Patil; Ashok S Kulkarni; Mr. Ashitosh P. Patil
venue: Open MIND
Tags: vulnerability; mathematical frameworks; network resilience; data integrity
abstract: This paper presents a comprehensive review of the recent trends and applications of mathematical tools in enhancing the cybersecurity of engineering systems. The increasing interconnectedness and complexity of industrial control systems (ICS), operational technology (OT), cyber-physical systems (CPS), and the Internet of Things (IoT) in engineering have amplified their vulnerability to cyber threats. This review explores the crucial role of mathematical frameworks from cryptography, coding theory, formal methods, network science, and game theory in addressing these challenges. We examine the underlying mathematical principles of key techniques within these areas and analyse their application in securing engineering communication, data integrity, system verification, network resilience, and strategic defence. Furthermore, this paper identifies current research challenges and highlights potential future directions for leveraging mathematical advancements to fortify the cybersecurity posture of critical engineering infrastructure.
Keywords: cybersecurity; engineering systems; mathematics; industrial control systems; cyber-physical systems; cryptography

title: Leveraging Large Language Models for ATT&amp;CK Technique Synthesis: Opportunities and Challenges
authors: Sameeruddin Shaik
venue: International Journal of Intelligent Systems and Data Science
Tags: AI; Machine Learning; Cyber Defense; Threat Analysis; Penetration Testing
abstract: The developing cybersecurity threats or large-scale attack vectors, coupled with the rising use of artificial intelligence (AI), are compelling researchers and practitioners to unite their forces in combating these issues through coordinated efforts. This paper investigates the use of LLMs developed with MITRE ATT&CK techniques, an established knowledge base that describes an adversary’s tactics, techniques and procedures based on real cyber operations. The experiment explores utilizing LLMs to generate code snippets, implementation ideas, and descriptive summaries corresponding to ATT&CK techniques to assist security researchers, educators, penetration testers, and red teams in developing a better understanding of adversarial behavior and defensive strategy. These abilities can enhance training, hasten security analyses, and create more credible evaluation testing grounds for detection and response mechanisms. Simultaneously, the availability of automated tools to code generators could raise a whole set of security issues, as they might lower the level of expertise required to replicate an offensive technique. Given these observations, careful governance, responsible application and proper safeguards ought to be exercised while applying LLMs in the domain of cybersecurity. By discussing the benefits and risks associated with LLMs, this paper attempts to present both sides of the coin in terms of the opportunities and challenges they present in relation to MITRE ATT&CK and modern cyber defences.
Keywords: Large Language Models; MITRE ATT&CK; Cybersecurity; Security Research; Adversarial Behavior

title: Blockchain for Secure and Transparent Systems
authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana
venue: Cybersecurity 5.0
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Corporate Records; Government Data
Tags: Blockchain Technology; Cybersecurity; Digital Resilience; Transparent Systems
abstract: Blockchain technology provides secure, transparent, and resilient systems for digital infrastructures across varying domains. The principal embrace of decentralization keeps intermediaries away, thus assuring data validity and trust among the players. In Cybersecurity 5.0, blockchain is a paramount enabler of proactive threat defense, where immutable data storage, traceable transactions, and consensus mechanisms are concerned. Further integration with artificial intelligence (AI) upgrades predictive analytics, intrusion detection, and automated response capacities. This combination thus guarantees a stronghold against data breaches, cyber fraud, and insider threats while maintaining compliance and accountability. The chapter discusses the principles, applications, and advantages of blockchain in creating secure and transparent systems and how its advent is transforming modern paradigms in cybersecurity, heralding a new era of digital resilience.
Keywords: Blockchain; Cybersecurity; Threat Defense; Data Integrity; AI Integration

title: Adversarial AI and Defensive Countermeasures
authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana
venue: Cybersecurity 5.0
Tags: Artificial Intelligence; Cyber Threats; Defense Strategies; Digital Security
abstract: With the advent of artificial intelligence (AI), cybersecurity has greatly changed, presenting new attack vectors and enhanced defense mechanisms. Adversarial AI entails any manipulation or misleading activity employed against a machine-learning model using AI techniques. These pose grave threats, from autonomous vehicles to financial infrastructures. This chapter presents the world of adversarial AI, including various forms of attacks such as evasion, poisoning, and model inversion. It also elucidates defense measures concerning robust model training, anomaly detection, and reactive methods of defense. Thus, the chapter equally mingles theory with practice to demonstrate the growing need for preemptive AI-led cybersecurity frameworks that can foresee, detect, and reject adversarial attacks. The discourse ends with future research and trends in adversarial AI defense, where resilient and ethical AI deployment is paramount for protecting digital assets.
Keywords: Adversarial AI; Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Defensive Countermeasures; Evasion Attacks; Model Inversion

title: An overview of security and privacy approaches to Brain-Brain Interfaces: Security architecture, fundamental consideration, and future directions
authors: Saeed Banaeian Far; Mohammad Reza Chalak Qazani; Azadeh Imani Rad
venue: Peer-to-Peer Networking and Applications
Tags: BBI; IoB; security architecture; defense framework; ethical deployment
abstract: The explosive rise of Brain-Computer Interfaces (BCIs) is unleashing the era of Brain-Brain Interfaces (BBIs) and the Internet of Brains (IoB), enabling seamless neural exchanges that could transform healthcare, collaboration, and human potential, yet at the peril of unprecedented neural data breaches, signal hijacks, and cognitive hijacking. Motivated by these looming threats amid Neuralink’s 2025 milestone of $$27+$$ human implants, this paper dissects the cybersecurity chasm in BBIs, unveiling a novel four-layered IoB architecture, from volition to ultra-tech channels, and a pioneering multi-tiered defense framework fusing neuro-encryption, AI anomaly detection, and post-quantum cryptography. Our contributions are 1) a layered blueprint fortifying neural pathways, 2) defenses slashing known threats by 90% in simulations, 3) countermeasures against mind-hacking via AI-mitigated synchronization, and 4) blueprints for blockchain neural controls and quantum-resilient comms. By establishing a secure foundation for BBI-based IoB networks, this work provides an essential roadmap for researchers and practitioners aiming to safeguard neural interfaces against emerging cyber threats. This study is a crucial step toward ensuring the ethical, secure, and scalable deployment of IoB systems, bridging the gap between cutting-edge neuroscience and advanced cybersecurity. With the increasing integration of brain-based communication technologies, the proposed security model serves as a cornerstone for future innovations, protecting cognitive privacy and enabling trustworthy brain-to-brain interactions.
Keywords: Brain-Computer Interfaces; Brain-Brain Interfaces; neural data; cybersecurity; neuro-encryption; AI anomaly detection; post-quantum cryptography; cognitive privacy; secure communication

title: The importance of encryption awareness, adoption barriers and encryption by default practices
authors: Imafidor Victoria; Shokefun Ebunoluwa; Valentin Maria
venue: World Journal of Advanced Engineering Technology and Sciences
Tags: sensitivity; user awareness; file encryption; security practices
abstract: Encryption is widely recognized as one of the most effective methods for protecting sensitive digital information from unauthorized access, data breaches, and device theft. Despite its importance, adoption among everyday technology users remains limited. This study examined encryption awareness, confidence in file encryption, barriers to encryption adoption, and attitudes toward encryption by default practices among young adult technology users. A quantitative survey methodology was employed using an online questionnaire distributed through both physical and digital recruitment channels. A total of 108 participants aged 18 years and older completed the survey. The findings indicate that many participants reported limited confidence in their ability to encrypt files when necessary. Lack of knowledge, uncertainty regarding encryption procedures, and perceived complexity were identified as common barriers preventing adoption. Survey responses also revealed that many participants would be more likely to utilize encryption if clearer instructions and educational resources were available. Support for encryption by default was high among respondents, suggesting a preference for security measures that do not require significant user intervention. The results align with previous research demonstrating that usability challenges and limited cybersecurity knowledge continue to hinder the adoption of encryption technologies. The findings suggest that relying on users to manually implement encryption may not provide adequate protection for sensitive information. Integrating encryption by default into devices and applications offers a practical approach for improving security while reducing the burden placed on individual users. Increased cybersecurity education and simplified security tools may also contribute to greater adoption and more effective protection of personal data.
Keywords: encryption; data protection; adoption barriers; cybersecurity education; encryption by default

title: Case Studies Across Sectors (Finance, Healthcare, and Government)
authors: Hewa Majeed Zangana
venue: Cybersecurity 5.0
Tags: AI integration; cyber resilience; data-driven intelligence; automation; Cybersecurity 5.0
abstract: This chapter is a detailed discussion of the way AI-driven strategies of cybersecurity are changing threat protection in three main domains: finance, healthcare, and government. Both case studies represent real-life examples of artificial intelligence (AI), machine learning (ML), and predictive analytics integration to identify, minimize, and avert emerging cyber threats. The discussion highlights the importance of automation, data-driven intelligence, and adaptive learning in making resilience against advanced attacks better. Financial AI is used to detect fraud and for real-time transaction monitoring. In healthcare, AI is used to safeguard patient data and keep the regulatory environment in check, and in the government, AI is used to boost national security and cyber defense operations. The chapter has used comparative knowledge and cross-sectoral analyses to emphasize the best practices, challenges, and new trends that are contributing to the development of Cybersecurity 5.0. The results indicate the importance of the fact that the integration of AI with proactive defense strategies not only reinforces the operational security but also transforms the future of digital trust and risk management.
Keywords: AI cybersecurity; machine learning; predictive analytics; cyber threats; financial fraud; healthcare security; government cybersecurity

title: Deepfake Detection Using Hybrid CNN-LSTM Architecture with Blockchain-Based Media Authentication
authors: T Priya; S Sandhiya
venue: Iconic Research and Engineering Journals
Tags: AI; cybersecurity; digital forensics; media integrity; video analysis
abstract: The rapid advancement of artificial intelligence has enabled the creation of highly realistic deepfake images and videos, posing significant threats to digital media authenticity, cybersecurity, and public trust. Existing deepfake detection techniques often rely on either spatial or temporal information, resulting in limited robustness against sophisticated manipulations. This paper proposes a hybrid CNN-LSTM framework integrated with blockchain-based media authentication for reliable deepfake detection and secure media verification. The Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) extracts discriminative spatial features from facial frames, while the Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network captures temporal inconsistencies across video sequences. To ensure media integrity, SHA-256 hashing is combined with blockchain technology to provide tamper-proof authentication and provenance tracking. The proposed model is evaluated using FaceForensics++, DFDC, and Celeb-DF datasets. Experimental results demonstrate high detection accuracy, improved robustness, and secure verification compared with existing approaches. The proposed framework offers an efficient solution for social media platforms, journalism, digital forensics, and cybersecurity applications.
Keywords: deepfake detection; CNN; LSTM; blockchain; media authentication

title: Blockchain-Assisted Cybersecurity for Solar Farm
authors: BoHyun Ahn; Taesic Kim; Kalyan Nakka; Jinchun Choi; Seerin Ahmad; Hee-Yong Kwon; Nathanial R. Handke; Trevor J. Reyna
venue: IEEE Transactions on Industry Applications
Tags: Cybersecurity Framework; MITM Detection; Firmware Security; Resilience
abstract: This article explores how blockchain (BC) technologies can improve cybersecurity of photovoltaic (PV) systems, specifically solar farms. First of all, a comprehensive BC-assisted security framework is proposed which has distinct stages: 1) Prevention stage including a solar farm membership service, solar asset management, secure BC data communication, secure boot verification, and self-signed certificate verification; 2) Detection and Incident Response stage including man-in-themiddle (MITM) attack detection, firmware attack detection, alert, and response; and 3) Recovery and Resilience stage including access control, firmware patching and rollback, and resilient control. Moreover, this article introduces a BC-integrated security module (SM) design providing an industry-deployable method of the proposed BC framework in the PV system. This article also provides practical cyberattack models targeting a commercial solar farm with real-world field testing methods. Finally, the testing results demonstrate that the proposed BCassisted system proactively detects MITM attacks, firmware modification attack, and malware attack, while ensuring the continuous operation of the solar farm during attack events.
Keywords: Blockchain; Cybersecurity; Solar Farm; Photovoltaic Systems; Incident Response

title: Strengthening the Nexus between Criminology and Cybersecurity
authors: Fosu Bora
venue: International Journal of Law and Societal Studies
Tags: cyber threats; law enforcement; security governance; high policing; low policing
abstract: Cybercrime is broadly defined in criminological literature as an umbrella concept that includes both conventional offences committed through digital means and offences that can only exist within networked environments. The former category, often termed ‘cyber-enabled crimes’, involves traditional crimes such as fraud and theft that are facilitated by technology, while the latter, ‘cyber-dependent crimes’, refers to acts like hacking and malware distribution that are intrinsic to digital systems. Similarly, cybersecurity operates as an expansive and interdisciplinary domain encompassing both academic research and applied practice. Within computer science and information security, it is generally understood as the set of policies, procedures, technologies, and behaviours aimed at safeguarding data, networks, systems, and digital infrastructure from unauthorised access, alteration, or disruption (NIST, 2018). Beyond its technical scope, cybersecurity has gained prominence across subnational, national, and international governance structures as states and institutions respond to escalating digital threats and transnational cyber risks. The relationship between cybercrime and cybersecurity has become increasingly interwoven. Cybercrimes are frequently framed as direct threats to cybersecurity, a development that has contributed to the growing involvement of national security institutions in cybercrime prevention, detection, and response activities. Despite these developments, however, the fields of cyber criminology and cybersecurity remain largely segmented in both theoretical and practical terms, thereby limiting opportunities for meaningful interdisciplinary engagement and knowledge exchange. This article adopts a conceptual and interdisciplinary analytical approach, drawing on existing criminological, cybersecurity, and security governance literature to examine the relationship between cybercrime and cybersecurity. It synthesises key theoretical perspectives and applies Brodeur's (2010) distinction between “high” and “low” policing as an analytical framework to explore the convergence of crime control and security governance in cyberspace. The article argues that stronger intellectual and operational linkages between cyber criminology and cybersecurity are necessary to effectively respond to the evolving nature of digital threats. Within Brodeur's framework, cybercrime is positioned at one end of the continuum, traditionally associated with the functions of low policing, while cybersecurity is situated at the opposite end, increasingly aligned with high-policing institutions concerned with intelligence, national security, and strategic risk management. By situating cybercrime and cybersecurity within a unified analytical framework, the article highlights the increasingly blurred boundaries between crime control and security governance in digital environments. This perspective contributes to a more integrated understanding of contemporary cyber threats and underscores the need for closer collaboration between cybercrime and cybersecurity researchers, policymakers, and practitioners. Ultimately, the article advances a unifying approach that promotes cross-fertilisation between the two fields and supports the development of more comprehensive and coherent responses to emerging challenges in cyberspace.
Keywords: cybercrime; cybersecurity; interdisciplinary; criminology; digital threats

title: A systematic review of cybersecurity quality metrics for Decentralized computational ecosystems
authors: Vishwas Dixit; Surendra Rahamatkar; Raghavendra Prasad
venue: Array
Tags: DCE; cybersecurity metrics; blockchain technology; privacy-enhancing methods; systematic review
abstract: Rapid advances in blockchain technology, distributed computing, federated learning, and privacy-enhancing methods have collectively given rise to what researchers now call the Decentralized Computational Ecosystem (DCE) an umbrella term covering digital infrastructures in which computation, trust establishment, and data governance are distributed across heterogeneous node networks rather than concentrated within centralised authorities. Despite a decade of accelerating output, the literature on DCE remains markedly fragmented: individual components are studied in isolation, and no prior systematic review has mapped cybersecurity concerns holistically across all five recognised DCE layers. This study attempts to fill that gap through a PRISMA 2020-compliant systematic review, applied with explicit attention to methodological rigour and reproducibility. A structured database search executed across IEEE Xplore, Elsevier ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, MDPI, and the ACM Digital Library between January and March 2025, covering publications from 2015 onward retrieved 147 unique records after de-duplication. Following title/abstract screening and full-text eligibility assessment, 101 peer-reviewed articles were retained for qualitative synthesis. These were organised into five DCE component categories: Distributed Ledger Protocols (DLP), Decentralized Compute Infrastructure (DCI), Privacy-Preserving Computation Protocols (PPCP), Decentralized AI and Data Marketplaces (DAIDM), and Decentralized Threat Detection Systems (DTDS). Thematic analysis of the included studies yielded six cross-cutting cybersecurity quality metrics and one system-level governance metric: threat detection accuracy, privacy protection strength, trust and verification transparency, attack resilience, scalability and performance stability, interoperability and composability, and governance, ethics and compliance. Coverage of these metrics was assessed systematically across all five DCE component layers. Persistent deficits are apparent in governance integration, cross-layer incentive alignment, and unified evaluation frameworks gaps that are characterised with specific design directions in the final sections of this paper.
Keywords: cybersecurity; decentralized ecosystems; blockchain; systematic review; quality metrics

title: AI-Driven Cybersecurity Framework: Threat Detection Techniques, Emerging Applications, and Future Challenges
authors: Parag Jain; Dr. Anish Kumar Choudhary; Dayanand Yadav
venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
Tags: Cyber Threats; AI Framework; Security Operations; Incident Response; Emerging Technologies
abstract: The increasing complexity and frequency of cyber threats have created a pressing need for advanced cybersecurity solutions capable of detecting and responding to attacks in real time. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a transformative technology in cybersecurity, enabling automated threat detection, predictive analytics, intelligent decision-making, and adaptive defense mechanisms. This paper presents a comprehensive review of AI-driven cybersecurity frameworks, focusing on threat detection techniques, emerging applications, and future challenges. The study examines the role of machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and anomaly detection in identifying cyber threats and enhancing security operations. Furthermore, it explores the growing adoption of AI in cloud security, Internet of Things (IoT) environments, software development, automated incident response, and Security Operations Centers (SOCs). Despite its advantages, AI-driven cybersecurity faces significant challenges, including adversarial attacks, privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, explainability issues, and regulatory compliance requirements. The paper identifies key research gaps and discusses future directions for developing resilient, transparent, and adaptive cybersecurity systems. The findings indicate that AI-driven cybersecurity has the potential to revolutionize cyber defense strategies while requiring continuous innovation to address evolving threats and ethical concerns.
Keywords: AI; cybersecurity; threat detection; machine learning; deep learning; anomaly detection

abstract: As State-sponsored cyber adversaries increasingly deploy evasive tactics against India’s National Critical Information Infrastructure (NCII), the NCII Securing air-gapped Advanced Persistent Threats (APT) is highly hindered by the limitations of legacy Security Information and Event Management (SIEM) system. As per the current scenarios the current Defense Networks suffer from severe “alert fatigue” among defense operators and are legally prohibited from utilizing modern, cloud-dependent artificial intelligence for the threat triage. The traditional perimeter defense has proven inadequate generating “alert fatigue” among defense operator. As the sovereign security mandates prohibits the usage of the cloud-dependent artificial intelligence, which turnout leaving the air-gapped networks heavily reliant on the manual forensic analysis. To resolve this critical bottleneck, this technical white paper will be outlining that our Defense Network now need to be updated to an entirely indigenous, on-premises zero-trust Cyber Threat Intelligence (CTI) pipelined architecture which is engineered explicitly for sovereign environments. By deploying an on-premised Machine Learning Triage Engine, the system autonomously ingests a very well encrypted endpoint telemetry, suppressing benign network noise and mapping high-confidence anomalies directly to the MITRE ATT&CK framework. By bridging the semantic gap between the raw machine logs and actionable military intelligence grading towards the real-time predictive situational awareness to the strategic commanders as this localized intelligence ecosystem establishes a self-reliant defense perimeter, and hence ensuring absolute data sovereignty and operational dominance in strict alignment that drastically reduces Mean Time to Detect (MTTD), and aligns with India’s strategic mandate for the Self-reliance (Atmanirbharata) in digital defense operations.
