abstract: This research examines the integration of artificial intelligence in India's digital forensic landscape, with particular emphasis on its application in sexual assault inquiries. As India confronts escalating cybercrime rates and increasingly complex digital evidence, forensic laboratories in the country have begun implementing artificial intelligence driven solutions to process and analyse electronic data. The study investigates specific artificial intelligence tools deployed by agencies such as the Central Forensic Science Laboratory and state police cyber cells, including facial recognition systems, automated malware analysis tools, among others. The paper encompasses this analysis in the instances of sexual assault forensics, where substantial backlogs and manual processing methods contribute to delayed justice. It discovers how artificial intelligence models, including automated biological evidence analysis, accelerated DNA matching, intelligent evidence prioritisation systems, and unconventional digital evidence processing, can potentially reduce evidence dispensation time from months to days, enabling faster filing of chargesheets within statutory limits. The research further examines how these technologies can be integrated with existing initiatives such as the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal and the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C) to create specialised pathways for rape and child abuse cases. Ethical and legal concerns are a major aspect when the usage of AI in forensics is put forward. The paper will sketch how the new Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam, 2023, deals with this amalgamation of AI and its interaction with India's constitutional framework, the new Digital Personal Data Protection Act (DPDP), and the existing IT Act. Additionally, it analyses recent judicial attitudes toward digital evidence and also compares the usage of AI forensic tools in different countries and how the usage has helped the police and judicial authorise to speed up the justice process. The research concludes by proposing a comprehensive ethical framework tailored to guide the responsible integration of AI in India's digital forensic ecosystem, balancing the benefits of AI, including drastically reduced evidence processing times, heightened detection competencies, and expedited judicial proceedings, with essential protections to algorithmic transparency standards and vigorous data protection safeguards. By potentially reducing investigation timelines from years to months, AI integration offers transformative potential for delivering timely justice to sexual assault survivors, which can resolve key loopholes in criminal investigations.
Keywords: AI; Digital Evidence; Forensics; Sexual Assault; India; Cybercrime; Ethical Framework

title: ForenGRAF-AI: An Explainable Graph-Temporal Artificial Intelligence Artifact for Digital Forensic
authors: Pedro Ramos Brandao
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Explainable AI; Forensic Soundness; Evidence Analysis; Decision Support System
abstract: Abstract Digital forensic investigation is increasingly constrained by the scale, heterogeneity, volatility, and legal sensitivity of contemporary digital evidence. Cloud infrastructures, mobile devices, endpoint telemetry, encrypted applications, containerized services, and adversarially manipulated logs have transformed digital forensics from a largely artifact-centered discipline into a problem of high-dimensional temporal reasoning under uncertainty. Artificial intelligence offers substantial opportunities to accelerate triage, prioritize evidence, reconstruct event sequences, and discover latent relationships among digital artifacts. However, opaque AI systems may undermine forensic soundness, reproducibility, interpretability, and evidential admissibility if they are not designed around forensic requirements. This article investigates the relationship between Digital Forensic Analysis and Artificial Intelligence and proposes ForenGRAF-AI, a complex yet feasible artifact for forensic investigation. ForenGRAF-AI is an explainable graph-temporal AI application that ingests heterogeneous forensic artifacts, constructs a signed temporal provenance graph, learns suspicious behavioral embeddings through graph neural networks and temporal variational modeling, estimates evidential relevance via Bayesian reasoning, and produces human-verifiable investigative hypotheses. The artifact is developed using the Design Science Research methodology, which is suitable when the research contribution is the construction and evaluation of an artifact intended to solve an identified organizational and technical problem [49]-[51]. The principal contribution is a mathematically grounded, explainable, and forensically constrained AI architecture for digital forensic triage and event reconstruction. Unlike conventional anomaly-detection systems, ForenGRAF-AI explicitly models evidential provenance, uncertainty, temporal causality, artifact reliability, and chain-of-custody requirements. The article presents the theoretical foundation, system architecture, mathematical formulation, data strategy, evaluation design, limitations, and implications for forensic practice. The proposed artifact is positioned not as an autonomous forensic decision-maker but as a decision-support system that assists qualified investigators while preserving transparency, repeatability, and evidential accountability.
Keywords: Digital Forensics; Artificial Intelligence; Graph-Temporal AI; Evidential Provenance; Event Reconstruction

title: Research on Incremental Network Intrusion Detection Based on Hunting Algorithm and Class Balance Strategy
authors: Wenqiang Yu; Xianfeng Guo; Xinyue Yan; Xi Chen; Make Mao
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: NIDS; AI; Machine Learning; Network Security; Continual Learning
abstract: Abstract With the continuous evolution of network environments and attack techniques, traditional network intrusion detection systems (NIDS) trained in a static manner struggle to effectively adapt to newly emerging attacks, while frequent model retraining incurs substantial computational overhead and maintenance cost. To address these challenges, this paper proposes an incremental network intrusion detection model, namely IDS-We, based on the Herding algorithm and a class-balancing strategy. The proposed method builds an exemplar memory mechanism, selects representative historical samples via Herding, and introduces a class-balanced scheduling strategy during incremental training to jointly manage new and old data. Under a limited storage budget, the method effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting and class imbalance, enabling continual learning of new attack types.We conduct systematic experimental analyses on three public network traffic datasets CIC-IDS2017, UNSW-NB15, and CSE-CIC-IDS2018 under three evaluation settings: in-dataset evaluation, cross-dataset evaluation, and extended evaluation. Experimental results show that the proposed model consistently outperforms existing incremental learning methods in both binary and multi-class tasks, achieving more substantial improvements in metrics such as F1-score and accuracy. In particular, under cross-dataset evaluation, the proposed method exhibits stronger generalization capability and more stable detection performance, validating its effectiveness and scalability for dynamic network environments and long-term intrusion detection deployment.
Keywords: Network Intrusion Detection; Incremental Learning; Herding Algorithm; Class Balance Strategy; Cybersecurity

title: The Impact of Darknet and Dark Web Environments on Cyber Sovereignty
authors: Agshin Pashayev; Samed Dursunov
venue: Dövlətin kibersuverenliyinin təmin olunmasının elmi-praktiki problemləri respublika konfransı
OSINT_Source_Types: Dark Web; Public Records; News Media
Tags: cybersecurity; digital transformation; legal regulation
abstract: In the context of digital transformation, the concept of state sovereignty is acquiring new dimensions, with the notion of cyber sovereignty becoming increasingly prominent. The borderless nature of the Internet and its distributed network architecture enable the rapid transmission of information beyond national boundaries, thereby reducing the effectiveness of traditional state control mechanisms. This study analyzes the Internet environment across three layers Surface Web, Deep Web, and Darknet and examines their impact on cyber sovereignty. The findings indicate that these technological characteristics complicate legal regulation and increase risks related to information security, including disinformation, manipulation, cyberattacks, and cyber threats. Consequently, the issue of cyber sovereignty requires a comprehensive approach that integrates legal, technological, and international cooperation frameworks.
Keywords: cyber sovereignty; darknet; information security; disinformation; cyber threats

title: Cybersecurity and the Art of Cyberwar
authors: Dan Shoemaker; Tamara Shoemaker; Amir Jabri
venue: CRC Press
Tags: cybersecurity; strategic defense; holistic approach; information warfare
abstract: The art of war is of vital importance to the state. It is a matter of life or death. Hence, it is a subject which can on no account be neglected.—Sun Tzu Why are we calling this war? It’s because the conflict in cyberspace is a matter of national concern, and we are, most assuredly, losing the current struggle. So, what do we do? The person who best understands war is a 2,300-year-old Chinese general who saw conflict as more about process and strategy than fighting. Which, in essence, is the holistic concept. Hence, this book is founded on two principles. First, cybersecurity is a state, not a technical solution. Accordingly, people and organizations must take active steps to both design and sustain a consistently secure operational process. Second, it’s given that you have not attained the desired state if you have failed to deploy all of the controls necessary to achieve it. The catch-all term for such an approach is “holistic.” A holistic control architecture is the only way to achieve adequate protection. Therefore, holistic cyber defenses embody a single, unified system of electronic, behavioral, and physical controls that enforce continuous security across all common attack surfaces. Why does the solution need to be holistic? It is because the cybersecurity function is responsible for securing three distinct and disparate types of attacks – electronic, human, and physical. And just as in war, the adversary doesn’t care which attack surface they breach. They only want your stuff, and they will do whatever it takes to get it. In that respect, then, the only practical approach to cybersecurity is to create an integrated, appropriately tailored defense against any viable threat … electronic, human, or physical. This book describes the lifecycle process for conceptualizing, implementing, and maintaining a holistic control solution. It centers on a well-defined process for planning, building, and ensuring comprehensive, in-depth cyber defense. In that respect, then, we will demonstrate why holistic security is the only way for an organization to identify and address all valid threats to its digital resources.
Keywords: cybersecurity; holistic security; cyberwar; cyber defense; threat management

title: Security of information resources in federal college of education libraries in northwest Nigeria
authors: Kayode Sunday John Dada; Hafsat Aliyu Mohammed; Diana Mallam; Emmanuel Oluwaseun Ajayi
venue: International Journal of Contemporary Security Studies
Tags: library; education; security measures; cyber threats; policy recommendations
abstract: This study investigates the security of information resources in Federal College of Education libraries in Northwest Nigeria, surveying 74 librarians using a descriptive survey design. A structured questionnaire based on a 4-point Likert scale (Strongly Agree = 4, Agree = 3, Disagree = 2, Strongly Disagree = 1) assessed perceptions of security measures, including policies, training, electronic systems, and physical safeguards. Data were analysed using the average weighted mean, with a benchmark of 2.50 indicating agreement. Findings reveal moderate security implementation, with only physical security measures scoring above the benchmark (M = 2.64). In contrast, security policies (M = 2.35), staff training (M = 2.12), and electronic systems (M = 2.41) were deemed inadequate. Key challenges include insufficient funding, inadequate training, weak policy frameworks, and erratic power supply, which exacerbate vulnerabilities to theft, mutilation, and cyber threats. These align with prior research highlighting resource constraints and low cybersecurity awareness in Nigerian libraries. The study recommends increased funding for advanced security infrastructure, regular training in cybersecurity, development of robust policies, and investment in alternative power sources, such as solar systems, to ensure consistent electronic security. By addressing these gaps, libraries can better protect resources critical for academic advancement. The findings contribute to the discourse on library security in resource-constrained settings, offering actionable insights for policymakers and library administrators to enhance resource protection and align with global standards. Future research should explore user perspectives and the cost-effectiveness of proposed interventions.
Keywords: library security; cybersecurity; information resources; Nigeria; vulnerability assessment

title: OSINT Report on Current Vulnerabilities in Indonesia
authors: WEI MENG
venue: Cambridge University Press (CUP)
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; Government Data; News Media
Tags: OSINT; vulnerabilities assessment; economic resilience
abstract: This report provides an open-source intelligence assessment of Indonesia’s principal national vulnerabilities as of May 17, 2026. The overall judgment is that Indonesia is not on the edge of systemic collapse. Macroeconomic growth, inflation, and reserve buffers continue to provide a measure of resilience. Its most dangerous vulnerabilities, however, do not sit in a single economic indicator. They lie in the coupled amplification among policy credibility, fiscal space, energy-import pressure, capital-market transparency, social protest, disaster exposure, cyber governance, and resource policy. If a Middle East energy shock, rating or index pressure, implementation failures in large social programs such as free meals, local protests, or major disasters emerge at the same time, Indonesia could move from a zone of manageable pressure into a zone of compound stress. The report divides the vulnerabilities into 10 categories and reviews them through evidence layering, an impact-probability matrix, trigger monitoring, alternative explanations, and scenario analysis. The core conclusion is that over the next 0-18 months, the main issue to monitor is not any isolated event but a chain of events linking declining fiscal credibility, rising foreign-investor risk premiums, expanding energy subsidies, defects in social-policy implementation, and disaster-related emergency fiscal burdens.

title: OSINT Engineering Assessment of Alleged Bribery Risk in Thai State Agencies
authors: WEI MENG; TING WU
venue: Cambridge University Press (CUP)
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; News Media; Government Data; Corporate Records
Tags: Bribery; Thailand; Risk Assessment; Transparency; Public Agencies
abstract: This report conducts an engineered open-source intelligence assessment of the alleged bribery risk survey concerning Thai state agencies, disclosed by Thailand’s private sector in May 2026. The core source base consists of the original JSCCIB/Zero Corruption/Puean Mai Thon survey page, a sequence of reports by The Nation Thailand, public responses from named agencies, Transparency International CPI/GCB indicators, and OECD/NESDC public information on Thailand’s OECD accession process and its move toward the OECD Anti-Bribery Convention. The report applies strict evidentiary downgrading. The survey results are sufficient to support the judgment that some state-agency interfaces carry elevated perceived bribery-risk in corporate contacts, licensing, regulation, enforcement, and procurement. They are not sufficient, by themselves, to support a legal finding that any specific agency or official has accepted a bribe. The integrated judgment identifies two concentrated risk dimensions. The first is high-contact-frequency risk: highway/traffic police, judicial-process agencies, subdistrict administrative organizations, the Marine Department, and the Department of Highways are reported as having high frequencies of alleged benefit solicitation in corporate contacts. The second is high-amount risk: the Pollution Control Department, the Marine Department, the Excise Department, the Revenue Department, and judicial-process agencies are reported in higher ranges for average alleged amounts. Counter-RAG counterevidence indicates that the Pollution Control Department and the Marine Department publicly disputed the conclusions and requested more granular evidence from JSCCIB. At the same time, the Ministry of Transport initiated a fact review. These counterpoints do not overturn the fact that the survey exists and has created reputational risk.
Keywords: OSINT; Bribery Risk; Thai State Agencies; Corruption; Survey Analysis

title: Red-Teaming the Feedback Loop: Adversarial Cascade Simulation in Synthetic Primary Care
authors: Florian Odi Stummer
venue: Cambridge University Press (CUP)
Tags: healthcare; artificial intelligence; security; feedback loops; cybersecurity
abstract: Administrative artificial-intelligence (AI) pipelines in primary care are vulnerable to cascade amplification when feedback loops are present. Whether the six adversarial attack classes catalogued in our earlier threat taxonomy can be deliberately triggered through realistic perturbations, and whether a distributional monitoring pattern can distinguish adversarial perturbation from accidental drift, has not been tested in silico. We extend our previously published five-node Synthea-based simulation of administrative AI in primary care (1,000 synthetic patients; 100 Monte Carlo iterations per scenario) with eight adversarial scenarios spanning single-node, coordinated multi-node, stealth-ramp, and supply-chain compromise patterns, plus a novel data-poisoning attack using the publicly available Medical-Triage-500 dataset (HuggingFace) validated against 41,470 patient encounters from the MedDialog/HealthCareMagic-100k corpus. Results: the stealth-ramp scenario (1 per cent perturbation magnitude over 100 feedback cycles) is the only configuration crossing the previously reported clinical-relevance threshold for cascade amplification (Cascade Amplification Factor > 1.2), with total error 2.94 versus baseline accidental-drift 0.31. Single-shot adversarial injection at 10 per cent magnitude without feedback reaches total error 0.39, only 23 per cent above baseline, operationally indistinguishable from noise. Coordinated attacks at the Documentation and Coding nodes produce 1.55 times the error of single-node attacks under identical magnitude and feedback. The data-poisoning attack produces an 11.7 per cent undertriage rate at population scale. We argue that adversarial-robustness assessment for clinical AI pipelines must address persistent low-magnitude perturbation through feedback loops, not only high-magnitude single-shot scenarios. An Ontological Intrusion-Detection Architecture as constructive response is developed in a companion paper.
Keywords: adversarial attacks; cascade amplification; AI in healthcare; data poisoning; Synthea simulation

title: PhishViT: A Vision Transformer-Based Framework for Phishing Detection from Webpage Screenshots
authors: Jean Chrysostome Ndayisabye
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: PhishViT; Machine Learning; Real-time detection; Visual analysis
abstract: Abstract Phishing attacks represent one of the most pervasive and economically devastating cyber threats, with conventional detection systems relying primarily on URL lexical analysis, DNS inspection, and HTML source-code heuristics. These text-centric approaches share a fundamental blind spot: they do not examine the visual rendering of webpages as perceived by human users, leaving a critical detection gap exploited by visual-layer spoofing attacks. This paper presents PhishViT , a Vision Transformer- based framework for real-time phishing detection that operates exclusively on webpage screenshots. Unlike methods that analyze URL strings or page source code, PhishViT learns discriminative visual representations directly from rendered webpage images using a fine-tuned Data-efficient Image Transformer (DeiT-Small) architecture. An automated Playwright browser pipeline captures live screenshots which are classified as phishing or legitimate, with interpretable attention rollout heatmaps generated for each prediction. The framework is developed through an iterative three-phase process, starting from an initial prototype (V1: 253 screenshots, 78.95% accuracy), expanding to a balanced dataset (V2: 642 screenshots, 96.91% accuracy), and culminating in a rigorous top-tier evaluation framework (V3) with comprehensive baseline comparison against ResNet50, EfficientNet-B0, and ViT-Base; 5-fold cross-validation confirming 85.23% ± 1.18% accuracy ; ablation study validating each design choice; and robustness evaluation under six visual perturbation conditions. V3 evaluation demonstrates that DeiT-Small achieves 91.75% accu- racy , 93.48% precision, 89.58% recall, 91.49% F1-score, and AUC-ROC of 0.9928 at only 5.44 ms inference latency, outper- forming EfficientNet-B0 and ViT-Base while achieving the best efficiency-accuracy trade-off. These results establish PhishViT as a viable, interpretable, and computationally efficient visual-layer phishing detection framework suitable for real-time browser ex- tension deployment.
Keywords: Phishing detection; Vision Transformer; Webpage screenshots; Cyber threats; Image classification

title: Zero trust architectures and cybersecurity frameworks for mitigating AI-enabled misinformation campaigns
authors: Shahed Al-Tamimi; Qasem Abu Al-Haija
venue: Combating Misinformation in the Age of Generative AI
OSINT_Source_Types: Social Media; Public Records; News Media; Forums & Communities
Tags: Disinformation; AI; Cybersecurity; Deepfake; National Security
abstract: The endemic artificial intelligence (AI) facilitated misinformation encompassing deepfake videos, fake content, and machine-based propaganda campaigns that pose a huge threat to digital trust, public discourse, and national security. This chapter discusses how Zero Trust Architectures (ZTA) and next-generation cybersecurity models can be an effective building block to counter disinformation in the contemporary world. Though focusing on transformation from the strict trust boundaries to continuous verification, ZTA enables secure content authentication, access management, and behavior monitoring at every layer of information flow. The technical overview of ZTA principles and their integration of AI with detection models, API controls, identity management, and blockchain-based proof-of-origin systems are also covered in the chapter. Apart from this, it aligns the aforesaid technologies with international standards such as the NIST Cybersecurity Framework, MITRE AT&CK, and ISO/IEC standards to counter misinformation. Through case studies and best practices from actual action, this chapter shows how layered, proactive measures are needed to counter synthetic media manipulation and recover the integrity of the information space. This book encourages a multidisciplinary collaboration for the purpose of developing a robust cyber infrastructure to withstand future rounds of AI-driven fraud.
Keywords: Zero Trust Architecture; Misinformation; AI; Cybersecurity Frameworks; Digital Trust

title: CEDF-CS: A Record-Level Data CondensationFramework for Resource-Efficient Intrusion Detectionin Industrial IoT and Heterogeneous Network Environments
authors: George Karraz; Anas Shahin
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Cybersecurity; IIoT; Resource Efficiency; Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Cybersecurity systems increasingly rely on deep learning for intrusion detection, yet such models demand large labeled datasetsand GPU hardware, rendering them impractical for resource-constrained Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT) environments. Thispaper introduces the Cybersecurity Data Condensation and Discriminative Feature Extraction Framework (CEDF-CS), amulti-level pipeline that compresses cybersecurity datasets by a factor of 32 while preserving and amplifying their discriminativestructure. The framework applies hierarchical record-pair fusion to label-sorted, Z-score-normalized network traffic data,followed by adaptive correlation-based feature selection, and trains lightweight classifiers (SVM and shallow neural networks)on the compact representation. A central finding is that the 32× compressed dataset serves as a faithful and sufficientrepresentation of the full-scale data: models trained exclusively on the compressed set and evaluated on the entire originaldataset achieve F1 = 0.994 on the WUSTL-IIoT dataset (binary, 630,000 records) and Pearson R = 0.985 on CICIDS2017(six-class, 2.93 million records). These results are obtained through purely linear operations (averaging and correlation) thatproduce feature spaces with discriminative properties typically associated with deep nonlinear architectures. The frameworkoperates without GPUs, reduces training time by over 90%, eliminates 58–59% of features, and preserves minority-classstructure even when the rarest attack class comprises only 0.06% of records.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection; Data Compression; Industrial IoT; Deep Learning; Feature Selection

title: Knowledge, Attitudes, and Behavioral Risk Patterns Associated with Cybercrime Involvement Among Nigerian University Undergraduates
authors: ADEDEJI ABDULRAHMON ALAYANDE; ADEBISI OLUWAJUWON ADENIRAN; TAIWO DORCAS ADEBOWALE; DAMILARE ADEOLU OLAWUNI; MARVELLOUS ADEOLA ADEDEJI; HABEEBULAH ABDULLAHI

title: Enhancing Advanced Persistent Threat Detection: An Exploration of Particle Swarm Optimisation and Genetic Programming Techniques
authors: ; Abdullah Mamun
venue: Victoria University of Wellington Library
Tags: APT Detection; Cybersecurity; Evolutionary Computation; Multi-phase Behaviours
abstract: Advanced Persistent Threats (APTs) are prolonged and carefully orchestrated cyberattacks that use stealth, persistence, and multi-stage techniques to evade detection. Identifying these attacks remains difficult due to limited and imbalanced datasets, subtle behavioural differences between early attack phases and benign traffic, and the complexity of modelling multi-phase behaviours. Traditional approaches often depend on extensive expert-driven feature engineering, which can be costly and difficult to update as threats evolve. This thesis aims to investigate how Evolutionary Computation (EC) methods, in particular Particle Swarm Optimisation (PSO) and Genetic Programming (GP), can be used to support APT detection and classification in the presence of dataset limitations, class imbalance, and evolving attack characteristics. The research explores three complementary directions: using PSO for early-phase APT detection, applying GP for evolutionary feature construction in multi-phase settings, and developing a multi-tree GP framework that evolves separate trees to generate class-specific constructed features. The thesis begins with a detailed analysis of four publicly available APT datasets, examining their feature characteristics, phase coverage, class imbalance, and preprocessing requirements. Baseline Machine Learning (ML) experiments using imbalance-aware metrics highlight how severe class imbalance, limited phase coverage, and feature-quality issues constrain performance, and provide a consistent evaluation framework for subsequent chapters. To address early-phase detection, the thesis proposes a cooperative coevolution PSO-based classifier (CMS-PSOC) that assigns a swarm to each class and optimises a geometric mean (G-mean) objective to improve performance across Benign, Reconnaissance, and Establish foothold traffics. Experiments on the DAPT-2020 dataset show that CMS-PSOC achieves competitive, low-variance performance, demonstrating effective alignment with imbalance-aware objectives. For multi-phase APT detection, the thesis introduces a single-tree GP feature-construction framework (GP–DT), where internal nodes of the evolved tree act as constructed features and are evaluated using a Decision Tree (DT) wrapper and other downstream classifiers. Results on SCVICAPT-2021, DAPT-2020, and Unraveled show that GP–DT often enhances or maintains performance, particularly on SCVIC-APT-2021 multi-class tasks. To further support phase-specific detection, a class-informed multi-tree GP method (FEGPDT) is proposed, evolving one tree per class to construct phase-targeted features. Experiments on SCVIC-APT-2021 demonstrate that FEGPDT achieves competitive balanced accuracy in both binary and multi-class settings and frequently outperforms or matches GP–DT and other evolutionary methods. SHAP-based analyses provide additional insight into the relevance of the constructed features. Across all contributions, the thesis provides a cohesive examination of how EC can complement existing ML approaches by supporting imbalance-aware optimisation, adaptive feature construction, and structured modelling of phase-specific behaviours. The findings offer practical guidance for designing APT detection pipelines and highlight areas where dataset design and evaluation practices can be improved to better support future research.
Keywords: Advanced Persistent Threats; Particle Swarm Optimisation; Genetic Programming; Machine Learning; Feature Construction

title: Industrialized Deception: The Collateral Effects of LLM-Generated Misinformation on Digital Ecosystems
authors: Alexander Loth; Martin Kappes; Marc-Oliver Pahl
venue: Companion Proceedings of the ACM Web Conference 2026
Tags: disinformation; generative AI; mitigation strategies; human perception; experimental tools
abstract: Generative AI and misinformation research have evolved since our 2024 survey. This paper presents an updated perspective, transitioning from literature review to practical countermeasures. We report on changes in the threat landscape, including improved AI-generated content through Large Language Models (LLMs) and multimodal systems -- addressing the adverse impacts of AI on information quality. This work focuses on our practical contributions: JudgeGPT, a platform to evaluate human perception of AI-generated news, and RogueGPT, a controlled stimulus generation engine for research. Together, these tools form an experimental pipeline for studying how humans perceive and detect AI-generated misinformation. Our findings show that detection capabilities have improved, but competition between generation and detection continues. We discuss mitigation strategies such as LLM-based detection, inoculation approaches, and the dual-use nature of generative AI.

title: Hybrid 1D CNN–BiLSTM Framework for Network Traffic-Based Intrusion Detection in Resource-Constrained IoT Environments
authors: Mustapha Ismail Kwari; N. Rajkumar; C Selvarathi; Rabiu Aliyu Abdulkadir; Muhammad Salahudeen Mansur
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: CNN-LSTM; DDoS; DoS; NF-ToN-IoT; Machine Learning
abstract: Abstract Heterogeneous Internet of Things (IoT) networks have expanded the cyber-attack surface beyond the capability of traditional signature-based intrusion detection, especially in resource- and latency-constrained environments. This study presents a hybrid deep learning model combining one-dimensional Convolutional Neural Networks (1D-CNNs) and bidirectional Long Short-Term Memory (Bi-LSTM) layers collectively termed the Convolutional Neural Networks – Long Short-Term Memory (CNN-LSTM) framework for multi-class intrusion detection using the NF-ToN-IoT NetFlow dataset (600,100 flows; five classes: reconnaissance, distributed denial-of-service (DDoS), denial-of-service (DoS), benign, and data theft). The Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE), z-score normalisation, and temporal sequence construction were used in response to a significant class imbalance (e.g., theft 0.32% vs. reconnaissance 78.42%). The proposed CNN–LSTM achieved 85.07% accuracy, outperforming Random Forest (77%), XGBoost (83%), and an RF–XGB–CNN/LSTM ensemble (82%), with macro-precision and macro-recall of 0.87 and 0.85, respectively. Per-class results showed excellent recognition of reconnaissance (F1 = 0.93) and theft (F1 = 1.00) but weak detection of DoS (recall = 0.05) due to confusion with DDoS. Learning-curve analysis confirmed stable convergence and limited overfitting (~ 2–3% gap). To address DoS/DDoS misclassification, the study suggests extending sequence windows, incorporating discriminative flow-level features (e.g., inter-arrival variance and connection churn), and applying reweighted or focal loss. Generalizability will be validated via effect-size reporting, McNemar and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests, and stratified K-fold cross-validation. Overall, the regularised CNN–LSTM model demonstrates superior performance on NF-ToN-IoT, emphasizing architectural and data-centric refinements for robust IoT intrusion detection.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection; IoT Security; Deep Learning; Network Traffic; Cybersecurity
affiliations: Vel Tech Rangarajan Dr. Sagunthala R&D Institute of Science and Technology; Shandong Xiehe University; Maryam Abacha American University of Niger

title: Advanced AI-Based Real-Time Industrial Safety Sentinel for Smart Hazard Detection and Workplace Safety
authors: Snehaprabha Jadhav; Prof. (Dr.) Yogini Kulkarni; Dr. Pramod A. Jadhav; Dr. Vinod H. Patil; Dr. Amol K. Kadam
venue: International Journal of Recent Technology and Engineering (IJRTE)
Tags: Safety Monitoring; Cyber-Physical Systems; Vulnerability Detection; Automation
abstract: Industrial environments — including factories, construction sites, warehouses, and chemical plants — continue to experience hazardous incidents due to PPE noncompliance, unauthorised zone entry, and unsafe proximity to workers. Simultaneously, web, IoT, and edge applications deployed in these environments remain vulnerable to well-documented cyber threats, including SQL Injection, XSS, and broken access control. This paper presents the Intelligent Integrated Cyber-Physical Safety and Security Framework (IICPSSF), a novel hybrid edge-cloud AIsystem that uniquely and simultaneously enforces (i) real-time vision-based physical industrial safety monitoring, and (ii) adaptive cybersecurity design pattern enforcement — governed by a shared Unified LLMAssisted Natural Language Rule Engine (ULNLRE). The edge layer employs YOLO-E, an open-vocabulary object detection model, for promptable real-time perception at approximately 60 FPS. At the same time, a deterministic symbolic rule engine enforces auditable safety and security policies. A Pattern Knowledge Base and contextaware adaptive selection engine handle cybersecurity pattern recommendations for web, IoT, and edge applications. The system achieves 92.5 perent precision, 90.7 percent F1-score, and 99.5 percent specificity on physical safety violation detection across four violation types and demonstrates effective coverage of six OWASP Top 10 vulnerability classes.
Keywords: AI; Industrial Safety; Cybersecurity; IoT; Edge Computing; Real-Time Monitoring

title: Securing Dynamic Spectrum Access: Primary User Emulation Attack Detection Using Location-Aware Methods in Cognitive Radio
authors: Ravikiran S. Anande; Suhas S. Patil; Rahul K. Patil
venue: Advancement in Engineering and Science
Tags: CRN; PUE Attack; TDOA; Spectrum Security
abstract: The escalating demand for wireless spectrum, driven by the proliferation of diverse applications ranging from critical financial transactions to national defence and healthcare services, has resulted in severe spectrum congestion. Cognitive radio networks (CRNs) have evolved into a promising solution to this scarcity, enabling secondary users to adaptively access and utilize underutilized spectrum belonging to primary users. However, the inherent open nature of CRNs renders them vulnerable to sophisticated security threats, most notably Primary User Emulation (PUE) attacks. In a PUE attack, a malicious entity mimics the transmission characteristics of a legitimate primary user, misleading secondary users and gaining unauthorized control of the spectrum. The paper investigates this important security challenge by proposing a novel detection approach relying on time-difference-of-arrival (TDOA) location verification. By accurately determining signal arrival time at multiple receivers, this method can accurately estimate the location of the transmitting source. This location information is then used to differentiate between legitimate primary users and malicious emulators. The efficacy of this approach is demonstrated through simulations, showcasing its capability to precisely identify and mitigate PUE attacks, thus improving the overall security and reliability of CRNs.
Keywords: Cognitive Radio; Primary User Emulation; Security; Location-Aware Detection; Spectrum Access

title: Mapping the Landscape of LLM Deployment in the Wild: Prevalence, Patterns, and Perils
authors: Xinyi Hou; Jiahao Han; Yanjie Zhao; Shenao Wang; Haoyu Wang
venue: Abstracts of the 2026 ACM SIGMETRICS International Conference on Measurement and Modeling of Computer Systems
OSINT_Source_Types: Public Records; News Media; Corporate Records
Tags: LLM Deployment; Security Risks; Cybersecurity; Vulnerability Assessment
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly deployed through open-source and commercial frameworks, enabling individuals and organizations to self-host advanced LLM capabilities. As LLM deployments become prevalent, ensuring their secure and reliable operation has become a critical issue. However, insecure defaults and misconfigurations often expose LLM services to the public internet, posing serious security risks. This study conducted a large-scale empirical investigation of public-facing LLM deployments, focusing on the prevalence of services, exposure characteristics, systemic vulnerabilities, and associated risks. Through internet-wide measurements, we identified 320,102 public-facing LLM services across 15 frameworks and extracted 158 unique API endpoints, categorized into 12 groups based on functionality and security risk. Our analysis found that over 40% of endpoints used plain HTTP, and over 210,000 endpoints lacked valid TLS metadata. API exposure was highly inconsistent: some frameworks, such as Ollama, responded to over 35% of unauthenticated API requests, with about 15% leaking model or system information, while other frameworks implemented stricter controls. We observed widespread use of insecure protocols, poor TLS configurations, and unauthenticated access to critical operations. These security risks, such as model leakage, system compromise, and unauthorized access, are pervasive and highlight the need for a secure-by-default framework and stronger deployment practices.
Keywords: Large Language Models; Security Vulnerabilities; API Exposure; TLS Configuration; Insecure Protocols

title: High-Performance Computing for Cybersecurity: A Systematic Literature Review
authors: Selahadin Nurga
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: HPC; Cyber Threats; Data Analysis; Security Methodologies; Research Gaps
abstract: Abstract A systematic literature review (SLR) of High-Performance Computing (HPC) applications in cybersecurity is presented in this work. Traditional security systems find it difficult to offer real-time detection, large-scale data analysis, and quick reaction capabilities as cyber threats increase in complexity, volume, and speed. HPC systems present a feasible answer to these problems because of their capacity for parallel computations and quick processing of large datasets. The structured technique used in this SLR includes systematic database searches throughout IEEE Xplore, the ACM Digital Library, ScienceDirect, SpringerLink, and Google Scholar, together with clear inclusion/exclusion criteria and a quality assessment of the chosen papers. The review synthesizes eighteen key papers that looked at distributed computing frameworks, GPU acceleration, parallel processing architectures, and hybrid AI-HPC systems and these papers were published between 2012 and 2024. Threat modeling, cyber training simulators, cryptanalysis, intrusion detection systems, and malware analysis are important application areas. The review organizes findings into three thematic categories: (1) HPC infrastructure and cybersecurity methodologies; (2) cybersecurity applications and use cases of HPC; and (3) security problems and advanced technologies in HPC-enabled environments. High-Performance Computing (HPC) platform significantly increases the speed of security operations, according to a comparison investigation. In cryptanalysis workloads, HPC can yield speed gains of 5× (times) to 100× (time). Additionally, it makes it possible to analyze network traffic in real time at speeds higher than 100 Gbps. But there are still a number of difficulties. Cost-effective deployment, ensuring intrusion detection real-time latency of less than 100 milliseconds, integrating HPC with current security operations, and safeguarding the HPC infrastructure itself are some of these problems. The lack of defined benchmarks for HPC security workloads, a lack of operational environment validation, and a lack of focus on side-channel attacks on HPC systems are among the research gaps identified in the article. Future research directions, such as post-quantum cryptography on HPC systems, creating Standard Tests for HPC Security Workloads, testing HPC for Intrusion Detection with Real Numbers, are discussed in the review’s conclusion.
Keywords: High-Performance Computing; Cybersecurity; Literature Review; Intrusion Detection; Malware Analysis; Cryptanalysis

title: Topological-Spectral Cybersecurity Models for Detecting Network Anomalies in Critical Infrastructure
authors: Murali Krishna Pasupuleti

abstract: Abstract: Topological-spectral cybersecurity models offer a rigorous framework for detecting, explaining and governing network anomalies in critical infrastructure. This manuscript develops an interdisciplinary architecture that integrates graph theory, topological data analysis, spectral statistics, causal inference, trustworthy machine learning, big-data engineering and policy governance. It argues that critical infrastructure networks cannot be protected through event-level detection alone because adversarial behaviour often appears as relational deformation, persistent structural change, spectral drift or cross-sector cascade exposure. The book advances a research design in which telemetry is transformed into dynamic graph evidence, statistical baselines are calibrated under uncertainty, machine-learning models are evaluated for robustness and reproducibility, and governance artifacts translate anomaly intelligence into accountable operational action. Across five chapters, the manuscript progresses from foundations and uncertainty to statistical explanation, predictive cyber-AI, scalable analytics lifecycles and sectoral policy translation. The global orientation includes realistic implementation contexts across South Asia, Europe, Africa and the Americas, with attention to legacy infrastructure, regulatory accountability, sparse telemetry, cloud concentration and critical-service continuity. The resulting monograph is designed as a doctoral-level reference for researchers, practitioners and policymakers seeking mathematically grounded, operationally usable and governance-ready approaches to critical infrastructure cybersecurity. title: DISCOURSE ANALYSIS FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF A CYBERGROOMING DETECTION MODEL ON ROBLOX
authors: Ana Paola Castañón Marroquín; Brenda Ailed Rodríguez Colis; Andrea Bazán Durán; Luis Enrique Colmenares-Guillen
venue: FapUNIFESP (SciELO)
Tags: cybercrime; child protection; text mining; Spanish communities
abstract: Cybergrooming represents a growing threat on online gaming platforms such as Roblox, where anonymity and frequent interaction among child users create conditions conducive to child abuse and sexual harassment. The objective of the research that led to this article was to identify linguistic patterns in the discourse of groomers in Spanish-speaking Roblox communities and incorporate them into a computational model for the automatic detection of this cybercrime through text. To this end, a mixed-methods approach was developed, integrating Corpus-Assisted Discourse Studies with the CRISP-DM data mining methodology. A specialized corpus of 25 conversations was compiled and processed, then subjected to detailed analysis. As a main result, a pattern of discursive organization consisting of a sequence of seven conversational modules with specific predictive value and a set of 21 functional lexicogrammatical patterns with 224 associated collocations were identified, described, and subsequently incorporated into a text classification model capable of distinguishing grooming conversations with 93.33% accuracy. In this way, the study demonstrated the efficacy of discourse analysis as a basis for the development of systems for the automatic detection of cybercrimes against minors.
Keywords: cybergrooming; Roblox; discourse analysis; text classification; linguistic patterns

title: An Evidence-Native OSINT Risk Assessment of Items Concerning Peaceland Foundation in the HNPW 2026 Report
authors: WEI MENG; TING LIU
venue: Cambridge University Press (CUP)

abstract: This report provides an evidence-native open-source intelligence assessment of items concerning the Beijing Peaceland Foundation in the HNPW 2026 Report. It examines the foundation’s listing as network/partner for a session on China’s civilian maritime medical rescue vessel and innovative humanitarian equipment, the related article output on humanitarian innovation, and the stated commitment to mobilize China’s private sector for humanitarian action in Southeast Asia. Publicly available materials indicate that Peaceland Foundation is a Beijing-registered Chinese nonprofit established in 2018, with activities in emergency rescue, disaster relief, refugee assistance, demining, and anti-poaching. The report also reviews public information on a 5,000-ton civilian oceangoing medical rescue vessel co-initiated by the foundation and launched in September 2025, including its stated medical, rescue, training, and relief-supply functions. The key finding is bounded: Peaceland Foundation’s appearance in HNPW 2026 suggests more than a one-off publicity event, but does not prove formal OCHA operational partner status or the existence of a mature maritime humanitarian operating mechanism. The most defensible interpretation is that the case represents an early signal of institutionalization, with Chinese civil-society philanthropy entering international humanitarian networks through maritime medical capacity, technology-enabled equipment, and private-sector mobilization. The report identifies potential for humanitarian response capacity, while assessing mid-to-high governance risks involving humanitarian principles, integrity, host-country consent, maritime medical compliance, data and technology ethics, private-sector accountability, and geopolitical interpretation. A structured composite risk index of 6.34/10 is presented as an analytic judgment tool, not a statistical fact.
Keywords: OSINT; Peaceland Foundation; Risk Assessment; Humanitarian Innovation; Geopolitical Risks

title: A Practical Cybersecurity Ontology Generator Based on Hierarchical Clustering and Multi-way Tree
authors: Yixuan Wang; Bo Zhao; Xiaofu Song; Jiahui Zhu
venue: International Journal of Interactive Multimedia and Artificial Intelligence
Tags: Ontology Generation; Data Integration; Cybersecurity
abstract: Cybersecurity ontology development is typically carried out by cybersecurity experts and ontology engineers. While some existing works focus on extracting cybersecurity knowledge from either textual or structured data, few address the challenge of handling both types of data simultaneously. This paper presents Locust, a tool integrating structured data and domain corpus for comprehensive cybersecurity ontology generation. We use open source cybersecurity specifications as structured input to build the skeleton of the ontology, and use the domain corpus to enrich and finalise the ontology. Additionally, we propose a methodology for filtering and simplifying the ontology using hierarchical clustering and multi-way tree. Experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in acquiring a cybersecurity ontology from specific domain data sources. Locust is implemented in Java and is available as an open source tool.
Keywords: Cybersecurity Ontology; Hierarchical Clustering; Multi-way Tree; Open Source Tool

title: Editor's Note
authors: Paulo Alonso Gaona-García
venue: International Journal of Interactive Multimedia and Artificial Intelligence

abstract: Recent advances in Artificial Intelligence (AI) applied to Human–Computer Interaction (HCI) have been characterized by the convergence of immersive technologies, semantic reasoning, and data-centric learning paradigms. In augmented reality (AR), AI enables real-time interaction by integrating computer vision and contextual understanding into dynamic environments, although it simultaneously introduces new security vulnerabilities that require robust AI-driven protection mechanisms. In parallel, AI-driven cybersecurity has evolved toward proactive and adaptive models that leverage machine learning for real-time threat detection, anomaly analysis, and predictive mitigation, significantly enhancing the resilience of digital systems. Ontologies further strengthen this landscape by providing structured, semantically rich representations of cybersecurity knowledge, facilitating interoperability, automated reasoning, and intelligent threat assessment. Additionally, advances in visual analytics and time series foundation models are enabling the processing of large-scale temporal and multimodal datasets, supporting more sophisticated data interpretation and decision-making processes in complex environments. Modern computer vision systems leverage deep learning architectures such as convolutional neural networks and vision transformers to extract high-level features, enabling accurate object recognition, pattern detection, and scene understanding. Advances in multimodal AI systems—capable of integrating text, images, audio, and video—have become essential for achieving more comprehensive and context-aware intelligence, especially in domains such as medical imaging and interactive systems. Based on these advances highlight, this regular issue presents the most notable research in this direction.

title: MRP-LLM: Multitask Reflective Large Language Models for Privacy-Preserving Next POI Recommendation
authors: Ziqing Wu; Zhu Sun; Dongxia Wang; Lu Zhang; Jie Zhang; Yew Soon Ong
venue: Proceedings of the 34th ACM Conference on User Modeling, Adaptation and Personalization
Tags: Multitask Learning; User Modeling; Data Privacy; Recommendation Systems
abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown promising potential for next Point-of-Interest (POI) recommendation. However, existing methods only perform direct zero-shot prompting, leading to ineffective extraction of user preferences, insufficient injection of collaborative signals, and a lack of user privacy protection. As such, we propose a novel Multitask Reflective Large Language Model for Privacy-preserving Next POI Recommendation (MRP-LLM), aiming to exploit LLMs for better next POI recommendation while preserving user privacy. Specifically, the Multitask Reflective Preference Extraction Module first utilizes LLMs to distill each user's fine-grained (i.e., categorical, temporal, and spatial) preferences into a knowledge base (KB). The Neighbor Preference Retrieval Module retrieves and summarizes the preferences of similar users from the KB to obtain collaborative signals. Subsequently, aggregating the user's preferences with those of similar users, the Multitask Next POI Recommendation Module generates the next POI recommendations via multitask prompting. Meanwhile, during data collection, a Privacy Transmission Module is specifically devised to preserve sensitive POI data. Extensive experiments on three real-world datasets demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed MRP-LLM in providing more accurate next POI recommendations with user privacy preserved.
Keywords: Large Language Models; Privacy Preservation; Point-of-Interest Recommendation; User Preferences; Collaborative Signals

title: A Structured Training Framework for Maritime Cybersecurity Education: The CyberSEA Case
authors: Germán de Melo Rodríguez; Aris Chronopoulos; Tomaz Gregorič; Lakhvir Singh; Wili Helenius; Monika Klein; Konstantinos Karampidis; Andrei Bautu; Natalia Wawrzyniak
venue: Maritime Transport Conference
Tags: Maritime Security; Cybersecurity Education; Incident Response; Human Factor
abstract: The increasing integration of digital systems into maritime operations has introduced new dependencies between shipboard IT and OT environments, exposing critical functions such as navigation, propulsion control, communication, and cargo management to cyber-related risks. While international regulatory [1] instruments require cyber risk management to be addressed within Safety Management Systems, practical implementation at the operational level remains inconsistent. A key limitation identified in both incident analyses and sector studies is the insufficient preparedness of maritime personnel to recognize and respond to cyber incidents. Existing maritime education and training frameworks provide limited coverage of cybersecurity, often treating it as a compliance or awareness topic rather than an operational competence. As a result, seafarers frequently lack system-specific knowledge, procedural guidance, and decision-making support for cyber-related events occurring during normal operations. The CyberSEA project was initiated to address this gap through the development of targeted, practice-oriented training resources for maritime professionals. One of its core outputs is a structured maritime cybersecurity training course designed to support operational readiness by focusing on realistic threat scenarios, procedural response, and the human element of cyber risk management. The course adopts a human-centred and operationally oriented approach, recognizing that seafarers play a critical role in both preventing and mitigating cyber incidents onboard vessels. The specific objectives of the course are to: Increase awareness of maritime-specific cyber threats and vulnerabilities across critical shipboard and shore-based systems; Enable recognition of early indicators of cyber incidents and abnormal system behaviour; Support informed and timely decision-making during cyber-related events; Enhance procedural competence in responding to cyber incidents in alignment with SMS and IMO guidance; Promote a culture of cyber risk awareness and shared responsibility within maritime organizations. A key methodological component was the development of scenario-based learning content [2]. Real-world maritime cyber incidents, documented attack cases, and technically plausible hypothetical scenarios were analyzed and transformed into structured training scenarios. These scenarios serve as the pedagogical backbone of the course, ensuring that learning outcomes are grounded in realistic operational contexts rather than abstract technical concepts. The course design aligns with contemporary principles of vocational education and adult learning, emphasizing modularity, contextualization, and applied learning. Learning outcomes were defined to reflect operational roles and responsibilities onboard vessels, ensuring relevance for officers, ratings, and shore-based personnel. The CyberSEA training course is organized into modular learning units, enabling flexible integration into maritime academies, vocational training programmes, and continuous professional development schemes. Each module addresses a specific cybersecurity theme while maintaining coherence within the overall course structure. Core thematic areas covered include: Fundamentals of maritime cybersecurity and the evolving threat landscape; Cyber vulnerabilities in navigation, propulsion, communication, and cargo systems; Human-factor vulnerabilities, including social engineering and phishing; Detection of cyber incidents and anomaly recognition; Procedural response to cyber incidents onboard and ashore; Integration of cybersecurity into Safety Management Systems; Regulatory and policy frameworks relevant to maritime cybersecurity. A distinguishing feature of the course is the integration of hands-on exercises and remote laboratory environments, allowing trainees to engage with simulated cyber threats in a controlled setting. These practical components are designed to reinforce theoretical knowledge and to develop situational awareness, procedural discipline, and confidence in responding to cyber incidents. Assessment activities embedded within the modules focus on knowledge comprehension and scenario-based decision-making rather than purely technical proficiency, reflecting the course’s emphasis on the human element. By combining system-specific risk analysis, scenario-based learning, and applied training methods, the course addresses limitations identified in existing maritime education frameworks. The main contribution of this work lies in translating regulatory requirements and cybersecurity principles into a practical training model tailored to maritime operations. The course design demonstrates how cybersecurity awareness, procedural competence, and human-centered learning can be integrated into a coherent educational framework supporting maritime cyber resilience.
Keywords: maritime cybersecurity; training framework; cyber risk management; operational competence; scenario-based learning

title: Artificial Intelligence–Driven Cybersecurity Frameworks for Securing Management Information Systems in Smart Enterprises
authors: Sani Lawal
venue: ScienceOpen
Tags: Cybersecurity Frameworks; Digital Transformation; Risk Assessment; Data Privacy; Dynamic Risk Mitigation
abstract: The rapid digital transformation of modern enterprises has increased the dependence of Management Information Systems (MIS) on interconnected networks, cloud platforms, Internet of Things (IoT) devices, and data-driven business processes. While these technologies improve operational efficiency and decision-making capabilities, they also introduce complex cybersecurity risks that traditional security mechanisms often struggle to address. Artificial Intelligence (AI) has emerged as a promising solution for strengthening cybersecurity by enabling real-time threat detection, predictive risk assessment, automated incident response, and adaptive security management. This paper examines the role of AI-driven cybersecurity frameworks in protecting Management Information Systems within smart enterprises. It explores how machine learning, deep learning, behavioral analytics, and intelligent automation can be integrated into enterprise security architectures to identify anomalies, prevent cyberattacks, and enhance organizational resilience. The study further discusses implementation challenges, including data privacy concerns, algorithmic bias, model transparency, and evolving threat landscapes. A conceptual framework is proposed to support continuous monitoring, proactive threat intelligence, and dynamic risk mitigation across enterprise environments. The findings suggest that AI-driven cybersecurity frameworks can significantly improve the confidentiality, integrity, and availability of organizational information assets while supporting sustainable digital transformation. The paper contributes to the growing body of knowledge on intelligent cybersecurity strategies for next-generation enterprise information systems.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Cybersecurity; Management Information Systems; Smart Enterprises; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Threat Detection; Incident Response

title: <b>Human-Computer Interaction in Cybersecurity: Leveraging Digital Systems to Combat Rural Banditry in Nigeria </b>
authors: Sanni Abubakar Omuya Ogirima; E. A. Oguntade
venue: International Journal of IoT, Embedded Systems and Industrial Automation
Tags: Counter-Banditry; HCI Design Principles; Digital Surveillance
abstract: Background: Rural banditry has become one of the most damaging security problems in Nigeria’s northwest, displacing over a million people and collapsing agricultural economies in Zamfara, Katsina, Kaduna, and Sokoto states. Nigerian security institutions have responded, in part, by deploying digital surveillance platforms, geographic mapping systems, and incident reporting tools. These investments, however, have largely failed to produce the operational improvements that policymakers anticipated. This study argues that a substantial part of that failure is attributable to poor Human-Computer Interaction (HCI) design: systems built for environments very different from the ones in which they are deployed, and for users very different from those who actually operate them. Objective: This study aimed to: (1) identify HCI-related deficiencies in digital security systems deployed for counter-banditry operations in northwest Nigeria; (2) assess the relationship between interface usability and system adoption among security personnel; and (3) propose a set of HCI design principles tailored to the Nigerian counter-banditry operational context. Methods: A concurrent mixed-methods design was used, combining a structured survey of 120 security personnel across three states with in-depth interviews of 15 key informants. Usability was measured using the System Usability Scale (SUS). Adoption frequency and perceived operational effectiveness were also captured. Pearson correlation analysis examined the relationship between usability and adoption rates. Qualitative data were analysed thematically using the six-phase framework. Results: The mean SUS score across deployed platforms was 48.3 (SD = 14.7), well below the threshold of acceptable usability, and only 23.3% of respondents recorded scores above 70. A statistically significant positive correlation was found between usability scores and system adoption rates (r = 0.63, p < 0.001). Only 38.3% of respondents reported daily or near-daily system use, and 31.7% reported that the system improved their operational effectiveness. Qualitative analysis identified five recurring barriers: interface complexity beyond user literacy levels, poor connectivity handling, English-only interfaces in predominantly Hausa-speaking operational environments, absence of participatory design, and dashboards that impair rather than support situational awareness. Conclusion: The study proposes five corresponding HCI design principles for counter-banditry security systems and recommends that HCI evaluation be embedded as a mandatory requirement in public security technology procurement in Nigeria.
Keywords: Human-Computer Interaction; Cybersecurity; Rural Banditry; Usability; Nigeria

title: DIGITAL EVIDENCE ACQUISITION FOLLOWING MINING AND NETWORK ATTACKS IN A PRIVATE BLOCKCHAIN
authors: Ali Hamadou; Rene Ndoundam; Abdoul Aziz Issaka Hassane; Mbopgue Timo Patrick Noel
venue: International Journal of Advanced Research
Tags: cybersecurity; private blockchain; evidence collection; methodology
abstract: The rapid adoption of blockchain technology has introduced new cybersecurity challenges, particularly in private blockchain environments where mining and network attacks pose significant threats. This study investigates the digital forensics process within private blockchain environments, with a specific focus on methodologies for acquiring digital evidence following mining and network attacks. In this context, we propose two complementary evidence acquisition models applied to Hyperledger Fabric: a post-mortem model using forensic disk imaging and hash verification (dd, sha256sum), and a live acquisition model using Hyperledger Explorer\\\'s REST API. Attack simulations including Denial-of-Service (DoS), 51%, and selfish mining attacks were conducted to validate the proposed models. The proposed models successfully enabled the identification and collection of user-generated and machine-generated evidence, including cryptographic transactions, node event logs, smart contract interactions, and network traffic metadata, while preserving chain of custody integrity. This work contributes a structured, practical methodology for blockchain forensics in private environments, addressing the unique challenges posed by the decentralized and immutable nature of blockchain systems.
Keywords: digital forensics; blockchain; evidence acquisition; mining attacks; network attacks; Hyperledger Fabric

title: THE CHALLENGES IN CYBER SECURITY – A REVIEW
