title: CRIMINAL LIABILITY FOR CYBERCRIMES: A COMPARATIVE LEGAL ANALYSIS OF THE LEGISLATION OF UKRAINE AND THE EUROPEAN UNION
authors: Dmitry Lopashchuk; Bogdan Krymchanin
venue: Metaverse Science, Society and Law
Tags: cyber law; cybersecurity; comparative study; international cooperation
abstract: This scientific study provides a comparative legal analysis of criminal liability for cybercrimes in Ukraine and the European Union. In particular, it examines theoretical approaches to understanding cybercrimes as an object of criminal law regulation, as well as the specific features of the legal framework establishing liability for such acts in the national legislation of Ukraine and in the legal acts of the European Union. It is determined that contemporary cybercrime is characterized by a high level of latency, transnational nature, technological complexity, and the capacity to cause significant harm to the information security of the state, human rights, and both public and private interests. The study also analyzes the common and distinctive features of the legal regulation of cybercrimes, approaches to defining their characteristics, and the specifics of establishing the limits of criminal liability for offenses in the field of information and communication systems. It is substantiated that the legislation of Ukraine generally complies with fundamental international and European approaches to combating cybercrime; however, it requires further improvement in terms of harmonizing terminology, clarifying certain elements of criminal offenses, and further developing mechanisms of international cooperation. It is concluded that the adaptation of national criminal legislation to modern European standards is an important prerequisite for enhancing the effectiveness of countering cybercrime in the context of digitalization and contemporary challenges to Ukraine’s national security.
Keywords: cybercrime; criminal liability; legal analysis; Ukraine; European Union

title: StormShield: Fingerprint-Based Detection and Mitigation of RRC Signaling Storms in O-RAN 5G RANs
authors: Noemi Giustini; Andrea Lacava; Leonardo Bonati; Stefano Maxenti; Michele Polese; Tommaso Melodia; Francesca Cuomo
venue: Proceedings of the 19th ACM Conference on Security and Privacy in Wireless and Mobile Networks
Tags: signaling storm; Malicious UEs; gNB resources; StormShield; O-RAN
abstract: 5G networks provide low-latency, high throughput, and massive connectivity, yet the control plane remains exposed to several security threats. Among the most common and impactful threats are Denial-of-Service (DoS) attacks, with Radio Resource Control (RRC) signaling storms being particularly effective and difficult to mitigate. In this attack, a malicious User Equipment (UE) aims to exhaust Next Generation Node Base (gNB) resources, preventing legitimate UEs from establishing a connection. Existing defenses are typically limited to detection, only evaluated through numerical simulations, and cannot discern between high-load network conditions and attacks. Most of them also assume static setups and do not take mobility into account. In this paper, we first evaluate the feasibility of the signaling storm attack by using the OpenAirInterface(OAI) 5G protocol stack. Then, we propose StormShield, a signaling storm attack detection and mitigation technique implemented as an xApp on an O-RAN Near-Real-Time (near-RT) RAN Intelligent Controller (RIC). It fingerprints and blocks Malicious UEs (MUEs) before gNB resources are exhausted. We prototyped our solution on an Over-The-Air (OTA) testbed with OAI, NVIDIA Aerial, and two different gNB setups. The first one leverages an USRP X410 Software-defined Radio (SDR) with 8.1 functional split; the second a commercial Foxconn Radio Unit (RU) with 7.2 functional split. Our experimental evaluation demonstrates that StormShield effectively prevents gNB resource exhaustion, identifying and blocking MUEs with an average detection accuracy of 97.6% within 106.5 ms from the beginning of the attack.
Keywords: 5G security; RRC signaling storms; DoS attacks; Network detection; Mitigation techniques
affiliations: Northeastern University; Sapienza University of Rome

title: Knowing your weaknesses is your greatest strength: Mapping CVE to CWE by leveraging CWE Hierarchy and fine-tuned LLMs
authors: Stefano Simonetto; Ronan Oostveen; Thijs van Ede; Peter Bosch; Willem Jonker
venue: Proceedings of the ACM Asia Conference on Computer and Communications Security
Tags: Cybersecurity; AI; Machine Learning; Weakness Identification
abstract:
Effective defense against threat actors requires that security professionals accurately identify the underlying weaknesses associated with common vulnerabilities and exposures (CVEs). This under standing is crucial for deploying appropriate defensive mechanisms and prioritizing remediation efforts. However, manually mapping CVEs to common weakness enumerations (CWEs) has become increasingly impractical due to the rapid increase of new CVEs and
the extensive, complex CWE taxonomy. In 2025, the number of CVEs awaiting analysis exceeded 25,000.

To automate the mapping between CVEs and CWEs, we propose to leverage two insights. To harness the power of large language models, we first fine-tune different language models to perform this mapping based on the vulnerability-to-weakness relation. Second, we propose a supervised framework leveraging the hierarchical structure of CWEs, where we first categorize vulnerabilities into
broad CWE classes (e.g., Injection, Buffer Overflow), which helps capture high-level patterns, and then utilizes specialized subnet works to distinguish fine-grained differences within each class.

Evaluated on a benchmarkthat covers 95% of all CVEs associated with a CWE, our approach improves F1-score by 5% over the best prior supervised method, demonstrating the value of combining model fine-tuning with hierarchy-aware classification.
Keywords: CVE; CWE; Vulnerability Mapping; Large Language Models; Automated Analysis

title: An Intelligent AI-Based Cybersecurity Frameworkfor Real-Time Threat Detection and Response
authors: Jasmine K S; Gayatri V K
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: cybersecurity; machine learning; real-time threat response; network traffic analysis
abstract: Abstract There is a need to monitor data from system logs and network traffics and analyze it to identify suspicious activities for security aspects. In this paper, an AI-based cybersecurity system is developed to identify and give response to threats in computer networks. The system collects It and uses AI techniques to understand patterns and detect possible threats. When a threat is detected, alerts are generated and basic response actions are performed. Watching logs and traffic nonstop and it spots odd signs that could mean something harmful is happening. Instead of just following fixed rules like older tools do, this approach learns how things usually behave to catch unseen threats. Pulling in info from many places, it uses basic smart tricks to find what stands out. Once it sees a possible danger, warnings pop up alongside steps taken like notifying users and blocking suspicious activity. Everything gets recorded for later analysis. Working in real time, the system handles different types of network data efficiently. A unified approach combines monitoring, detection, and response into a single flow, improving detection speed and reducing response time. The system is simple, flexible, and suitable for small-scale environments while allowing future enhancements.
Keywords: AI-based cybersecurity; threat detection; real-time monitoring; network security; data analysis

title: Security challenges in large-scale IoT systems
authors: Sowmya T Rao; Anuj Kumar
venue: Advanced Investigation Strategies for IoT Forensics
Tags: Internet of Things; cybersecurity; large-scale systems; attack surface; security challenges
abstract: The untapped explosion of the Internet of Things (IoT) has revolutionized industries and everyday life by connecting a vast collection of heterogeneous devices into vast, evolving networks that energize applications ranging from smart cities to industrial automation, healthcare, and intelligent transportation. But this is a massive scale, and heterogeneity brings enormous security challenges that conventional security models can barely manage. This chapter explains the distinctive capabilities of security threats of large-scale IoT implementations, starting with a critical examination of their multi-level hierarchies, including a large range of constrained devices, communication protocols, and cloud-edge systems, all of which contribute to developing an extensive attack surface. It also examines the diversity of cyberattacks specific to such environments, including distributed denial-of-service (DDoS) attacks, hijacking of devices, data breaches, spoofing, and physical tampering, emphasizing how attackers assault weaknesses in the perception, network, and application layers. With the resource constraints and scalability requirements of IoT devices, the chapter discusses existing standards and customized security solutions such as lightweight cryptography, identity and access management schemes, machine learning-based anomaly detection, blockchain for trust establishment, and decentralized security frameworks. How much of this new technology, such as edge and fog computing, in achieving localized security controls and real-time response to threats, is helpful is also discussed. Realistic case studies of industrial and smart city IoT deployments offer tangible illustrations of security issues and mitigation techniques in actual large-scale deployments. Lastly, the chapter offers future work directions such as quantum-resistant cryptography, Artificial Intelligence (AI)-based adaptive defense solutions, and looking for unifying security frameworks that can evolve with the fast-paced era of IoT. Along the way, images and formal analysis make it possible to have a solid grip, providing readers with the information they require to survive and obtain today&s;s and tomorrow&s;s complex-scale, state-of-the-art IoT systems.
Keywords: IoT security; cyber threats; DDoS attacks; lightweight cryptography; machine learning; smart cities

title: Best practices in IoT forensics
authors: Manish Thakral; Keshav Kaushik; Farhan Shaikh; Anita Devare; Manoj H Devare
venue: Advanced Investigation Strategies for IoT Forensics
Tags: Internet of Things; Digital Forensics; Cybersecurity; Best Practices
abstract: The Internet of Things (IoT) has introduced connection in most appliances and different industrial objects. Although it is evident that such interconnection provides high levels of convenience and efficiency, the problem of digital forensics is apparent here. Over the past few years, studying the IoT device-involved mishaps necessitates the application of unique methods to ensure the safety and efficiency of approaches used in evidence collection and analysis. This chapter aims at discussing various strategies of performing IoT forensics so as to deal with the difficulties that characterize such devices. They will start by looking at the type of environment that IoT operates in, the different devices that are in use, the different communication channels and data interfaces. It is imperative that forensic professionals comprehend these nuances as part of their endeavors to penetrate the manifold arrangements of IoT networks. The primary problem to address in IoT forensics is therefore the large and heterogeneous amount of data from connected objects. This type of saturation can prove problematic when using traditional methodologies of forensic analysis, meaning that new methods and means of both data acquisition and analysis must be developed. This chapter outlines the processes of investigating IoT devices for digital evidence, how to acquire and preserve it while still observing chain of custody and integrity. Additionally, IoT devices cannot be relied on as having installed standard security features, hence opening themselves to exploitation. This puts into question not only for device owners but also for forensic practitioners when confronted with infected systems or media. This chapter presents how to evaluate IoT devices’ security status and how to identify that a device has been tampered with or accessed illicitly IoT forensic purposes. Further, the question of bureaucratic law and ethics also remains a focal point of concern especially understanding rights of privacy and protection of data for IoT forensics purposes. Offenders have to operate within these numerous legal systems sometimes concurrently with ensuring that the methods used by the investigators do not violate the forensic norms. Last but not the least, final section of this chapter paves way to look into the future trends of IoT forensics, the prime areas that are already in their nascent stage such as the advent of new and enhanced forensic tools and technique, influence of artificial intelligence and machine learning in forensics, and changing dynamics of threats. Consequently, this chapter will offer a brief on the established IoT forensics best practices as an effort to empower the forensic investigators, law enforcement agencies, and cybersecurity professionals to better handle the myriads of difficulties that stem from the constantly increasing IoT devices populace.
Keywords: IoT Forensics; Digital Evidence; Data Acquisition; Chain of Custody; Security Evaluation; Forensic Tools; Artificial Intelligence

title: Confident yet Concerned: Inconsistencies in Computing Students’ Attitudes on Cybersecurity
authors: Victor Adama; Robert Biddle; Nalin Arachchilage; Danielle Lottridge
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: cybersecurity education; student awareness; phishing susceptibility; online safety
abstract: Abstract Today’s young adults are most immersed in technology, leading in feelings of powerlessness in man-aging online privacy across many platforms, and particularly susceptible to phishing attacks. This raises questions about their general, wide-ranging attitudes to-wards and management of cybersecurity. How do young, tech-savvy adults approach cybersecurity? We seek a better understanding of their cybersecurity knowledge, attitudes and experiences, in particular in addressing deceptive online communications. We surveyed a group of ‘lead users’: computing university students (n = 236). By combining thematic analysis of open-ended responses with quantitative data, we provide insights into their experiences and perceptions. While students demonstrate reasonable cybersecurity awareness, their cyber-security experiences vary, and inconsistencies exist around their practices, perceptions of responsibility, and sup-port structures. Findings also reveal four key thematic tensions: 1) Computing students are knowledgeable yet have persistent incorrect beliefs, 2) They learn more about keeping safe from sources outside the classroom, 3) They have limited assistance and have fallen victim to cybercrime, and 4) Many are confident, yet others are concerned about their own safety and responsibility. Through cluster analysis of attitudes, we identify two groups, with one feeling less prepared, less confident, yet expressing a desire to learn more. Established measures of intentions and objective knowledge were correlated to preparedness. Self-efficacy correlated to confidence and predicted cluster membership.
Keywords: cybersecurity; attitudes; students; phishing; online privacy
affiliations: University of Auckland; Carleton University; RMIT Europe

title: Comprehending Students/Teachers' Motivations in Cybersecurity/AI-Powered Metaverse Education Applications
authors: Mishall Hammed Al-Zubaidie; Rakhimberdiev Kuvonchbek; Khayitova Oydinoy; Naskath Jahangeer
venue: Securing the Metaverse in the Era of Scientific Competition
Tags: Education; Virtual Reality; Augmented Reality; Cybersecurity in Education; IoT
abstract: E-learning has become an important pillar of all aspects of life. In educational contexts, the Internet of Things, augmented reality, and virtual reality are all incorporated into the metaverse (MV), a network of linked virtual worlds that allows for realistic dimensional experiences. Examining the possible effects, such as privacy/ security, in this context is crucial as the use of MV is growing in many fields, including e-education security. Therefore, using the technology acceptance model (TAM) and hedonic consumption behavior theory (HCBT) is important to determine the acceptability of MV security in supporting the educational environment. The chapter supports the significance of TAM, HCBT, trust, identity, privacy, and security framework (TIPS), and understanding students'/teachers' security issues in understanding the adoption of the MV in e-education. Also, this chapter outlines the incentives for students and teachers to adopt MV in education systems. Finally, this chapter provides recommendations and strategic insights into adopting MV security in educational systems.
Keywords: Metaverse; E-learning; Cybersecurity; Privacy; Security; Technology Acceptance Model; Hedonic Consumption Behavior
affiliations: Thi Qar University; Tashkent State University of Economics; Nord University

title: Federated Learning, Temporal Convolutional Networks, Electric Vehicle Charging Infrastructure, Intrusion Detection, Cybersecurity, Privacy-Preserving Machine Learning
authors: Mohammed Gamal Ragab; Hitham Alhussian; Said Jadid Abdulkadir; Majdy Eltahir; Ayed Alwadain
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Cybersecurity; AI; Machine Learning; Electric Vehicles; Intrusion Detection
abstract: Abstract The rapid growth of electric vehicle (EV) charging infrastructure has increased exposure to cyberattacks, while conventional centralized intrusion detection remains poorly suited to distributed and privacy-sensitive EVSE environments. This study proposes a federated learning framework based on a Dual-Attention Temporal Convolutional Network (DA-TCN) for collaborative cyberattack detection without centralized data sharing. The model combines dilated causal convolutions with channel and temporal attention to capture complex dependencies in multimodal EVSE telemetry. To improve federated optimization, we introduce Federated Stochastic Weight Averaging (FedSWA) and client-local mixup augmentation, which together enhance generalization and robustness across distributed clients. Evaluated on the CICEVSE2024 dataset, the proposed framework achieved 99.18\% accuracy and 98.95\% macro F1-score, outperforming a centralized baseline (98.96\% accuracy) while maintaining perfect recall for benign and cryptojacking traffic. With an inference latency of 7.21~ms per batch and a model size of 4.07~MB, the framework is well suited for real-time edge deployment. A complementary Isolation Forest module provides unsupervised zero-day anomaly detection. These results demonstrate that federated learning can deliver accurate, lightweight, and deployment-ready intrusion detection for privacy-preserving EV charging infrastructure.
Keywords: Federated Learning; Intrusion Detection; Electric Vehicle Charging; Cybersecurity; Privacy-Preserving; Temporal Convolutional Networks
affiliations: Universiti Teknologi Petronas; King Khalid University; King Saud University

title: TOSSS: A CVE-based Software Security Benchmark for Large Language Models
authors: Marc Damie; Murat Bilgehan Ertan; Domenico Essoussi; Angela Makhanu; Gaetan Peter; Roos Wensveen
venue: Proceedings of the 12th ACM International Workshop on Security and Privacy Analytics
Tags: AI; Security Assessment; Vulnerability; CVE-based; LLMs
abstract: With their increasing capabilities, Large Language Models (LLMs) are now used across many industries. They have become useful tools for software engineers and support a wide range of development tasks. As LLMs are increasingly used in software development workflows, a critical question arises: are LLMs good at software security? At the same time, organizations worldwide invest heavily in cybersecurity to reduce exposure to disruptive attacks. The integration of LLMs into software engineering workflows may introduce new vulnerabilities and weaken existing security efforts.

title: Innovative approaches and techniques in digital forensics
authors: Manish Thakral; Keshav Kaushik; Farhan Shaikh; Anita Devare; Manoj H Devare
venue: Advanced Investigation Strategies for IoT Forensics
Tags: digital evidence; cybercrime investigation; data acquisition; anomaly detection
abstract: Digital technological enhancement over the past ten years has been a broad area since the most sophisticated and voluminous digital evidence came onto the scene. This chapter aims to discuss advanced approaches in the context of the digital forensics domain, which present the most recent methods and tools used in digital crime investigation. Digital forensics is defined as the process for the identification of electronic evidence, the preservation and investigation of digital evidence from computers, mobile phones, and networks. The main objective in a civil or criminal case is to search for and offer “admissible evidence” in a case. Among the most significant progresses made in the field of digital forensics is the enhancement of complex approaches to data acquisition. Database techniques in general are not very effective in situations when data is encrypted or fragmented. Modern techniques help forensic specialists to get past encryption, retrieve files that have been deleted, and restore damaged data. Some of these techniques are memory analysis, which deals with analyzing volatile memory with a view to searching for evidence that is not stored on the hard disk, and live forensics, which deals with the analysis of a running system to capture data. Another significant area of advancement is the use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) in digital forensics. AI and ML algorithms can process large volumes of data quickly and identify patterns that might be missed by human investigators. These technologies are particularly useful in sorting through massive datasets, recognizing suspicious activity, and predicting potential security breaches. For example, anomaly detection algorithms can identify irregularities in network traffic, which might indicate a cyber-attack. Network forensics has also progressed more dramatically, especially in regard to network traffic analysis for monitoring and investigation of cybercrimes. Some of the advanced methods are deep packet inspection, which inspects the data part and the header of the packet when it goes through a checkpoint, and network flow analysis, which analyzes the pattern of data traffic within networks in order to detect abnormality. In addition, the application of blockchain in digital forensics is being developed as a methodology that guarantees the incorruptibility of the evidence. Blockchain, as the easiest explanation, can help to maintain a record of the evidence chain of custody and thus improve the sanctity of the digital forensic procedure.
Keywords: digital forensics; evidence preservation; AI in forensics; network forensics; blockchain; memory analysis; live forensics

title: Mapping the field of open-source investigations
authors: Stephen D. Reese; Azza El-Masri
venue: The Routledge Companion to Journalism Education
OSINT_Source_Types: Social Media; Public Records; News Media; Forums & Communities
Tags: human rights; investigation; accountability; verification
abstract: Open-source intelligence (OSINT) exploits the abundance of publicly available information, social media, and other user-generated online content, which enable investigations into human rights, conflict zone, and other issues. With a combination of technology, forensic research, and journalism, this new globalised field has gained prominence from projects involving diverse contributors, such as the massive investigation into the 2021 US Capitol riot, spanning communities of citizen “sleuthers”, NGOs, and professional journalists. Extending beyond formal news organisation boundaries, harnessing the power of crowd-sourcing and providing a “show your work” kind of transparency make open-source an important development for journalism. This chapter considers the underlying principles and opportunities that open-source presents and how it compares to allied fields like fact checking and to related skills of “data journalism”. We argue that as it grows in popularity, open-source has the potential to strengthen journalism to the extent that routinised practices develop, driven by institutional values of accountability and verification.
Keywords: OSINT; open-source investigations; journalism; crowd-sourcing; fact checking

title: Exploring the Advances of Artificial Intelligence in Cryptocurrencies and Darknet Forensics
authors: Ramy El-Kady
venue: Encyclopedia of Modern Artificial Intelligence
OSINT_Source_Types: Dark Web; Public Records; News Media
Tags: Blockchain Forensics; Dark Web Analysis; AI in Forensics; Cryptocurrency Investigations
abstract: This article explores the digital forensics of cryptocurrencies and the dark web, highlighting the role of blockchain, computers, and mobile phones in their formation and evidence gathering. It also discusses the use of artificial intelligence and machine language in dark web forensics. The article highlights the need for immediate research in digital cryptocurrency forensics, particularly in cryptocurrencies like Monero, Ethereum, Verge, and Dogecoin, and the gap in host-based cryptocurrency forensics. Cryptocurrency forensics mostly looks at public blockchains using clustering heuristics and machine learning-based analysis to find anonymous entities or help with investigations. The Elliptic Dataset, a significant resource, has been developed to study machine learning and graph-based methods in Bitcoin forensics based on blockchain technology, providing a wealth of information for researchers in the field. Blockchain-based forensics research is progressing organically alongside technological advancements, offering a promising future.
Keywords: Cryptocurrency Forensics; Darknet; Artificial Intelligence; Blockchain; Machine Learning
affiliations: National Police Academy; Dubai Police Academy

title: PERUN: Protecting Sensitive Cyber Ecosystems from Upcoming Next Generation and AI-generated Malware Threats [preprint]
authors: Marek Pawlicki; Aleksandra Pawlicka; Jörg Keller; Wojciech Mazurczyk; Rafał Kozik; Michał Choraś
venue: Communications in Computer and Information Science
Tags: cyber threats; critical infrastructure security; Horizon Europe; malware detection
abstract:
The increasing sophistication and frequency of cyberattacks pose significant risks to critical infrastructures, essential services, and digital ecosystems across the European Union. Addressing challenges such as polymorphic malware, encrypted malicious communications, and AI-generated attacks requires integrated, scalable, and trustworthy cybersecurity solutions. The PERUN (Protecting Sensitive Cyber Ecosystems from Upcoming Next Generation and AI-generated Malware Threats) project, funded within the Horizon Europe framework, develops advanced artificial intelligence-driven tools and methodologies for threat detection, vulnerability assessment, and incident response. The project focuses on enhancing the security and resilience of critical digital infrastructures while supporting European technological sovereignty and compliance with regulatory and ethical frameworks, by integrating innovative AI technologies and sector-specific protection strategies.

title: A Bibliometric Analysis on Cybersecurity in Human Resource Management
authors: Saranya Suriyamoorthy
venue: Empowering Emerging Economies through Innovation, Resilience, and Sustainability
Tags: cyber threats; HR management; research trends; data security
abstract: In the modern dynamic environment, human resources collect the information (personal identifiers, salary information, and employment history), process it, and store inconceivable volumes of data about their employees. They send this data over networks on a daily basis. This kind of data is targeted by cybercriminals, resulting in cybersecurity threats. This is a serious threat to the functionality and security of different networks and systems. Cyberthreats are increasing at an alarming rate and have gained traction in recent years. There has been literature available on cybersecurity and HR, yet the literature does not highlight any research trends. As a result, the study aims to assess previous research in the field of cybersecurity in the HR area and offer insights about important contributors, publication trends, and changing research avenues in this field. Data is gathered from the Scopus database between 2012 and 2024. The inclusive criteria include the publications on keywords like “cybersecurity” and “HR” with an emphasis only on the English language. Visualization is created with the use of Bibliometrix in R Studio. The results show the common trends and publication patterns in the field of cybersecurity and the HR area. Finally, the study offers some suggestions based on the key future directions found in the body of existing literature.
Keywords: cybersecurity; human resources; bibliometric analysis; data protection; publication trends

title: Quantum Attacks: Emerging Threats and Advanced Countermeasures in Cybersecurity
authors: Supreet Kaur Sahi; Vandana Kalra; Sahaj Khurana
venue: Progressive Computational Intelligence, Information Technology, and Networking
Tags: Quantum Attacks; Cyber Threats; Encryption Vulnerabilities; Security Protocols
abstract: With rapid improvement quantum computing classical cryptographic systems are facing significant risks. The rise of quantum computing imposes a shift in cryptographic strategies. In this paper quantum attacks are explored and their implications for cybersecurity are presented. This study highlights the vulnerabilities of RSA, ECC, and symmetric encryption against quantum attacks. Different post-quantum cryptography strategies are discussed in this paper. Real-world scenarios and potential implementations of quantum-resistant security protocols are also discussed in this paper. This paper highlights open challenges in scalability, cost, and adoption of quantum-safe encryption.
Keywords: Quantum Computing; Cybersecurity; Cryptographic Systems; Post-Quantum Cryptography; RSA; ECC

title: Medical Device Cybersecurity in the Era of <scp>AI</scp> and Machine Learning
authors: Rebecca M. Basta; Waqar Anwar
venue: Cybersecurity for Medical Devices
Tags: Cybersecurity; Healthcare; Artificial Intelligence; Vulnerability; Ethics; Regulations
abstract: This chapter examines the transformative integration of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) into medical devices and the unique cybersecurity challenges this creates. AI/ML capabilities—including diagnostic imaging analysis, predictive patient deterioration detection, and real-time insulin dosing optimization—are discussed alongside the technical complexities of model maintenance, drift mitigation through remote recalibration, and the opacity of black-box decision-making. Novel AI-driven attack vectors are analyzed in depth: data poisoning that corrupts training pipelines to skew clinical algorithms, model inversion and theft through crafted queries that extract sensitive patient data or proprietary logic, adversarial input generation that causes diagnostic misclassification through imperceptible perturbations, and algorithmic bias that produces systematically inequitable patient outcomes. Strategies for securing AI training and operational pipelines include data provenance tracking, anomaly detection in training datasets, encrypted model parameters, and human-in-the-loop oversight. Regulatory and ethical considerations address transparency requirements, informed consent for AI-driven care, and cross-border data compliance. Future-proofing practices combine adaptive defenses, threat intelligence integration, and automated security operations.
Keywords: AI; Machine Learning; Medical Device Cybersecurity; Data Poisoning; Model Inversion; Adversarial Attacks; Algorithmic Bias

title: Comparative Analysis of Game-Theoretic Intrusion Detection Models for Cybersecurity Using NSL-KDD, KDDCup99, and UNSW-NB15 Datasets
authors: Abhishek Prithvi Teja
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: cybersecurity; game-theoretic models; detection systems; reinforcement learning
abstract: Abstract Modern intrusion detection systems operate in adversarial environments where attackers continuously adapt their behavior to evade detection. Traditional machine learning approaches often treat intrusion detection as a static classification problem and fail to explicitly model strategic attacker-defender interactions.This work presents a comparative analysis of three game-theoretic intrusion detection frameworks: Evolutionary Game Theory IDS, Repeated Stackelberg Security Game with SHARP/SUQR and Q-Learning, and Naive/Hierarchical Q-Learning IDS. The proposed frameworks are evaluated using NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and KDDCup99 benchmark datasets. Results demonstrate that binary intrusion detection consistently outperforms multiclass classification while Stackelberg-SHARP/SUQR provides the most realistic attacker-defender modeling and Evolutionary Game Theory offers the highest interpretability. The study highlights the potential of game-theoretic reasoning and reinforcement learning for adaptive cybersecurity defense.
Keywords: intrusion detection; game theory; cybersecurity; machine learning; adaptive defense

title: From Ciphers to Future Cybersecurity: Engaging High School Students with Emerging Cryptographic Techniques through Hands-on Activities
authors: Mille Skovhus Lunding; Karl-Emil Kjær Bilstrup; Line Have Musaeus; Anna Hallenberg; Anne Kirstine Overgaard; Sophia Yakoubov; Marianne Graves Petersen
venue: Proceedings of the 25th Annual ACM Interaction Design and Children Conference
Tags: Education; Emerging Technologies; Child-Computer Interaction; K-12
abstract: Emerging cryptographic techniques have the potential to transform foundational societal infrastructures, creating a need to teach their possibilities and limitations to support children’s and youths’ agency in this transformation. With this aim, we first surveyed cryptography experts (n=10) about which cryptographic techniques high school students should be taught. Next, we explored how one of the identified techniques, multi-party computation (MPC), can be taught in high school through a co-design process with five teachers. This process led to the design of four hands-on activities, which were evaluated with 96 high school students. Our findings demonstrate how high-school students can engage with an emerging cryptographic technique through hands-on activities that strategically black-box mathematics. We outline future research directions for teaching emerging cryptographic techniques in K-12 education and discuss how child-computer interaction can support children and youth in exploring future opportunities of cybersecurity.
Keywords: Cryptography; Cybersecurity; High School Education; Hands-on Activities; Multi-Party Computation

title: Cultivating Computational Empowerment in K-9 Education through Critical Hope and Transformative Agency
authors: Ane Vielandt Jensen
venue: Proceedings of the 25th Annual ACM Interaction Design and Children Conference
Tags: K-9 Education; Child-Computer Interaction; Cybersecurity; Theoretical Frameworks
abstract: This PhD project explores how K-9 students’ Computational Empowerment (CE) can be cultivated through the lenses of critical hope (CH) and transformative agency (TA). The project is theoretically grounded in Pedagogy of Hope and Cultural‑Historical Activity Theory (CHAT) and empirically conducted through Participatory Design (PD) activities with K-9 students and teachers within K-9 cybersecurity education. It extends existing Child-Computer Interaction (CCI) research by contributing: 1. Insights into cybersecurity matters relevant to K-9 students and the implications for strengthening their CE through TA, 2. An age‑appropriate cybersecurity vocabulary aimed at K-9 students’ CE, 3. Empirically grounded design principles for integrating CH into PD activities aimed at CE, and 4. Theoretical underpinnings for cultivating K-9 students’ CE through CH and TA.
Keywords: Computational Empowerment; Cybersecurity Education; Participatory Design; Critical Hope; Transformative Agency

title: Advanced Techniques and Innovations in Deepfake Detection: A Comprehensive Research Perspective
authors: Priya Sharma; Diya Ahuja; Shobha Tyagi; Neha Tyagi
venue: Progressive Computational Intelligence, Information Technology, and Networking
Tags: Deepfakes; AI; Detection Techniques; Multi-modal Synchronization; Cyber Fraud
abstract: Recent advances in generative models such as GANs and autoencoders have enabled the creation of synthetic media, raising concerns for digital trust and its implications across journalism, politics and cybersecurity. Such manipulations undermine conventional verification methods and raise serious concerns for politics, journalism and cybersecurity. The increasing realism and sophistication of synthetic audio and video highlight the need for detection techniques that are robust, scalable and adaptable. This paper provides an exhaustive study of modern innovations in deepfake detection, including self-supervised learning, hybrid CNN-transformer models, adaptive patch-based attention, biometric signal analysis and multi-modal synchronization techniques. Authors explored each methodology&s;s theoretical foundation, architectural design, real-world implementation, advantages and limitations. This review concludes by proposing future research directions that combine deep learning, signal processing, cryptographic techniques and ethical frameworks to combat synthetic media fraud effectively.
Keywords: Deepfake Detection; Synthetic Media; Generative Models; Cybersecurity; Digital Trust

title: Fuzzy AI-Driven Intelligent Agents for Intrusion Detection in Wireless Sensor Networks
authors: A Firos; Seema Khanum
venue: Modern Wireless Communication Systems and Networks
Tags: AI; Cyber Threats; Security; Detection Systems; WSN
abstract: Today, wireless sensor networks (WSNs) have a prominent place in cybersecurity and support numerous applications, from environmental monitoring to national defense. Nevertheless, as far as the inherent vulnerability of WSNs to unauthorized intrusion is concerned, this may be a serious risk that must be managed with proper security. In this regard, the chapter presents a new idea of using fuzzy artificial intelligence (AI) to make intelligent agents in tracing intrusions in WSNs. In this chapter, Fuzzy AI is an ideal model to accurately and reliably uncover latent security vulnerabilities. Extensive attack situations are studied using the WSN-DS dataset as well. This system uses a fuzzy logic-based approach to analyze the information gathered by sensor nodes, allowing the intelligent agent to identify both normal and intrusive behaviors at fine-grained levels. The system applies fuzzy AI to manage the uncertainty and imprecision that frequently accompany sensor data, resulting in a large increase in detection performance. This decision action is refined through continual learning and improvement by the intelligent agent to ensure that it adapts dynamically according to new types of intrusion tactics, creating a more effective response. Experimental results are reported from an extensive testing of the WSN-DS dataset to explain that the fuzzy AI-based intrusion detection methodology performs significantly better than traditional intrusion detection systems (IDS). By utilizing the proposed method, an increased detection rate will be achieved with fewer false positives; this translates to a more effective cybersecurity landscape for WSNs while maintaining operational efficiency. This research contributes to cybersecurity, providing scalable and efficient solutions to protect WSN from sophisticated intrusions. This paves the way for a safer and more robust WSN. Through the integration of fuzzy AI, this study highlights the potential of intelligent agents to improve WSN’s security mechanisms and makes important advances in combating cyber threats in an increasingly connected world.
Keywords: Wireless Sensor Networks; Fuzzy AI; Intrusion Detection; Cybersecurity; Intelligent Agents

title: Implementing SDG 16 Goals with Artificial Intelligence
venue: Wiley
Tags: AI; Governance; Sustainable Development; Global Challenges; Institutional Strengthening
abstract: Discover how AI-powered solutions can transform global governance and legal systems with this essential guide to leveraging emerging technologies for peace, justice, and stronger institutional frameworks. In a world rife with challenges like corruption, cybercrime, legal inefficiencies, human rights violations, and weak institutional frameworks, AI-powered solutions present an unprecedented opportunity to improve transparency, legal systems, and security altogether. This book explores the role of artificial intelligence as a transformative agent of peace, justice, and effective institutions. Drawing on literature from international relations, conflict studies, political science and machine learning, this book considers relationships between artificial intelligence and Sustainable Development Goal 16, focusing on how emerging technologies can support governance, law enforcement, conflict resolution, and democratic practice. Positioning itself between technological innovation and policy, this book provides actionable perspectives to leverage AI responsibly in building stronger institutions and crafting a just, peaceful society. Readers will find the volume: Draws from academics, policymakers, AI researchers, and legal experts to present cutting-edge research, case studies, and policy recommendations on the applications of AI for governance; Explores in detail how artificial intelligence can be used to fight misinformation, improve electoral integrity, and cope with global security threats; Structured with thematic sections that provide a multi-disciplinary view of the effects of AI on peace, justice, and the resilience of institutions. Audience Government officials, international organizations, technology developers, legal practitioners, and scholars dealing with AI holistically for sustainable governance.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Sustainable Development Goals; Governance; Legal Systems; Transparency; Cybercrime; Peace; Justice

title: Event intelligence
authors: Michael McDonagh; Charles Swanson
venue: Event Security and Leadership
OSINT_Source_Types: Social Media; Public Records; News Media
Tags: global events; digital resilience; cyber intrusions; public trust; perception warfare
abstract: In the arena of global event management, operational success is no longer defined solely by physical infrastructure or crowd control; it now hinges on strategic dominance within an increasingly complex and contested digital environment. This chapter will look at the critical vulnerabilities of major international events to a spectrum of digital threats, ranging from opportunistic cyber intrusions to coordinated, state-sponsored attacks and weaponised misinformation campaigns. As high-profile events become prime targets for malign actors, the digital battlefield emerges as a frontline of risk with profound implications for safety, reputation, and continuity. The chapter interrogates the inherent fragilities within the digital ecosystems that support modern events, including ticketing systems, communication platforms, security networks and live broadcast feeds, and unpacks the growing sophistication of adversaries seeking to exploit them. It further examines the erosion of public trust through the deliberate spread of disinformation, highlighting how perception warfare can be as disruptive as technical compromise. In response, this chapter advocates for the integration of advanced multi-provider open-source intelligence (OSINT) capabilities and the implementation of robust, adaptive digital resilience strategies. By outlining proactive, intelligence-led approaches to risk mitigation, from threat detection and incident response to public assurance and post-event analysis, it argues that mastery of the digital domain is now a strategic imperative. Safeguarding the integrity, security and reputational capital of global events demands a paradigm shift: one that treats cyberspace not as an auxiliary concern but as a decisive theatre of operation.
Keywords: event management; digital threats; cybersecurity; disinformation; intelligence-led risk mitigation

title: Compatibility Between Marxist and Islamic Economic Thought
authors: Yasushi Suzuki
venue: Toward a ‘Constitutional’ Socialist State
Tags: economic thought; exploitation; capital allocation; ICT; S-Money
abstract: Abstract The chapter observes that the Abrahamic religions prohibit interest primarily because it is seen as a source of exploitation and injustice. Marx shared this concern, arguing that interest lacks any objective economic basis and is instead determined by bargaining power, allowing systematic exploitation under capitalism. However, even a socialist economy requires mechanisms to mobilize idle funds for productive investment, and Marx did not fully address how socialism could manage investment risks and uncertainties. This raises an open question: whether advances in information and communications technology (ICT) and artificial intelligence might enable new monetary forms – such as labour money or Socialist Money (S-Money) – that mitigate exploitation while facilitating efficient capital allocation.
Keywords: Marxist economics; Islamic economic thought; interest prohibition; capitalism; socialism; information technology; artificial intelligence

title: Analysis of Cybersecurity Threats and Security Modeling Approaches
authors: Kirandeep Kaur
venue: Sustainable Developments in Computer Engineering, Green Technology and Smart Systems
Tags: cyber threats; security modeling; IT security; risk assessment
abstract: A model of computer security refers to a plan of defining and implementing security policies. A security model can be based on a formal model of access rights, a computational model, a distributed computing model, or none whatsoever. Threat modelling consists of the process of identifying and sharing data on possible risks to a certain system or network. Security threat modelling will allow an IT team to understand threats and their possible impacts on the network. There are many models and approaches, which have been put forward to manage the cyber security issue. This study will look at these models, their deficiencies, and past strategies in minimizing such risks. Also, the paper provides recommendations on further research.
Keywords: cybersecurity; threat modeling; security policies; risk management

title: Verification and Validation of Performance with Dissemination of Best Practices in District Energy and CHP for Enhanced Resiliency, Energy Efficiency, and Cybersecurity
venue: Office of Scientific and Technical Information (OSTI)
Tags: energy efficiency; cyber threats; system reliability; decarbonization
abstract: This report contains the results of the International District Energy Association’s work to analyze, validate, and verify performance data of existing district energy systems and identify industy best practices for the purpose of improving system reliability, resiliency, and efficiency, and to accellerate decarbonization. In addition to a technical evaluation of the surveyed systems and identification of a series of technical performance metrics, the report illustrates the accompanying operations and financial best practices employed by surveyed systems to fully serve their customer base. Additionally, the third chapter of the report describes the current landscape of cybersecurity threats and counteracting measures, and recommends a series of steps for effectively guarding highly networked district energy systems against cybersecurity attacks.
Keywords: district energy systems; cybersecurity; performance validation; best practices; resiliency

title: Bridging Knowledge and Behavior: A Mixed-Methods Study of Adolescent Cybersecurity Literacy and Its Implications for Child Protection in Jordan
authors: Mohammed Ghallab; Sahar AlMakhamreh
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: cybersecurity; education; qualitative research; quantitative research; ecological systems theory; social construction theory
abstract: Abstract The rapid digitalization of adolescents' lives has introduced unprecedented child protection challenges, yet limited research has examined cybersecurity literacy among adolescents in the Global South. This explanatory sequential mixed-methods study investigated the extent of cybersecurity literacy among Jordanian adolescents aged 14 to 17, the digital threats they encounter, and potential social work intervention models. In the quantitative phase, 625 adolescents completed a validated electronic questionnaire measuring cybersecurity knowledge and behavior. In the qualitative phase, focus group discussions and semi-structured interviews were conducted with 20 participants, including students, parents, teachers, and school counselors. Quantitative findings revealed a moderate overall level of cybersecurity literacy (M = 3.63, SD = 0.726), characterized by a significant knowledge-behavior gap: knowledge was high (M = 3.79) while behavior remained moderate (M = 3.49). The most prevalent digital threats were hacking attempts (28.1%), harmful content (23.5%), and cyberbullying (16.7%). Notably, 39.4% of adolescents had received no cybersecurity training, and only 1.3% reported threats to their schools. Regression analysis identified training as the strongest predictor of both literacy and threat reporting. Qualitative findings illuminated barriers including shame culture, fear of parental punishment, and a lack of practical skills. Grounded in Bronfenbrenner's Ecological Systems Theory and Social Construction Theory, the study proposes a storytelling-based intervention model for enhancing online resilience, offering actionable implications for child protection practice and policy.
Keywords: cybersecurity literacy; adolescents; child protection; Jordan; digital threats; social work intervention

title: Selecting Optimal Cybersecurity Measures for Power Systems Using Complex Intuitionistic Fuzzy Rough Frank Aggregation Operators
authors: Ahmad Idrees; Meraj Ali Khan; Ibrahim Al-Dayel; Tahir Mahmood
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Decision Making; Cyberattacks; Reliability; Stability
abstract: Abstract In modern power systems, reliability, stability, and cybersecurity (CS) robustness against cyberattacks are of utmost importance due to the growing reliance on digital technologies. In order to reduce cyberattacks, a comprehensive CS evaluation approach for power systems is required. However, the selection of most optimal CS solution requires handling the uncertainty and imprecision in data. For this, we introduced a multi-criteria decision-making (MCDM) model in the framework of complex intuitionistic fuzzy rough sets (CIFRSs). CIFRSs are very useful for addressing decision-making situations in which experts must overcome both complexity and roughness to make a conclusion. To cope the MCDM approach, we developed the Frank operational laws based on CIFRS. Additionally, we introduced aggregation theory named complex intuitionistic fuzzy rough (CIFR) frank weighted average and geometric aggregation operators (AOs) which are employed in the constructed technique of MCDM. After that, a case study is conducted to demonstrate the applicability of the proposed approach in “selecting optimal CS measures for power systems”. The results highlight the robustness of CIFR Frank AOs in managing complex decision-making scenarios. At the end, a comparative analysis is conducted with the existing methods that validates the effectiveness and reliability of the proposed approach. MSC 2020 Classification: 03E72, 94D05.
Keywords: Cybersecurity; Power Systems; Multiple Criteria Decision-Making; Fuzzy Sets; Aggregation Operators
affiliations: International Islamic University, Islamabad; Islamic University

title: AMLID: An Adaptive Multi-Layered Deep Learning Framework for Intelligent Intrusion Detection
authors: Rohan Chaudhary; Nityadeep Sharma; Gautam Tyagi
venue: Sustainable Developments in Computer Engineering, Green Technology and Smart Systems
Tags: Cybersecurity; Machine Learning; Real-time Detection; Scalability
abstract: The increase in cybersecurity threats has led to the emergence of adaptive intrusion detection systems that can learn with the changing characteristics of attack. This paper proposes an Adaptive Multi-Layered Intrusion Detection (AMLID) framework that combines the most advanced deep learning model containing Convolutional Neural Networks (CNNs), long short-term memory (LSTM) networks, attention mechanisms, and ensemble learning. The uniquely hybrid technology of AMLID combines adaptive feature weighting, multi-scale temporal modeling, and hierarchical decision, which allow for real-time and robust detection capabilities. The AMLID framework has achieved an overall accuracy of 98.92%, a precision of 98.25%, and an F1-score of 95.96% on CICIDS2017, CSIC2010, NSL-KDD, UNSW-NB15, and Sysmon logs. This shows AMLID is effective and has elevated, adaptability and scalability against evolving vectors of attack.
Keywords: Intrusion Detection; Deep Learning; CNN; LSTM; Adaptive Systems

title: AI-Driven Digital Forensics for Police Investigations
authors: Kiranbhai R. Dodiya; Bhagirath Gohil
venue: Enhancing Evidence Preservation With Blockchain
Tags: Artificial Intelligence; Cyber Investigations; Evidence Triage; Fraud Detection; Synthetic Media Authentication
abstract: This chapter examines the role of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in enhancing digital forensic investigations for cybercrime detection and response in modern India. Rapid digitalisation has increased the scale and sophistication of cyber offences, challenging conventional investigative methods. This chapter per the authors explores how AI technologies—including machine learning, natural language processing, computer vision, and predictive analytics—support intelligent evidence triage, behavioural analysis, fraud detection, and synthetic media authentication. It also addresses implementation challenges such as skill gaps, infrastructure limitations, legal admissibility, and algorithmic bias. The chapter highlights the need for governance frameworks, explainable AI, and capacity building to ensure responsible adoption. AI-driven digital forensics is presented as a strategic pathway toward more efficient, scalable, and intelligence-led cybercrime investigations in India.
Keywords: AI; Digital Forensics; Cybercrime; India; Machine Learning; Natural Language Processing

title: Regulatory and Admissibility Challenges
authors: Pradip Kumar Kashyap; Nirbhay Kumar Sharma
venue: Enhancing Evidence Preservation With Blockchain
Tags: blockchain technology; legal issues; evidentiary rules; cybercrime prosecution
abstract: The chapter critically analyzes regulatory and admissibility issues arising from the use of blockchain evidentiary in court. However, as blockchain is increasingly being adopted in the field of digital forensics and criminal investigation, law enforcement and judicial authorities around the globe are encountering considerable challenges in assessing blockchain technology's reliability, authenticity and compliance with current evidentiary rules and procedures. The chapter discusses how the nature of digital evidence has changed over time, the new legal issues that blockchain immutability and decentralized structure creates, and its significant impact on cybercrime prosecutions. It covers a range of admissibility considerations, regulatory deficiencies, authentication issues, privacy concerns and precedent. The main objective of this study is to fill the gap between technological innovation and judicial acceptance, so evidence collected via blockchain can be withstand in strict court procedures, and enhance the global combat against cybercrime.
Keywords: blockchain; evidence; digital forensics; admissibility; regulatory challenges; cybercrime
affiliations: Rayat Bahra University; Mohammad Ali Jauhar University

title: Cross-Border Evidence Sharing
authors: Pooja; Saurabh Chandra
venue: Enhancing Evidence Preservation With Blockchain
Tags: Evidence Sharing; Cybercrime; Blockchain; Legal Processes; International Law
abstract: Cybercrime has gone global, making the exchange of evidence a critical component in the fight against it in criminal investigations. Typical processes like Mutual Legal Assistance Treaties (MLATs) are time-consuming, cumbersome and frequently insufficient for time sensitive digital evidence. In this chapter, the author illustrates how blockchain technology could help transform the way the world enters into international collaboration by answering some of the key questions, including how can blockchain technology enable the secure and immutable exchange of evidence in international legal processes and execute it without compromising the principles of national sovereignty. The use of blockchain can provide a plausible chain of custody, interestingly, requests and requests can be automated using smart contracts, and privacy preserving architectures are also possible, establishing trust between countries.
Keywords: Cross-Border Evidence; Cybercrime; Blockchain Technology; International Collaboration; Digital Evidence; Chain of Custody; Smart Contracts

title: Criminal Investigations With Blockchain Technology
authors: Divya S. Khurana; Bhrigu Raj Mourya; Om Prakash Kannaujia
venue: Enhancing Evidence Preservation With Blockchain
Tags: Blockchain Technology; Criminal Investigations; Immutability; Privacy-Preserving Methods; Legal Compliance
abstract: The chapter investigates how blockchain technology can be implemented to solve some major challenges in criminal investigation, particularly with respect to identifying some of the serious vulnerabilities found in a digital forensics investigation and the evidence handling procedure of cybercrime. Volatile, easily tampered nature of traditional digital evidence often means that traditional digital evidence is susceptible to tampering, is difficult to formulate, and may not be admissible in court without problems with the chain of custody. The key characteristics of blockchain immutability, decentralization, cryptographic hashing, and audit trails provide a secure and efficient way to capture physical evidence at time of collection to when it enters the courtroom. It focuses on that the multi-agency partnership as well as privacy-preserving methods and case studies should be examined, together with technical architectures and legal compliance, including admissibility criteria.
Keywords: Blockchain; Digital Forensics; Cybercrime; Evidence Handling; Chain of Custody
affiliations: Rayat Bahra University; Mahaveer Academy of Technology and Science University

title: Ingress phase
authors: Michael McDonagh; Charles Swanson
venue: Event Security and Leadership
Tags: Event Security; Safety Planning; Technological Solutions; Crowd Behavior; Risk Management
abstract: The ingress phase of any global event encompasses the journey from attendee arrival to venue entry, and I believe it is far more than a security process; it is a critical determinant of an event‘s safety, operational efficiency and enduring reputation. In support of the other chapters, I want to explore the multifaceted strategic considerations essential for mastering ingress, defining it as an introductory element that helps shape the attendee experience from the ‘ formal’ outset. We now need consider the core components of effective ingress management, including meticulous strategic planning and dynamic capacity calculation, advanced crowd and queue management techniques and comprehensive security and access control measures. The indispensable human element, encompassing staffing awareness, training and proactive communication, is highlighted as crucial for influencing crowd behaviour and ensuring compliance. Furthermore, this chapter examines the transformative role of technology, from seamless digital ticketing and biometric authentication to AI-powered crowd analytics, real-time surveillance, hostile vehicle mitigation (HVM) and counter-drone solutions, all of which are revolutionising ingress security and efficiency. Drawing lessons from failures such as Astroworld, Love Parade and Hillsborough, the chapter underscores the severe consequences of planning deficiencies, operational breakdowns and systemic vulnerabilities, emphasising the critical need for resilient planning and an organisational culture prioritising safety. Finally, it addresses emerging threats, including cybersecurity risks to digital systems and the impact of disinformation and social media on crowd psychology, alongside persistent staffing challenges.
Keywords: Ingress Management; Event Safety; Operational Efficiency; Crowd Management; Security Measures; Digital Ticketing; Biometric Authentication; AI Analytics; Cybersecurity Risks; Disinformation

title: Ransomware and artificial intelligence: a comprehensive systematic review of reviews
authors: Therdpong Daengsi; Phisit Pornpongtechavanich; Paradorn Boonpoor; Kathawut Wattanachukul; Korn Puangnak; Kritphon Phanrattanachai; Pongpisit Wuttidittachotti; Paramate Horkaew
venue: Bulletin of Electrical Engineering and Informatics
Tags: Ransomware Defense; AI in Security; Systematic Review; Cyber Threats; Hybrid Models
abstract: This study provides a comprehensive synthesis of artificial intelligence (AI), especially machine learning (ML) and deep learning (DL) in ransomware defense. Using a “review of reviews” methodology based on the PRISMA, this paper gathers insights on how AI is transforming ransomware detection, prevention, and mitigation strategies in the past five years (2020-2024). The findings highlight the effectiveness of hybrid models, which combine multiple analysis techniques such as code inspection (static analysis) and behavior monitoring during execution (dynamic analysis). The study also explores anomaly detection and early warning mechanisms before encryption that tackle ransomware’s growing complexity. It also examines key challenges in ransomware defense, such as techniques designed to deceive AI driven detection, and the lack of strong and diverse datasets. It highlights AI’s role in early detection and real-time response systems, enhancing scalability and resilience. With the systematic review of reviews approach, the contributions of this study are systematically consolidating research insights from multiple review articles, identifying effective AI models, and bridging theory with practice to foster collaboration among academia, industry, and policymakers. Future research directions are anticipated and practical recommendations for cybersecurity practitioners are provided. Finally, it presents a roadmap for advancing AI-driven countermeasures, for the protection of key systems and infrastructures against evolving ransomware threats.
Keywords: Ransomware; Artificial Intelligence; Machine Learning; Deep Learning; Cybersecurity; Anomaly Detection; Threat Mitigation

title: Synthetic Hate
authors: Lev Topor
venue: Routledge
Tags: Hate Speech; AI; Extremism; Moderation Challenges; Political Disinformation
abstract: Synthetic Hate investigates how extremists exploit artificial intelligence (AI) to modernize the world’s oldest hatred. Antisemitism – rooted in religious discrimination, medieval blood libels, Nazi propaganda, and contemporary Islamist and far-right conspiracies – has found new life through generative tools that can produce persuasive text, images, audio, and video at scale. Drawing on documented cases and controlled demonstrations, the book shows how large language models (LLMs), deepfakes, bots, and recommendation systems enable cheap, rapid, and adaptive propaganda – memes that evade moderation, fabricated “evidence,” synthetic voices, and narrative laundering that spreads across platforms and into mainstream feeds. The result is not “new” hate, but hate that is faster, more convincing, and harder to police. Crucially, Synthetic Hate goes beyond diagnosis, and it lays out a practical counterstrategy of technical safeguards, platform accountability and regulation, and education and resilience, so policymakers, researchers, and practitioners can blunt AI-amplified antisemitism and hate without sacrificing democratic values.
Keywords: Artificial Intelligence; Antisemitism; Disinformation; Generative Tools; Propaganda

title: Quantum Autoencoders for Anomaly Detection in Cybersecurity
authors: Rohan Senthil; Swee Liang Wong
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Quantum Computing; Cyber Threat Detection; Autoencoders; Data Analysis
abstract: Abstract Anomaly detection in cybersecurity is a challenging task, where normal events far outnumber anomalous ones with new anomalies occurring frequently. Classical autoencoders have been used for anomaly detection, but struggles in data-limited settings which quantum counterparts can potentially overcome. In this work, we apply Quantum Autoencoders (QAEs) for anomaly detection in cybersecurity, specifically on the BPF-extended tracking honeypot (BETH) dataset. QAEs are evaluated across multiple encoding techniques, ansatz types, repetitions, and feature selection strategies. Our results demonstrate that an 8-feature QAE using Dense-Angle encoding with a RealAmplitude ansatz can outperform Classical Autoencoders (CAEs), even when trained on substantially fewer samples. The effects of quantum encoding and feature selection for developing quantum models are demonstrated and discussed. In a data-limited setting, the best performing QAE model has a F1 score of 0.87, better than that of CAE (0.77). These findings suggest that QAEs may offer practical advantages for anomaly detection in data-limited scenarios.
Keywords: Anomaly Detection; Quantum Autoencoders; Cybersecurity; Machine Learning

title: Signal Quality and the Silence Trap in Collaborative Cybersecurity Governance
authors: Jiguang Wang; Yi Ren
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: cybersecurity governance; evolutionary game theory; crowdsourced regulation; vulnerability detection
abstract: Abstract Collaborative cybersecurity governance relies on “societal sensors” to detect vulnerabilities, yet regulators must filter noisy reports under pronounced information asymmetry. Existing evolutionary game models typically adopt a “perfect monitoring” assumption, obscuring the structural conditions under which incentives remain effective. By incorporating a signal-verification perspective into a tripartite evolutionary framework, this study endogenizes verification precision and false-report penalties as determinants of system stability. The model identifies a critical signal-quality threshold below which the system enters a “Silence Trap”: user participation becomes weakly responsive to incentives, and higher monetary rewards alone fail to restore collaboration. We also identify a “Deterrence Paradox,” whereby harsher penalties for unsubstantiated reporting can suppress valid signals unless paired with sufficiently strong verification infrastructure. These findings shift attention from reward tuning to capacity-first governance, highlighting that the sustainability of crowdsourced regulation is conditional on verification precision as a foundational complement to monetary incentives.
Keywords: collaborative cybersecurity; societal sensors; information asymmetry; signal quality; verification precision; deterrence paradox
affiliations: Shanxi University of Traditional Chinese Medicine

title: International and Local Legal Frameworks for Cybersecurity and Regulatory Advances and Gaps
authors: Ricardo A. Barrera-Cámara; David H. Fuque-Ehuan; Alejandro Fuentes-Penna; Fernando E. Sánchez-Martinez
venue: Secure Digital Infrastructure and Cyber Resilience in Smart Government Systems
Tags: Legal Frameworks; Cyber Resilience; Sustainable Development; Digital Technologies
abstract: The increase of digital threats and the uneven development of regulations in distinct parts of the world generate significant challenges in data management, the creation of standards for new technologies, and the protection of infrastructure. These differences affect global goals linked to sustainable development objectives, as well as addressing issues related to the safe and responsible use of digital technologies. The study employs qualitative documentary research to analyze laws, regulations, frameworks, and technical standards. The results of the analysis show advances in technological security regulations, as well as the existence of areas that need greater attention to meet the challenges that new technologies demand. Congruent, flexible, and ethical regulatory frameworks are required to strengthen cyber resilience and global sustainability.
Keywords: Cybersecurity; Regulatory Frameworks; Data Management; Digital Threats; Technological Standards
affiliations: Universidad Autónoma del Carmen; El Colegio de Morelos

title: Cybersecurity Risk Assessment of Smart Home IoT Ecosystems in the MENA Region
authors: Hameed Almubark; Hamed Al-Raweshidy; Jenan Moosa Hasan; Ahmed Jedidi
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Cybersecurity; IoT; User Awareness; Risk Management
abstract: Abstract The Internet of Things (IoT) is increasingly embedded in smart homes, industrial systems and healthcare environments, creating new requirements for low latency, bandwidth efficiency and robust security. However, many IoT devices remain difficult to secure because of limited processing capability, storage capacity, energy resources and fragmented communication protocols. This study investigates security and privacy concerns associated with IoT adoption in smart-home and related environments, with a particular focus on users in the MENA region. An online questionnaire was distributed to Arabic-speaking participants, resulting in 164 valid responses from 12 countries. The results show that users are highly concerned about privacy invasion, data theft, device hacking and unauthorized access, while their protection practices remain inconsistent. More than half of the respondents reported a need for additional support to secure existing IoT devices rather than replacing them. The findings also show that commonly used protection mechanisms include strong passwords, two-factor authentication, firmware updates, antivirus software, firewalls and VPNs, although users still require clearer guidance, checklists and professional support. Based on the survey results and related literature, the paper discusses practical recommendations for strengthening IoT security through user awareness, network protection, device-level controls, edge computing and blockchain-enabled approaches.
Keywords: IoT Security; Smart Home; Risk Assessment; Privacy Concerns; MENA Region
affiliations: Brunel University of London; Ahlia University; Applied Science University

title: Enhancing Cybersecurity in Cloud Computing Environments through Zero Trust Architecture: A Multi-Layer Adaptive Framework with Simulation-Based Evaluation of Attack-Surface Reduction
authors: mohsin bashir hakak
venue: Springer Science and Business Media LLC
Tags: Cybersecurity; Cloud Computing; Security Framework; Risk Management; Network Security
abstract: Abstract The migration of critical workloads and sensitive data into cloud computing environments has dissolved the traditional network perimeter and invalidated the implicit-trust assumptions of conventional security architectures. Zero Trust Architecture (ZTA), formalised in National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) Special Publication 800-207, instead evaluates every request against contextual signals before authorisation. This paper proposes a multi-layer adaptive Zero Trust framework spanning identity, device, network, application/workload and data, unified by a continuously computed trust score whose weights are derived by the Analytic Hierarchy Process.
